title: A rare family of barn owls moved into Manhattan. New Yorkers are captivated
summary: Manhattan’s Upper West Side has been reveling in the company of its latest celebrities: A family of barn owls nested in a water tower atop a building near Central Park
story: NEW YORK -- Manhattan's Upper West Side has been reveling in the company of its latest celebrities: A family of barn owls nested in a water tower atop a building near Central Park.

This is the first documented instance of barn owls nesting in Manhattan in modern history, according to one expert, and the owls have attracted nightly crowds of people in the street eager to get a glimpse of the elusive birds.

“It was, like, totally shocking,” Andrew Farnsworth, a migration ecologist at the Cornell Lab of Ornithology, said of the barn owls. “To the best of our knowledge, like the collective birding knowledge, there hasn’t been a nest in, you know, in Manhattan, at least in recorded history.”

Word of the barn owl family didn't get around until last week, when Elisabeth Williams, an Upper West Side resident, notified a local news outlet on Oct. 6 that she and her husband saw multiple owls at the water tower atop a building on West 75th Street close to Central Park West.
The couple had previously seen a single owl on an apartment windowsill a few days earlier and were shocked even then, Williams recalled.
“In a place like Manhattan, you normally really have to go out of your way to encounter nature,” she said. “And here it was, just sort of right outside our window.”

It's not the first time that birds have captivated New Yorkers. Residents have fallen in love with American woodcocks, who are known to stop in Midtown Manhattan’s Bryant Park every year as they migrate north in early spring. After Flaco the Eurasian eagle-owl died in 2024, dozens of mournful fans gathered to say goodbye to the beloved creature who flew around Manhattan and became a joy to many after someone let him out of his zoo enclosure the previous year. Then there was Pale Male, a red-tailed hawk who nested above Fifth Avenue for three decades before dying in 2023.

But barn owl sightings in New York City parks are very rare, according to the New York City Department of Parks & Recreation. New York is at the northern fringe of the barn owl's range and the barn owl population has declined “at an alarming rate” over time, according to the state Department of Environmental Conservation.

“There’s lots of excitement among New Yorkers, both birders and non-birders alike, about these owls because owls really capture the attention,” said Jessica Wilson, executive director of NYC Bird Alliance. “They’re magical, they’re nocturnal, they are secretive, they’re not commonly seen, especially on the Upper West Side of Manhattan. And to have this chance to see these birds is really thrilling.”
Photographers and casual onlookers have gathered on the street on a nightly basis to spot the owls.

“I’ve only seen one barn owl ever, and that was in California,” said Val Coleman, a retired New York City resident who was on the Upper West Side earlier this week trying to spot the owls. “At dusk, we hope they will come out to hunt. We hope they don’t eat poisoned rats with rodenticide in ’em.”

David Barrett, a Manhattan-based birder who runs the popular social media account, Manhattan Bird Alert, said he’s observed at least one adult barn owl and five fledglings at the water tower. He’s also seen an adult owl carrying rodents back to the water tower. There are believed to be two adult owls, and some photographers have claimed to have seen six fledglings, Barrett added.
“Having one barn owl is a rarity, but it’s not national news. Having a family, for the first time ever, breeding in Manhattan in recorded history, that’s special news,” Barrett said.

Before the recent barn owl sightings, Williams and her husband heard periodic screeching noises outside going back to early September. They initially assumed it was a bird of some kind but were skeptical when a phone app indicated the noise was from a barn owl.
Thomas Obersteiner said that he first heard bizarre screeching and wailing noises from outside one evening in mid-September. It sounded like someone was “being murdered outside,” he said.
“That lasted for two or three weeks, every night, sometimes more, sometimes less, coming from different directions,” Obersteiner added. “But I had no idea what that was.”

On multiple occasions, Obersteiner or his wife ran into their children's bedroom after mistaking the owls' screech for a child in pain, he said. It wasn't until he saw a news report that he realized that owls were making the sounds.
Farnsworth said the screech is typical of barn owls, who use it to communicate with one another. The screech is like a “horror movie kind of experience,” he said.

Obersteiner, who said his roof deck is “probably the best location in town right now” to watch the owls, has been letting nature photographers access that perch to observe the owls “almost every night” since news of the barn owls spread. On one night last week, 20 people had gathered.
“We can’t say no because it’s so much fun and these people are so serious,” Obersteiner added. “It's beautiful.”
Williams and her husband were not bird watchers before the barn owl family moved in to the water tower. But that may change soon after their “delightful” experience.
“I think we’re about to become birders,” Williams said.
Kelety reported from Phoenix.

title: Employee arrested after listening device found in OpenAI conference room, FBI and the company say
summary: An engineer at OpenAI has been charged with secretly installing a recording device inside a conference room in what officials say was an effort to capture sensitive conversations about the company’s technology
story: An engineer at OpenAI has been charged with secretly installing a recording device inside a conference room in what officials say was an effort to capture sensitive conversations about the company’s technology

WASHINGTON -- An engineer at OpenAI has been charged with secretly installing a recording device inside a conference room in what officials said Tuesday was an effort to capture sensitive conversations about the company's technology.

The employee, identified as a 35-year-old Saudi national named Abdulrahman Alfozan, was arrested Friday, a week after the ChatGPT maker discovered an audio recording device hidden in the conference room, according to a criminal complaint filed in federal court in San Francisco.

The complaint did not identify the company, but the company confirmed in a separate statement that it had discovered a “sophisticated recording device that was hidden inside one of our offices," reported the finding to the FBI and fired the employee.

“We used our models to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier. We referred the matter to the FBI, and we’re grateful to the agents and prosecutors who moved quickly to make an arrest. The FBI’s investigation is ongoing and we will continue to support their work,” an OpenAI spokesperson said.
“At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data. The employee was terminated,” the statement said.
The complaint does not detail what Alfozan might have wanted to do with any captured communications.

Alfozan made his first court appearance Tuesday on a charge of using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. It was not immediately clear if he had a lawyer who could speak on his behalf.
The recording device was found September 30 concealed in toilet paper and inserted into a USB port on the back of a television in the conference room, according to the complaint.

Though the conference room where the recording device was found did not have a camera at the time it was installed, closed-circuit television footage inside the company's offices revealed that Alfozan was near the conference room on a half-dozen occasions last month despite not having any authority to access the space, the complaint says.
The company subsequently added a camera to the room that last week captured Alfozan entering and checking behind the television where the recording device was installed, according to the FBI.
The complaint also he also used a productivity tool to make multiple inquiries about the company's building addresses, meeting rooms, meeting-room capacities and calendars.
Before his arrest last week, the complaint says, Alfozan left an unattended bag in a different room in the building that included his wallet, identification and another recording device.

title: Police confiscate robot that groped 16-year-old girl, probe whether young men were at the controls
summary: German authorities have opened an investigation into possible sexual harassment involving a robot
story: German authorities have opened an investigation into possible sexual harassment involving a robot

COLOGNE, Germany -- COLOGNE, Germany (AP) — German authorities opened an investigation into possible sexual harassment after a robot controlled by two young men touched the buttocks of a 16-year-old girl and made thrusting movements toward her, police said.

Police in the western city of Cologne responded after the incident overnight Saturday to Sunday in which the robot's suspected 16-year-old owner and a 19-year-old companion were said to have filmed the alleged assault.
They were said to have streamed the incident and commentated on it online.

Cologne police spokesman Christoph Bermel said the two male teenagers have not been charged but are considered suspects, and investigators were examining whether the robot's movements were preprogrammed or controlled in real time.
Police were unfamiliar with this type of incident, he said.
“We have not been aware of this phenomenon so far," Bermel told The Associated Press, saying it was "new territory for us.”

Emergency teams that were dispatched to the scene near a fast-food restaurant found the robot in the trunk of a vehicle, Cologne police said in a statement on Monday. The robot and the two young men's mobile phones were confiscated.
North Rhine Westphalia Police Cologne, on Facebook, posted an image of the red-and-gold robot lying on the ground.
The robot, said to be 120 cm (about 3 ft 11 inches) tall, was dressed in a white tank top, black sweatpants and wearing a gold chain and sunglasses. It also had what appears to be a fake mustache.
Videos circulated on the internet show two young men escorting the robot toward a group of women, bumping into one and hugging others, on a lively nighttime street.
One of the men repeatedly shouts at the robot and pulls it backward after it makes sexual gestures, prompting laughter among people in the area.
On the police's Facebook account on Tuesday, officers criticized inappropriate comments and warned that sharing or joking about such incidents can worsen the impact on any victim.
Associated Press writer Jamey Keaten in Geneva contributed to this report.

title: What to Stream: Katseye, 'VisionQuest,' 'Tenzing' and a new 'Castlevania' game
summary: New streaming entertainment options are arriving this week, including a tribute to Norm Macdonald and a new Marvel series
story: New streaming entertainment options are arriving this week, including a tribute to Norm Macdonald and a new Marvel series
A new album from Katseye and the Marvel series “VisionQuest” are some of the new television, films, music and games headed to a device near you.

Also among the streaming offerings worth your time this week, as selected by The Associated Press’ entertainment journalists: Judd Apatow's tribute to Norm Macdonald, “Dopamine Chamber” from Fontaines D.C. and a new entry in the “Castlevania” video game series.

— Director Judd Apatow pays affectionate tribute to Norm Macdonald with the documentary “Norm: The Tale of Norm Macdonald” (Netflix). Apatow’s film about the stand-up comedian, who died in 2021, plays with Macdonald’s still constant ubiquity on social media, where bits and late-show appearances still regularly flood the feeds of comedy fans. — Jennifer Peedom’s “Tenzing” (Apple TV) is a biopic and historical drama about an often unsung hero of mountaineering: Tenzing Norgay. Genden Phuntsok and Tom Hiddleston star as Tenzing and Edmund Hillary, respectively, in Peedom’s film about the first climbers to ever summit Mount Everest. Co-starring Willem Dafoe.

— “The Death of Robin Hood” (HBO Max) stars Hugh Jackman as a grizzled and violent outlaw little like most contemporary versions of Robin Hood. Michael Sarnoski (“Pig,” “A Quiet Place: Day One”) eschews cheerier mythologies for a brutal telling of the medieval tale. In my review, I wrote that it “drains the blood, and life, out of an old English legend.”
— AP Film Writer Jake Coyle

— Call Katseye the great, global girl group experiment of the decade. The band officially debuted at the end of 2023, created by the Hybe Corporation and Geffen Records in a TV competition process that was documented on the Netflix series “Popstar Academy: Katseye.” That feels like ancient history now. Today, they’re easily one of the biggest groups on the planet, and their swift ascent is further documented in a new film, “Katseye: Wild Heart,” available to stream on Disney+/Hulu.

— If the Irish post-punk band Fontaines D.C. is still unknown to you — that’s sure to change. Their last album, 2024’s “Romance,” was certified platinum in the U.K. off the strength of its singles “Favourite” and “Starburster.” Their latest album, “Dopamine Chamber,” is on track to be one of the biggest rock releases of the year, from the trip-hop-adjacent “Tongue” to the dizzying “Marianne.” (If their pop-and-then-some experiments are not enough of an incentive to press play, just know that Rosalía appears on the track “Where Is Gone?,” their first guest feature. That’s unexpected!)

— When it comes to Riot Grrrl, the ’90s feminist movement, some names loom larger than others in cultural memory. At the forefront is Kathleen Hanna, the feminist punk pioneer and celebrated Bikini Kill frontwoman, as well as acts like Bratmobile. The list should also include Heavens to Betsy, the duo of drummer Tracy Sawyer and singer-guitarist Corin Tucker (who would later form Sleater-Kinney with Carrie Brownstein.) On Friday, they will release “Baby’s Gone,” a newly unearthed demo tape originally recorded in February 1992 by Bratmobile’s Molly Neuman — and two 7-inch EPs. It’s a miracle for followers of the DIY musical underground and a gift for others just discovering it now (perhaps in no small part due to Olivia Rodrigo’s Daisy Chain Festival)?
— AP Music Writer Maria Sherman

— Paul Bettany returns as Vision in the Marvel series “VisionQuest,” that closes out the WandaVision trilogy. Vision is now a fugitive after the events of “WandaVision,” with authorities hunting him down. James Spader reprises his role as Ultron, an evil artificial intelligence that built Vision to be his own ultimate physical form. The first two episodes drop on Wednesday on Disney+.

— “Hollywood Arts,” a sequel to the Nickelodeon sitcom “Victorious” that ran from 2010 to 2013, arrives on Netflix. It follows Daniella Monet’s Trina Vega, a down-on-her-luck actress with no teaching credentials who takes a substitute job at her old high school. Original stars Victoria Justice and Ariana Grande are not among the main cast, but Justice has said she may make a cameo in the future. The first 13 episodes drop on Thursday and the second half of the season will premiere at a later date.

— Before Jason ever picked up a machete, his mom was doing the bloody work. A new “Friday the 13th” prequel series called “Crystal Lake” goes back to where the legend began. It's an eight-episode series starring Linda Cardellini as Pamela Voorhees, who is Jason's mom. The full season debuts Thursday.
— AP Writer Alicia Rancilio

— William, the hero of “Valor Mortis,” takes the title (which means “the value of death”) a bit too literally. He has already died fighting for Napoleon, but somehow he has come back to life. That unholy resurrection gives William some wicked supernatural powers to go along with his slick swordplay. Meanwhile, Napoleon’s endless war has corrupted a broad chunk of 19th-century Europe, so hordes of “plague-ridden abominations” have joined the fight. Polish studio One More Level, best known for the cyberpunk slasher “Ghostrunner,” promises demanding first-person combat in a haunted alternate history. Take up arms Tuesday on PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X/S and PC.

— While we’re messing around in France, let’s travel back in time to 1499 for “Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse.” A new protagonist, Rose Belmont, has inherited the mighty whip known as the Vampire Killer. Dracula has been defeated for good, but his castle has plunked itself down in Paris and all sorts of demons — not to mention Joan of Arc — are on the loose. The 2D, side-scrolling action of Konami’s 1986 original has recently inspired dozens of imitators like “Dead Cells,” and the studios behind that cult hit have taken the reins here. Whip it good starting Thursday on PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X/S, Switch and PC.
— Lou Kesten

title: Judge denies gag order request in Cornell sex assault civil case
summary: The judge called the request a "'side show' meant to muddy the waters and distract from the merits of the claims and defenses involved in this case."
story: The judge called the request a "side show" meant to "muddy the waters."

A New York judge on Friday rejected a request to impose a gag order in the civil case brought by a former Cornell University student who alleged she was sexually assaulted at a fraternity house in 2024, calling the request a "'side show' meant to muddy the waters and distract from the merits of the claims and defenses involved in this case."
Judge Phaedra Perry-Bond said the public statements made by Jane Doe's attorney that one of the men named in the civil lawsuit used to justify the request "express nothing more than [his] opinions."

"Expressing opinions on the case or reporting on how the litigation has impacted clients cannot alone serve as a factual basis for limiting an individual's First Amendment rights," Judge Perry-Bond wrote. "While the Court agrees that [he] should not make statements that certain parties spoliated evidence, especially where, as here, no discovery has yet to take place, those isolated statements, without more, are insufficient to show the serious risk of prejudice required by precedent and the United States Constitution."
The judge encouraged the attorneys in the case to work together to prevent their clients from facing threats, harassment, and doxing.

"The Court believes that given the notoriety of doxing related to this case, it would serve all parties' interests to work together to ensure their clients and others may be safeguarded, to the extent possible, from being inundated with threats or harassment from malicious outside actors," she wrote.
Perry-Bond also rebuked the lawyer who requested the gag order for including in a court filing an email exchange with an attorney for one of the other men.

"The Court will not tolerate its docket being used to generate media controversy, and this Court does not tolerate attorneys, especially attorneys who are not even involved in this case, engaging in mudslinging," she wrote.

The attorneys requesting the gag order had asked for "narrowly tailored restrictions" that would prevent lawyers and parties in the civil case from commenting on the allegations outside of court, arguing in their motion that a gag order would limit "possible juror prejudice" and prevent the potential release of sensitive information that could lead to " threats, doxing, intimidation, and extrajudicial contact."

In a statement responding to the motion response, an attorney for Jane Doe, Thomas Giuffra, argued that the attorney for one of the men "has tried to rebut the claims in this case by engaging in a wholesale leaking of confidential documents, giving interviews calling Ms. Doe's story into question and calling her lawsuit immoral. These attempts to shift the narrative have not been successful."

A then-undergraduate student identified only as Jane Doe made a complaint to campus police in November 2024, three weeks after the alleged incident occurred, that she had been sexually assaulted by a group of men at the Chi Phi fraternity house. She filed a civil suit against seven men and the university alleging that she had been drugged and raped.
The men denied all of the allegations.
The university has said it takes allegations of allegations of sexual violence "extremely seriously" and that it "investigated and adjudicated the allegations consistent with university policies."
The school said it conducted a "thorough" Title IX investigation and "issued a range of sanctions, which included expulsions and suspensions from Cornell.

This week, Cornell University President Michael Kotlikoff announced that all parties and social events at fraternity houses are suspended for the rest of year while the university considers whether fraternity life can continue at the Ivy League school.

"It is clear that women on our campus continue to question whether they are safe. We must meet this moment by acknowledging where we have fallen short and taking meaningful action," Kotlikoff said Tuesday.
No criminal charges have been filed, but an investigation by the New York attorney general is ongoing.
The case has rocked the university and started conversations about treatment of sexual assault allegations on college campuses across the country.

title: Bend, Oregon, shooting: Suspect ID'd, had attended elementary school, police say
summary: Three children and one teacher are dead after a shooter forced his way into a Bend, Oregon, elementary school and opened fire, authorities said.
story: The shooting occurred at Silver Rail Elementary School.

The mass shooting at a Bend, Oregon, elementary school on Thursday that left three children and one teacher dead took place inside a special needs classroom, authorities said at a news conference, identifying some of the victims and the suspected shooter.

Three boys, ages 5, 8 and 11, and the teacher died at the scene, police said. At a news conference on Friday, authorities identified the teacher as 25-year-old Megan Lambert, and one of the boys as 5-year-old Rhoam Summer. The names of the other two children killed are not being released at the request of their families, police said.

The suspected shooter, a 16-year-old armed with a twelve-gauge shotgun, was fatally shot by a community member who saw the teen going into the Silver Rail Elementary School and pursued him inside, according to Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz.
In another "heroic" act that may have saved lives, he said another teacher tackled the shooter to the floor and tried to take the gun away from him.

A 7-year-old girl and a 54-year-old teacher were wounded in the gunfire and were taken to the hospital with critical injuries, police said. The child was in serious but stable condition on Friday, and the teacher -- identified by her family as Becky Drury -- suffered serious but non-life-threatening injuries, police said.

Police identified the suspected shooter on Friday as Griffin J. John II, a Bend resident who formerly attended Silver Rail Elementary School. The suspect had been a special needs student at the school, school officials confirmed. He was not currently enrolled in the school district, according to the police chief.
Preliminary information indicates the 16-year-old suspected shooter used a pump-action shotgun believed to be purchased by his mother, multiple sources told ABC News.

"How the suspect got the weapon and ammunition remains part of the active criminal investigation, and I will not be able to address any of that portion today," Krantz said at a press briefing on Friday.
A motive also remains under investigation, police said.
"It will require substantial investigative time to continue that, but that is the answer we're seeking as well," Krantz said. "We may never get that full answer, but we want it."
The incident began unfolding shortly before 1 p.m. PT Thursday, police said.
At 12:59 p.m., police received a call from a driver who reported being shot at multiple times by a person with a long gun, the police chief said. The vehicle was struck three times.

Shortly afterward, the Deschutes County dispatch center began receiving multiple 911 calls that a shooter had entered Silver Rail Elementary School. The school was directed to go into lockdown at 1:01 p.m, Krantz said.
The shooter "forced" his way inside the school by shooting at the glass panes of locked doors multiple times, according to the police chief.
"The suspect went directly into the classroom, immediately to the left of the entry doors, where he fired as many as 15 rounds overall," Krantz said.
Officers arrived on the scene at 1:02 p.m., police said.
All of the shooting victims were located in that special needs classroom, he said. The suspect was also shot in the classroom and died at the scene, he said.
A Maverick 88 pump-action 12-gauge shotgun was located near the suspect, who had approximately 44 remaining rounds of 12-gauge ammunition, according to the chief.
Police said the shooter was fatally shot inside the classroom by a 36-year-old community member who had seen the teen firing at the truck and then followed him into the school, Krantz said.
His family on Friday identified him as Kaylub Giamanco, a father with two daughters who attend Silver Rail Elementary School.

Giamanco -- a lifelong Bend resident -- was driving near the school when he heard the commotion and ran inside, according to his family, who said he regrets not being able to save more lives. His family confirmed he has a concealed carry permit.

"He is not seeking recognition, but instead wishes to express his gratitude to the first responders, school personnel, and community for the outpouring of love and support," the Giamanco family said in a statement.

Police also commended another teacher who threw her cellphone at the shooter after he entered the classroom. The police chief said the teacher then "tackled him and fought to take the firearm from him," and that she "almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed." The police chief did not identify the teacher, and noted that she was uninjured.
Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek thanked teachers, staff and first responders who rushed to the scene and thanked the community member who she said "heroically intervened to stop further loss of life."
Following the shooting, police said they evacuated the school room by room. A reunification site for families was set up at a nearby church.
Bend-La Pine Schools Superintendent Steven Cook called the shooting an "unthinkable tragedy" and said, "We are heartbroken. We are horrified."

Thousands of community members gathered for a candlelight vigil Thursday night at Drake Park in Bend. A makeshift memorial has also grown outside the elementary school, with mourners leaving flowers, candles, toys and stuffed animals.
Kotek ordered flags at Oregon public institutions to be flown at half-staff on Friday from sunrise to sunset in remembrance of those who lost their lives at Silver Rail Elementary School.
Classes, activities and athletic events at all Bend-La Pine Schools were canceled Friday, school officials said.

"A school should be a safe place where children can learn and feel secure. What happened today should never happen," Bend Mayor Melanie Kebler said at Thursday's press briefing. "Like so many in our community, I'm struggling to make sense of a loss that feels unimaginable."

A school resource officer was not at the elementary school at the time of the shooting, a police spokesperson said, noting that he officer oversees multiple schools and was at a nearby campus at the time.

The shooting sparked a large police presence as law enforcement and first responders raced to the school. Over 150 law enforcement officers and first responders have been involved in the investigation, police said.
"Everything they were doing seemed highly trained and highly prepared for this," Caleb Weis, who was riding his motorcycle near the school at the time, told ABC News.
"I didn't see as many phones out recording as you see on many other occasions, just a kind of a shock factor and an immense amount of respect for the law enforcement, first responders," he said.

FBI Director Kash Patel said the agency was on the scene assisting in the investigation. Agents with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives were also responding, according to a source.
Some parents who heard the sirens came to the school and anxiously awaited information.
"There's really no way to prepare for something like this," one father told ABC Bend affiliate KOHD.
ABC News' Alyssa Pone and Lisa Sivertsen contributed to this report.
Editor's Note: Police have corrected their initial spelling of the 25-year-old teacher's name. The correct spelling is Megan Lambert.

title: Zelenskyy urges support for new US sanctions on Russia after Trump puts them on hold
summary: Zelenskyy calls Trump's decision to put them on hold "unfortunate."
story: Zelenskyy calls Trump's decision to put them on hold "unfortunate."

KYIV, Ukraine -- Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy urged supporters Saturday to speak out in defense of new U.S. sanctions against Russia, hours after President Donald Trump signed an executive order pausing a sweeping package of restrictions targeting the Russian economy.
The White House decision has further raised fears that Ukraine could be left exposed to Moscow’s escalating assaults with winter approaching.

Russian attacks overnight killed at least four people, including an ambulance driver, and wounded dozens, officials said. Ukrainian drones killed a woman in a Russian border region and disrupted flights at Moscow's airports, according to Russian authorities.

In a statement on social media, Zelenskyy described Trump's move to put sanctions on hold as unfortunate, but did not directly criticize the U.S. leader despite deepening tensions between Ukraine and Washington in recent days.

“A decision was unfortunately made in America to completely disregard the Lindsey Graham Act, which was supposed to impose truly effective pressure on Russia to bring this war to an end,” Zelenskyy wrote.

He separately thanked Democrats and Republicans who backed the legislation. He said blocking it would encourage Russia to continue killing, and limiting Ukraine’s ability to retaliate against Russian attacks would not bring peace.

“Nevertheless, we very much hope — and I personally hope — that the president of the United States of America will do everything possible to make (Russian President Vladimir) Putin stop the killing, stop the attacks on our energy infrastructure, and end this war,” he said.

Asked about contacts with Washington, Zelenskyy said that Ukraine’s lead negotiator, Rustem Umerov, met with U.S. presidential envoy Jared Kushner, who is also Trump's son-in-law, on Friday. He said that the U.S. was working to arrange a trilateral meeting with both him and Putin. He said it could take place in the Middle East, Europe or the U.S.

Named after late South Carolina Sen. Lindsey Graham, the legislation had sought to clamp down more quickly on the flow of financial resources fueling Russia's 4 1/2-year-old war against Ukraine. The bill had sought to sanction Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers that keeps Russian energy moving.

Trump personally signed the legislation just last month and his move came just two days before a deadline set in the law itself for its implementation. Trump told Congress that the pause was in the national interest but gave no further details.

Sen. Richard Blumenthal, who co-drafted the bill, criticized Trump's move, saying the president turning his back on “the majority of Americans, their representatives in both houses of Congress, and our European allies.”
“These waivers have nothing to do with our national security, and everything to do with sucking up to Vladimir Putin,” Blumenthal said.

Trump’s unexpected decision comes a week after he had agreed to purchase diesel from Russia to try to bring down global energy prices, despite that potentially hurting Ukraine. Republicans and Democrats alike say the purchase will help Russia execute its war against Ukraine — without making a difference to global fuel prices, which are elevated mostly due to Trump’s war on Iran.

Zelenskyy said that Kyiv was investigating sudden speed restrictions on Ukraine’s use of Starshield, the military-grade version of SpaceX’s Starlink satellite internet service, which is the backbone of Ukraine’s drone operations and communication.

The restrictions, imposed without warning early Thursday, cut the internet data connection when a communication terminal moves faster than 160 kph (100 mph). The cap forced Ukrainian drones to fly slower than usual, making it easier for Russian weapons to target or evade them.
Zelenskyy said that there were no similar restrictions in European Union countries and apply only to Ukraine. "In other words, this is a planned operation,” he said.

It was unclear who was responsible. SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk said this week that the U.S. government owns and controls the system, with decisions about its use resting with the U.S. military and, ultimately, the president. The Pentagon has not answered questions from The Associated Press sbout the restrictions.
Trump told reporters Friday that he did not order restrictions on the system. He also doubted that the disruption came from Musk.
“Well, I don’t know if it was anybody, but it wasn’t me, and I don’t think it was Elon,” Trump said. “And from what I understand, it’s the same as it’s always been.”
Moscow carried out a massive strike on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, targeting more than 15 sites across the country, Zelenskyy said.
“The sheer scale and unrelenting pace of Russia’s strikes, specifically against our energy sector, are unfortunately having severe consequences,” he said.
Ukraine’s air force said it intercepted all four of Russia's cruise missiles and most of 332 attack drones it fired overnight.

Russia’s heavy bombardment of the power grid ahead of winter has been an annual feature of the war, aimed at wearing down Ukraine’s appetite for the fight by denying civilians heat and running water. Ukrainian officials have warned that Russia is stockpiling ballistic missiles for more attacks in the coming months.

Russian attacks killed three people in the Ukrainian city of Sloviansk, Vadym Liakh, head of the city military administration, said Saturday. A Russian strike also killed an ambulance driver in Ukraine’s Kherson region, head of the local military administration Yaroslav Shanko said. The strike, which used guided bombs, wounded at least 33 others, he said.
A Russian woman was killed in a Ukrainian drone attack in the Russian border region of Belgorod, local officials said.
Russia’s Ministry of Defense said Saturday that its forces shot down 610 Ukrainian drones overnight over 15 Russian regions, as well as the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea and the Black Sea.

Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said that more than 100 drones were shot down en route to the capital. More than 350 flights were canceled or delayed at Moscow airports, local media reported, as planes were grounded in response to incoming drones.
The Kremlin announced Saturday that Putin approved a government program to help restore trade and logistics facilities damaged in drone attacks.
Davies reported from Manchester, England.
Follow the AP’s coverage of the war in Ukraine at https://apnews.com/hub/russia-ukraine

title: How Elon Musk is bankrolling GOP’s hopes in Texas Senate race
summary: New campaign finance filings show the major role billionaire Elon Musk is playing in bankrolling GOP efforts against Democrat James Talarico in Texas.
story: The world’s richest man is spending more than $150 million against Talarico.
New campaign finance filings reveal the major role billionaire Elon Musk has played in bankrolling Republican efforts against Democrat James Talarico in his home state of Texas.
In fact, Musk appears to be the chief sponsor of a prominent group supporting Republican Ken Paxton, according to new filings with the Federal Election Commission.
On Sept. 9, the first day of the GOP midterm convention in Dallas, Musk gave $75 million to the Senate Leadership Fund (SLF), the main Senate Republican super PAC.
One day later, SLF transferred $75 million to Texas PAC, which was founded a few weeks earlier to back Paxton in his Senate race against Talarico.
On Sept. 23, Musk made another $83 million contribution to SLF. The group then transferred that sum to Texas PAC the next day.
Texas PAC reported receiving the sum of those two payments -- totaling $158 million -- in its latest report.
The transfers have allowed the Senate GOP group to support Paxton without diverting resources away from Republicans in other competitive races across the country.

Republicans are trying to maintain their four-seat majority in the Senate in November and are currently locked in competitive races in North Carolina, Maine, Iowa, Ohio, Kansas and Alaska, in addition to Texas.
Democrats are defending open Senate seats in Michigan, New Hampshire and Minnesota.
The support directed to Texas PAC is just one element of Musk's more than $276 million in spending on the midterms -- close to what he spent on the entire 2024 presidential election.
Among other efforts, he has also pumped more than $76 million into AMERICA PAC, his super PAC helping the GOP target and turn out low-propensity Trump voters even though Trump is not on the ballot.

From July to September, Musk also gave $20 million to the Congressional Leadership Fund, the main House Republican super PAC; $10 million to another super PAC supporting Paxton; $10 million to the Republican Governors Association; and $2 million to the Republican Attorneys General Association.
A spokesperson for SLF did not immediately return a request for comment.

“If Democrats take control of Washington and win key gubernatorial and attorney general races this November, then America risks becoming a socialist, woke and borderless country,” Andrew Romeo, a spokesman for America PAC, told the New York Times. “These robust investments have allowed the G.O.P. apparatus to get its message out so Republicans can have a fighting chance to defy history.”
Many Democrats out-raised their GOP opponents in some competitive House and Senate races, according to new FEC filings.
Talarico, for example, raised $64 million in the third quarter -- a record for Senate races -- compared to Paxton's $18 million in the same time period.
But Republicans continue to enjoy a massive advantage in spending and support from outside political groups, such as Musk's, that have helped their candidates target voters.

title: Georgia's Senate and governor races test Trump's political influence
summary: Trump plays a significant role in Georgia's races, with Democrats working to tie their GOP opponents to Trump’s unpopular policies on the economy and war with Iran.
story: Trump has played a significant role in Georgia's races.
President Donald Trump on Friday returned to Georgia -- a key battleground state in the upcoming and high-stakes midterm elections -- to hold a midterm rally in Dalton.

The state has closely watched Senate and gubernatorial races this year, with GOP Senate candidate and current Rep. Mike Collins trying to unseat incumbent Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff, while businessman and GOP candidate Rick Jackson faces former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms in the race for governor.
The president plays a significant role in both of these races, with Georgia Democrats working to tie their Republican opponents to Trump's unpopularity and policies on the economy and war with Iran.

The Republican nominees for Senate and governor have employed diverging strategies on how to deal with Trump. Collins has leaned into his ties to the president in hope of turning out Georgia’s MAGA base, and Jackson has distanced himself from Trump to appeal to the moderate coalition that propelled current Georgia Republican Gov. Brian Kemp to victory.
ABC News ranks the Senate race in Georgia as likely Democrat and the gubernatorial race as a toss-up.
Collins has stuck by Trump in a political bet that drawing out Georgia's MAGA base will give him his best shot at winning in November.

During his debates against Ossoff, Collins dodged questions on the Iran war and Trump's tariff policy -- issues that remain unpopular with many Americans because they have driven up the cost of goods and gas. A recent Fox News poll found that majorities of Americans disapprove of how Trump is handling tariffs (69%) and about 6 in 10 (59%) oppose U.S. military action against Iran.
When he was asked in the first debate if he would defend the Iran war, Collins said that Trump "had every right to go in there and make sure that Iran does not get a nuclear weapon."

Pressed on high diesel prices tied to the Iran war in the second debate, Collins said that "diesel prices are high. Diesel price is high. The supply is coming. The supply is coming now, and the prices will continue to come down."

At this time last year, the Georgia Senate race was the election to watch, with Republicans hoping to flip the Senate seat held by Jon Ossoff, the only Senate Democrat up for reelection this year in a state that Trump won in 2024. But over the past year, Collins' missteps, closeness to Trump, and a political environment shaped by affordability and the Iran war have left Democrats confident Ossoff will face minimal challenges in his reelection bid.

The major Democratic PAC supporting Senate candidates pulled advertising funding from the race as it pours its funds into what it sees as other opportunities in red states -- sending a vote of confidence to Ossoff, who also continues to dominate in fundraising, according to a report in the Washington Examiner earlier this week. Ossoff announced he raised $33 million in the third quarter of the year, according to Federal Election Commission data.

Collins confirmed he would be attending Trump's rally in Georgia on Friday, writing on social media that he was excited to welcome the president back to Georgia. Trump last campaigned in Georgia on July 22.

After campaigning to be "Trump's favorite governor" during the Republican primary, Jackson, a billionaire health executive and political newcomer, didn't mention Trump's name once in his debate earlier this month against Bottoms. When Bottoms tried to tie Jackson to the president, Jackson instead aligned himself with popular two-term Gov. Kemp.

"Let me tell you something. I don't owe anybody anything. Nobody's ever told me what to do. My No. 1 priority is Georgians. It's you. And I will stand up to anybody, just like Brian Kemp has done. He works with both parties, both presidents and he stands up when he disagrees,” Jackson said in the debate.

Though Trump initially endorsed Jackson's opponent, Georgia Lt. Gov. Burt Jones in the Republican primary and runoff. The president endorsed Jackson when he became the nominee, and the two appeared together onstage during Trump’s July visit to Marietta, Georgia.
Jackson will attend Trump's rally on Friday.

Jackson has spent more than $100 million on his gubernatorial race, massively outspending Bottoms as she works to make the election a referendum on Trump and high costs. History is not on Bottoms' side: Georgia hasn't elected a Democrat for governor since 1998.

title: Trump administration threatens to prosecute local California election workers
summary: The DOJ sued over claims the state hasn't purge noncitizens from voter rolls.
story: The DOJ sued over claims the state hasn't purged noncitizens from voter rolls.

The Trump administration is escalating its feud with California over allegations of noncitizen voting, threatening on Friday to criminally prosecute election workers who knowingly tabulate ballots belonging to noncitizen voters.

"The legal consequences for either facilitating or ignoring a federal crime are significant," Trent McCotter, the acting deputy attorney general, wrote in a letter to Los Angeles officials. "Noncitizen voting in a federal election is a federal crime--and knowingly facilitating such conduct is equally unlawful."
McCotter continued: "If persons knowingly tabulate ballots cast by individuals identified by federal agencies as noncitizens, they risk becoming aiders and abettors to a federal crime."
President Donald Trump reposted the letter to his social media platform. In a follow-up post resharing the letter, Trump wrote "They will all go to jail for a long period of time!!!"

The Justice Department's threat to hold election workers criminally liable for noncitizen voting is not the Trump administration's first such salvo. Over the summer, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin similarly warned that election officials "can be held accountable by fines, by penalties, and even depending on how far it goes, prison time."

Trump has made the issue of noncitizen voting a personal fixation despite scant evidence that it is widespread. The Justice Department has promoted dozens of arrests in recent weeks of alleged noncitizens who have voted in past cycles. But even those examples fall far short of the sort of figures that would tilt the scales in any outcomes.
McCotter's threat to prosecute local election officials comes one day after the DOJ sued California over claims that the state has refused to purge noncitizens from its voter rolls.

Earlier this week, McCotter sent letters to the Los Angeles County Clerk and California Secretary of State demanding California voting officials access a password-protected thumb drive that DOJ officials said contained thousands of names of potential non-citizens believed to be on the state's voter registration list.

The letters gave a two-day deadline for the officials to confirm they were conducting a review and also moving to segregate any potential ballots that may have been returned from individuals whose names were on the thumb drive.
California characterized the request as legally baseless and a last-ditch effort by the Trump administration to intervene in the state's election process.

"The USDOJ's relentless efforts to unlawfully gain access to states' protected voter data and purge voter rolls serve only to cause chaos and fuel public distrust in our elections," California Secretary of State Shirley Weber said.
Experts overwhelmingly agree the lawsuit is unlikely to succeed. But they fear the consequences of publicly calling election outcomes into question could damage confidence in democracy.
Sean Morales Doyle, a voting expert at the Brennan Center, told ABC News on Friday that the Trump administration appears to be "laying the groundwork to challenge results after Election Day."
"They're putting a nail in the wall for something to hang their hat on later," Morales Doyle said.

title: Iran live updates: Trump admin prepares options, including 'mother of all bombs'
summary: A dozen people were killed Saturday during a "brutal" attack at the King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, the Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation said.
story: Officials have prepared a range of options for the president to consider.
President Donald Trump announced "major combat operations" against Iran on Feb. 28, with massive joint U.S.-Israeli strikes targeting military, government and infrastructure sites.

Despite a memorandum of understanding signed by both countries in June aimed at ending the war, talks broke down and the U.S. and Iran renewed strikes, with the strategic Strait of Hormuz as the primary flashpoint.
Across the region, fighting in Yemen between the Iranian-backed Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni forces has intensified in recent weeks and the militia group has also launched strikes on Saudi Arabia.
