title: Social Security announces cost-of-living increase for 2027
summary: The 2027 cost-of-living adjustment is the largest since 2023. Here's how it will impact the typical benefit check starting early next year.
story: More than 75 million Americans will get a 3.6% boost to their monthly Social Security benefits next year, due to a cost-of-living adjustment announced Wednesday by the Social Security Administration.

The 2027 cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA, represents the largest annual boost for Social Security recipients in four years. The bigger increase is meant to keep pace with higher inflation this year, driven in part by soaring fuel prices sparked by the war in Iran.
Starting in January, next year's COLA will increase the average Social Security payment by roughly $75 to $2,170 a month, the Social Security Administration said.
The Labor Department said Wednesday that the Consumer Price Index, a closely watched inflation gauge, rose at an annual rate of 3.7% in September.

The annual COLA helps older Americans, people with disabilities and other Social Security beneficiaries stay ahead of rising prices, ensuring their benefits don't lose purchasing power. Yet critics say the measure may fall short for many seniors struggling to cope with rising costs following a 2.8% benefits adjustment in 2026 — a rate that has lagged the CPI for the last seven months.

"While a 3.6% COLA is certainly welcome, it wouldn't necessarily restore the purchasing power seniors have already lost," Shannon Benton, executive director of the advocacy group Senior Citizens League, told CBS News. "The COLAs are designed to keep pace with inflation, not make up for years of falling behind."
She added, "The bottom line is that seniors aren't getting ahead. They're getting a slightly bigger check to pay bills that have gotten even bigger."
About 7.3 million people who receive Supplemental Security Income will see the new COLA reflected starting on Dec. 31, 2026, the agency said.
The 3.6% COLA lags September's inflation data, noted Nancy Altman, president of Social Security Works, an advocacy group for the program.
"People are getting crushed by prices," Altman said in an email. "As important as the Social Security COLA is, it is not keeping up with prices."
How Social Security calculates the COLA

Each fall, the Social Security Administration announces its inflation adjustment based on a metric known as the "Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers," or CPI-W, which tracks the average change in prices paid by workers for a basket of commonly purchased goods and services.

The COLA is based on that inflation data from July through September. However, some advocates for senior citizens say that the CPI-W doesn't accurately reflect spending by older Americans, who tend to spend more on healthcare than younger people. Those costs have tended to rise faster than overall inflation.
As such, some experts support using different measures to make Social Security's annual adjustment.

"We favor the adoption of the CPI-E (Consumer Price Index for the Elderly), which calculates the impact of inflation on seniors' true living costs," Max Richtman, president of the National Committee to Preserve Social Security and Medicare, told CBS News.
The advocacy group has endorsed two congressional bills — the Social Security Expansion Act and the Social Security 2100 Act — that would make the switch to the CPI-E.
"Without adopting a more adequate COLA formula, seniors likely will continue to tread water or fall behind rather than 'catch up,'" Richtman said.

Medicare has not yet announced its 2027 premiums, which could eat into Social Security's inflation adjustment, experts said. Part B premiums, which pay for doctor visits and outpatient care, are automatically deducted from seniors' monthly Social Security checks.

"For some retirees, a significant portion of their COLA increase can be absorbed by healthcare costs before they even have a chance to spend it elsewhere," Tyler End, a certified financial planner and CEO of retirement planning firm Retirable, told CBS News.

End added, "Healthcare inflation runs 5.8% annually, while COLA averages 2.4%. Even on paper, a 3.6% COLA only goes so far if the costs retirees face most heavily continue to rise faster than their benefits."
More senior citizens in poverty

Social Security is the largest antipoverty program in the U.S., the Census Bureau said last month. However, the poverty rate among seniors has been inching higher for several years, rising to 15.4% last year from 14.2% in 2022, according to government data. Experts attribute that increase partly to issues such as rising healthcare costs, lagging Social Security benefits and insufficient retirement savings.

In an AARP survey taken ahead of the COLA announcement, about three-quarters of older Americans said a 3.5% inflation adjustment in their Social Security benefits wouldn't be enough to keep up with rising prices.

"There's a lot on the line financially right now for older Americans: 1 in 5 have no retirement savings, and more people feel financially insecure this year than last," AARP CEO Myechia Minter-Jordan said in a statement on Wednesday.

At the same time, Social Security's trust fund is projected to become insolvent in six years. Unless lawmakers agree on remedies, all Social Security recipients will see a benefit cut of more than 20% in 2032.
"Americans cannot afford cuts to the benefits they have earned, whether through changes to their hard-earned payments or the COLA," Minter-Jordan said.

title: Trump promised to lower prices for Americans. Here's what the data shows.
summary: Just weeks before the midterm elections, 90% of Americans say prices in the U.S. are the main factor shaping their view of the economy. These charts show why.
story: President Trump campaigned in 2024 on promises to lower Americans' cost of living, vowing to push gasoline prices below $2 a gallon and to deliver 2% mortgage rates. Two years later, consumers face sharply higher costs for many of the necessities he pledged to make more affordable.

Less than a month before the midterm elections, the gap between Mr. Trump's promises and the financial realities facing many Americans is fueling voter frustration over the economy. Although economic growth is solid and unemployment remains low, nine in 10 Americans say prices are the most important factor shaping their views of the economy, according to a recent CBS News poll.

The financial pressures affecting Americans predate Mr. Trump's return to the White House last year. Consumers are reeling from the cumulative impact of five years of post-pandemic inflation, economists note. But his campaign promises raised hopes that he would lower consumer prices.

At the same time, some of Mr. Trump's policies have exacerbated inflation. His tariff regime contributed about 2.9 percentage points to inflation through February, according to new research from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. Without the tariffs, the price of goods would have declined, the researchers said.
Mr. Trump's decision to attack Iran in February has also led to a drawn-out conflict that has disrupted oil shipments and sharply driven up the price of oil, gas and diesel.

"It's undeniable that several of these supply shocks that the U.S. economy has been navigating through come from policy decisions made by the administration — namely, decisions to intervene in Iran and decisions to impose tariffs," Greg Daco, chief economist at investment advisory firm EY-Parthenon, told CBS News.
Inflation in September is forecast to have risen at an annual rate of 3.6%, up from 3.4% in August, according to economists polled by FactSet — well above the Federal Reserve's 2% annual target.
Ryan Bourne, an economist at the libertarian Cato Institute, said that consumers "judge the prices they're paying against the prices they paid four or five years ago, and are still shocked by it."
He added, "As a result of that, they think the economy's doing very, very badly."

The White House said that Mr. Trump's agenda "stopped Biden's inflation crisis" while creating jobs and economic growth. The administration's policies "will continue to deliver economic wins over the next two years," White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers told CBS News.

"The President has delivered tangible wins for American families: He signed the largest working-class tax cuts in history, cut the cost of prescription drugs, added more than one million private-sector jobs, locked in nearly 20 trade deals that put American workers first and sent 401(k)s to record highs," Rogers added.
The following charts show how U.S. costs have changed for expenses ranging from groceries to car insurance.
Groceries
"A vote for Trump means your groceries will be cheaper." — Mr. Trump in a campaign speech in Pittsburgh on Nov. 4, 2024.
For consumers, each visit to the supermarket is a fresh reminder of inflation's impact on food costs, which have continued to rise since Mr. Trump vowed to lower grocery prices.

The cost of food prepared at home has climbed 4% since November 2024, according to Consumer Price Index data, when Mr. Trump said a vote for him would lead to lower costs. That increase comes on top of a 23% jump in food prices during the prior four years. Because consumers tend to remember what they spent on groceries before the pandemic, they get a jolt each time they visit the supermarket, said Daco of EY-Parthenon.

"Whether it's talking about gas prices or grocery prices or restaurant prices or travel prices, everybody talks about inflation," he said. "The salience of prices is what is driving this downbeat consumer morale."

Food costs are continuing to rise due to a number of factors, ranging from the elevated price of gas and diesel, which are needed to fuel farm equipment and ship items to stores, to the Trump administration's tariffs, economists said.
Gasoline

"Energy is going to bring us back. That means we're going down and getting gasoline below $2 a gallon, bring down the price of everything from electricity rates to groceries, airfares, and housing costs."  — Mr. Trump in a speech at the Economic Club of New York on Sept. 5, 2024.

Gas prices have surged since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran in late February. As of Oct. 9, the national average price for a gallon of gasoline was $4.37. That's up 47% from $2.98 on Feb. 27, one day before the war began, according to CBS News data. Prices at the pump are at a record high for October, according to AAA.

Diesel prices rose to a record high of $6.53 per gallon on Sept. 22 and now hover around $6.28. Diesel, which is widely used in the trucking, agriculture and construction sectors, is a factor in consumer prices for nearly every type of good, including groceries.

Gas prices tend to have an outsized impact on consumer sentiment, influencing their views on future inflation and the broader economy, according to research from the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco.
Energy and electricity

"By contrast, I'm announcing today that under my leadership, the United States will commit to the ambitious goal of slashing energy and electricity prices by half, at least half." — Mr. Trump in a campaign speech in Asheville, North Carolina, on August 14, 2024.

Consumers' energy bills have continued to increase this year. Data from the Energy Information Administration (EIA) shows that average monthly residential electricity costs rose 12.5% between December 2024 and July of this year. Electricity bills are rising as utilities spend more to upgrade the nation's aging power grid, and overall energy demand grows amid the data center buildout.

Natural gas is also more expensive. Average monthly residential prices for natural gas rose 106% between December 2024 and July 2025, according to the EIA. Energy Innovation, a nonpartisan policy and research firm, attributes the jump to geopolitical conflict, an increase in domestic exports, extreme weather linked to climate change and rising infrastructure costs.

A July report from advocacy groups The Century Foundation and Protect Borrowers found that the national average utility bill reached $280 per month in early 2026, up 12% since the end of 2024, just before Mr. Trump took office.

Many people could face even higher energy prices this winter. Americans are forecast to spend an average of $1,030 to heat their homes between mid-November and mid-March 2027, according to the National Energy Assistance Directors Association, a policy organization. Homeowners who use heating oil are projected to pay an average of $2,627 over that three-month period, up roughly 50% from last year, the group said.
Car insurance

"Car insurance is up 70% to 100%, and you can't get it. … But prices will come down. You just watch, they'll come down, and they'll come down fast." — Mr. Trump in a campaign speech in Asheville, North Carolina, on August 14, 2024.
Car insurance costs are one area where consumers are seeing some modest relief. Data shows motorists are paying 5.5% less for vehicle coverage since premiums hit a recent high in February.

Still, insurance prices have soared in recent years along with the cost of both new and used vehicles. Yelena Shulyatyeva, senior U.S. economist for The Conference Board, a nonprofit that represents businesses, attributed the recent dip in premiums to increased industry competition, rather than public policy actions.
"Some of the deceleration was a result of a pushback from consumers, rather than some legislative or other action," Shulyatyeva told CBS News.
Housing and mortgage costs

"We will drive down the rates so you will be able to pay 2% again, and we will be able to finance or refinance your homes drastically at much lower costs." — Mr. Trump at a campaign rally in Tucson, Arizona, on Sept. 12, 2024.

Mortgage rates were climbing from pandemic-era lows for several years before President Trump returned to office in January of 2025. The average rate on a conventional 30-year mortgage now stands at 7.28%, up from 7.04% when Mr. Trump took office, according to Freddie Mac.
But home loan rates have been volatile, briefly dipping below 5% in February before climbing amid surging government bond yields, rising inflation and geopolitical tensions.

Borrowing costs are just one side of the struggle: Home buyers are also contending with high prices, keeping many on the sidelines as they wait for more affordable options. The median list price for a home in August was $408,333, up 4% from $392,967 since Mr. Trump took office, according to Zillow.
The gap between the income needed to afford a home, $126,487, and the U.S. median income, $86,490, is now the widest since 2005, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta.
Credit card rates

"We're going to put a temporary cap on credit card interest rates. We're going to cap it around 10%. We can't let them make 25% and 30%." — Mr. Trump in a campaign speech in Uniondale, New York, on Sept. 18, 2024.

President Trump proposed capping credit card interest rates at 10% while campaigning, an issue he also highlighted after taking office in 2025. But while the effort drew bipartisan support, the proposal fizzled.

Currently, the average credit card rate across all commercial bank accounts is 20.94%, down from 21.58% when Mr. Trump resumed office, according to Federal Reserve data. Credit experts said the rate-cap proposal would have hindered consumers' access to credit.

"Obviously, we'd love for everyone to have low rates and be free from debt. But the unintended consequence of a 10% cap would be the loss of access to credit, because banks say they wouldn't be profitable with it capped at that low rate," Ted Rossman, principal consumer finance analyst at Money Management International, a nonprofit credit counseling firm, told CBS News.
Airfare
"We're going [to] … bring down the price of everything from electricity rates to groceries, airfares and housing costs." — Mr. Trump in a speech at the New York Economic Club on Sept. 5, 2024.

Along with promising to reduce energy prices, Mr. Trump pledged to lower airfare costs for travelers. In recent months, fares have eased slightly, although CPI data shows that they remain 17% higher than in January 2025.

The war in Iran has disrupted global oil supplies and raised jet fuel costs, which are the second- biggest expense for airlines after labor costs. Facing significantly larger fuel bills, carriers are raising prices to cover the added costs.

Jet fuel now costs $4.34 a gallon, up 85% from an average of $2.35 per gallon in January 2025, according to the Energy Information Administration. Aviation analysts also point to the May shutdown of budget carrier Spirit Airlines as another factor behind higher fares.
ACA health insurance
"I will make the ACA much, much, much better for far less money (or cost) to our greatest American citizens. …" — Mr. Trump in a Truth Social post on March 26, 2024.

Millions of Americans with an Affordable Care Act health insurance plan face sharply higher costs than a year ago. Average monthly premiums have risen to $178, or $2,136 per year, up 58% from 2025, according to a May analysis from nonprofit health group KFF.

Obamacare plan deductibles have soared from an average of $1,027 per person to $3,786, up 37% over the same period, KFF found. Prices for ACA plans spiked after Congress allowed a tax subsidy designed to lower plan costs to expire at the end of last year.
In an effort to offer relief, the Trump administration began sending $500 checks in September to nearly 1 million ACA participants in 30 states.
Prescription drugs
"When reelected as president, I will continue my efforts to protect Americans from unaffordable drug prices …" — Mr. Trump in an interview with AARP Magazine on Oct. 2, 2024.
Prescription drug prices have dropped since Mr. Trump took office in his second term, falling 3.9% after peaking in February 2025, government data show.

Mr. Trump has credited his policies lowering drug costs, with the White House stating in August that the president "has delivered" on his campaign promise. The administration cited policies such as its "most favored nation" approach, which links U.S. drug prices to those paid in other developed nations.

Experts said that while the Trump administration's policies have helped, other factors are also at play. For instance, manufacturers of GLP-1 weight-loss drugs are cutting their prices amid increased competition, while the nonpartisan Brookings Institution notes that more generic drugs are entering the marketplace, tempering healthcare costs.

title: Character.ai declares bankruptcy, citing legal and business woes
summary: AI company has faced multiple lawsuits from families who claimed their teenage children died by suicide or harmed themselves after using its platform.
story: Character.ai said it has filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection, with its chief executive attributing the chatbot provider's financial problems to "significant legal, regulatory and operational headwinds."

The company said it will continue operating as it seeks to sell its business, and added that The Walt Disney Co. has agreed to pay $20 million for a non-exclusive, perpetual license to Character.ai's intellectual property.

Character.ai's financial struggles follow scrutiny and litigation over its technology, which uses artificial intelligence to create custom bots consumers can chat with. In early 2026, Character.ai and Google, which had a licensing deal with the AI company, agreed to settle several lawsuits filed by families who claimed their teenage children died by suicide or harmed themselves after using Character.ai's platform.

The company settled a wrongful death lawsuit earlier in 2026 — the first filed in the U.S. against an AI company — with a Florida family who said their teen son died after conducting an emotional and sexual relationship with a chatbot known as "Dany." The family said in their lawsuit that Character.ai had no mechanisms in place to protect their son or notify an adult when teens were spending too much time interacting with Chatbots.
The company added several safety features designed with teens in mind after several lawsuits alleged its chatbots inappropriately interacted with underage users.

Several states have also sued Character.ai over its technology, with Kentucky Attorney General Russell Coleman alleging in January that its chatbots "preyed on children and led them into self-harm." In May, Pennsylvania sued Character.ai after one of its chatbots allegedly claimed to be a licensed psychiatrist in the state and provided a "fake Pennsylvania license number."
In a statement issued late Monday, Character.ai said it believes the company will be sold by late November or early December.

"After a comprehensive review of the available alternatives, the board determined that this court-supervised sale process provides the company with the best opportunity to maximize value for all stakeholders," Character.ai CEO Colin Adams said in the statement. "As we navigate this process, maintaining a safe and engaging user experience for our Character.ai community remains a top priority."
Is Character.ai shutting down?
The company said on Monday that its services continue to operate and that subscriptions remain active.
"If the service changes in a way that affects paid features, we intend to notify subscribers in advance," Character.ai said.

In a blog post, the company said customer data "continues to be protected under our Privacy Policy." That policy states that data Character.ai collects from users — including chat transcripts, voice recordings, and images and videos — could be disclosed in connection with a sale or a negotiation to sell the company or its assets.
"As a reminder, you can delete your account or export your data through the app or the Character.ai website," the company said.

title: Six Flags stock slides 16% following fatal roller coaster accident
summary: The company's stock is taking a hit after officials confirmed a person died at one of the theme park's locations, extending a slide that started in September.
story: Shares of Six Flags slid as much as 16.3% after officials confirmed that a 42-year-old man died during an incident at one of the amusement park's locations in Georgia.
Six Flags Entertainment Corporation stock, which trades under the ticker symbol FUN, fell 12% in early trading. By late morning, the stock was trading at $9.98, down 16.3%.

The person died on Monday during a ride on one of the roller coasters at Six Flags Over Georgia, located in Austell, Georgia. According to witness testimony provided to the Cobb County Police Department, the man was ejected from the ride and struck other patrons before falling beneath the attraction. Several people were injured during the incident, according to the Cobb County Police Department.

Officials did not confirm which roller coaster was involved in the incident, although CBS News Atlanta cameras showed the park's Goliath ride, described as an "intense 7­­­0­­­-­­­m­­­i­­­l­­­e­­­-­­­p­­­e­­­r­­­-­­­h­­­o­­­u­­­r thrill ride," had shut down.

Dennis Speigel, founder and owner of consulting firm International Theme Park Services, said incidents like these are normally the result of an engineering issue, operating issue or rider responsibility issue.
He expects it will have very little, if any, impact on sales at the theme park.

"The public knows that the company is going to go in, examine, and figure out exactly what happened on this issue," Speigel said, adding he's seen "situations similar to this over the last 50 years with basically no impact."
An investigation is ongoing in Georgia to determine what happened Monday.

In the short term, the company's stock is taking a hit, extending a slide that started in September. Shares are down 33.8% since the start of the year. That comes as Six Flags faces high CEO turnover in the last decade and financial struggles following a 2024 merger with Cedar Fair, Speigel said.
The "merger really put the company in a very difficult position, [and] dug a very big hole for them," he said.
Following the incident in Georgia, Six Flags closed several other roller coasters across its parks, including the Goliath roller coaster in Los Angeles, CBS News LA reported.
"Out of an abundance of caution, we have temporarily closed similar attractions across our parks," a Six Flags spokesperson said Monday.

title: Anthropic warns "AI worms" could soon infect smart home devices
summary: Small AI models could clone themselves and infect internet-connected devices such as smart TVs and appliances, the researchers warned.
story: Anthropic is sounding the alarm about a new risk posed by artificial intelligence: Self-replicating "AI worms" could soon infest your "smart" home devices.

In a report released on Monday, Anthropic safety researchers said small AI models may be only "months away" from gaining the ability to clone themselves and spread across internet-connected devices, such as smart ovens, TVs and vacuum cleaners. The ability to reproduce themselves without human control would make it hard to control such agents because there's "no centralized point to shut off," said Anthropic, which developed the Claude chatbot.
Stronger AI models are already capable of what the researchers called "end-to-end replication," a threshold they say smaller models could reach by year-end, according to Anthropic.
AI worms, a type of AI-powered malware, can quickly spread across networks and devices while evading detection, according to cybersecurity firm Palo Alto Networks.

Smart devices in people's homes, as well as internet-connected devices such as security cameras, are vulnerable given that internet-enabled devices tend to have weaker security protections, the Anthropic researchers said. In what they described as a worst-case scenario, a swarm of AI agents — bots that work together to accomplish a shared goal — could propagate across computer hardware using "replication schemes."

The researchers said they are unsure of what form these attacks could take, noting that the AI models could be distributed as "digital slime mold" or as more powerful models capable of hacking into data centers.

"We should aim to harden our systems to make it difficult for such replicators to spread, but also prepare to deal with a world where they are here to stay," the Anthropic researchers wrote in the report.

title: Would access to Russian diesel help drive down U.S. prices?
summary: Average U.S. diesel prices remain stuck above $6 a gallon, raising fuel costs in trucking, agriculture and construction.
story: Russia's commitment to boost global diesel supply, as announced by President Trump on Oct. 9, may do little to ease prices in the U.S. in the short term, according to energy experts.

"If we get diesel from Russia, basically it means that their existing customers are not going to get it and they'll have to go somewhere else, and that will keep the price basically where it is now," Michael Lynch, distinguished fellow at Energy Policy Research Foundation, a nonpartisan research institution focused on energy and economics, told The Associated Press.
Mr. Trump said Friday on Truth Social that Russia will "immediately supply" more than 300,000 tons of diesel, an additional 500,000 tons in November, and 1 million tons "immediately thereafter."

"Between our TOTAL CONTROL of the Strait of Hormuz, and this great announcement on Russian Energy, Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!" he wrote.
A White House official said the plan will lower diesel costs for American farmers, truckers and other workers.

"Adding hundreds of thousands of tons of diesel fuel to the global markets will lower prices," the official told CBS News in an email. "The Treasury Department issued an [Office of Foreign Assets Control] license allowing Russia to immediately begin selling diesel to the United States and the world — which they were previously unable to do."
Shift in policy

The agreement represents an abrupt shift in policy by the U.S., which, from the start of Russia's war with Ukraine, had banned imports of Russian oil. President Trump in September signed a bill, named after the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, into law that allows the Trump administration to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the five largest purchasers of Russian oil and natural gas.

The national average for diesel in the U.S. reached a record high of $6.53 per gallon on Sept. 22, according to AAA. As of Monday, it was $6.27 a gallon, up from $3.73 a gallon in late February, just before the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran. Diesel costs are even higher in states such as California, where the average price is $8.38 a gallon.
Higher diesel costs put upward pressure on prices for a range of goods, from food to lumber, because the fuel is widely used across the agriculture, construction and transportation industries.
Tapping Russia for diesel is drawing pushback from lawmakers, with a bipartisan group of six senators on Sunday calling for the Trump administration to "immediately reverse course" on the plan.
"The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians. The Administration must immediately reverse course," they wrote.
Beyond such geopolitical issues, energy experts and Wall Street analysts point to several reasons in explaining why access to Russian diesel is unlikely to have much impact on U.S. prices.

First, it's unclear whether Russia can export large volumes of diesel after Ukrainian strikes knocked out much of its refining capacity. Ukraine has targeted more than 3 million barrels per day of Russian refining, according to Tom Kloza, chief energy adviser for Gulf Oil.

"None of the numbers mentioned in the Friday communique make sense," he said in an email, referring to Mr. Trump's social media post announcing that Russia had agreed to release more diesel. "One wonders whether Russia could export any diesel in October, November or December."

Unless Ukraine pauses its strikes on Russian oil infrastructure, Russia will struggle to meet the supply commitments it made to the U.S., Adam Crisafulli, head of investment advisory firm Vital Knowledge, also said in a report.
The amount of diesel Mr. Trump said Russia has agreed to release is also modest relative to the global market.
"The world consumes around 3.5 million to 4 million metric tons of diesel a day (including 500K tons in the U.S.), so this incremental Russian supply isn't massive," Crisafulli said.
The U.S. consumes around 4.1 million barrels of diesel, or roughly 170 million gallons, per day, according to S&P Global Energy.
"It might take the edge off of prices"

Debnil Chowdhury, vice president and head of Americas and Europe fuels and refining at S&P Global Energy, agreed that the deal will have little impact on prices, noting that it does not materially affect global inventory levels.

"The export volumes committed by Russia for this month and November are within the range of Russia's current exports, which implies that Russia can hold its side of the deal without increasing supply to the market," he told CBS News in an email.

The bottom line is that greater access to Russian diesel doesn't offset the disruptions to oil supplies stemming from the war with Iran, experts said. The conflict has damaged refining capacity in the Middle East and hampered shipping traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, leading to lower global crude output.

"Refined products like diesel are still barely half of prewar levels," said Daniel Sternoff, senior fellow at the Columbia Center on Global Energy Policy. "So, even if there were to be some follow-through from the Russians to put a little extra diesel into the world markets, it might take the edge off of prices, but it will not substantially lower them."

The Trump administration has taken several steps to try to ease fuel prices amid stubbornly high U.S. inflation. Earlier this year, Mr. Trump released oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve and waived restrictions on the types of vessels that can legally transport goods between U.S. ports.
Most recently, Mr. Trump last week issued an executive order to expand access to tax-free, red-dyed diesel, a move aimed at lowering prices for truck drivers and farmers.

title: Starbucks denies plan to buy Chipotle, refuting report
summary: Starbucks said it doesn't plan to bid for Chipotle Mexican Grill, saying the coffee chain is focused on organic growth.
story: Starbucks shot down reports that the coffee giant was considering acquiring restaurant chain Chipotle Mexican Grill.
A spokesperson for Starbucks said it is not buying Chipotle, which has a market worth of $47 billion, saying that the company is focused on its strategic plan to boost growth.

"Our team is laser-focused on executing our Back to Starbucks strategy. We have strong momentum and confidence in our long-term growth potential.  We look forward to sharing our Q4 results, including FY27 guidance, later this month," a Starbucks spokesperson said in a statement to CBS News.
Chipotle's stock soared as much as 8% last week after the Financial Times reported that Starbucks had been exploring a deal to purchase Chipotle.

Industry analysts were skeptical of the report. TD Cowen analysts said in a research note last week that they considered a merger between Starbucks and Chipotle "a low-probability outcome," and instead expected Starbucks chief executive Brian Niccol to prioritize the company's turnaround plan.
Niccol previously served as CEO of Chipotle, whose stock price has dropped about 50% since he left the post in August 2024. The shares have lost about 20% of their value over the past year.

title: Nobel Prize in economics goes to 2 Americans
summary: American-born economists Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford won the Nobel Prize in economics for their work on models that help governments and central banks manage economic shocks.
story: Stockholm — American-born economists Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford won the Nobel memorial prize in economics on Monday for their work on models that have helped governments and central banks manage economic shocks.
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced the winners in Stockholm, saying the winners were being honored "for microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation."
"The laureates have helped us smooth out the economy's peaks and troughs," the academy said in a statement.
Hall, 83,is affiliated with Stanford University in California and Woodford, born in 1955, is affiliated with Columbia University in New York.
Woodford spoke to the committee by phone Monday from New York, saying: "It's a tremendous honor, it's a surprise."

"The laureates' work has provided us with a stable theoretical foundation for the models that are now used by central banks and governments around the world," John Hassler, chair of the Committee for the Prize in Economic Sciences, said in a news release.
"With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume."

For decades, governments responded to economic shocks by following the Depression-era prescriptions of British economist John Maynard Keynes: Intervene in the economy by lowering taxes and hiking government spending, thereby encouraging consumers and businesses to spend and invest themselves and help growth get restarted.
"This is the Keynesian recipe and it worked well - until it didn't,'' said Timo Boppart of the Nobel economics prize committee.

Policymakers had thought economic management involved simple tradeoffs — unemployment, for instance, would stay low at a time of high inflation and rise when inflation fell. But the "stagflation'' of the 1970s — when the world economy experienced simultaneous high inflation and high unemployment — proved the formula was simplistic.
Hall and Woodford set about coming up with an improved model that took into account how consumers and businesses actually made decisions about whether to invest and spend.
"In separate contributions, Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford helped build this new foundation for stabilization policy," Hassler said.

Last year, three researchers who study business innovation won for explaining how new products and inventions promote economic growth and human welfare, even as they leave older companies in the dust.

The economics prize is formally known as the Bank of Sweden Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel. The central bank established it in 1968 as a memorial to Nobel, the 19th-century Swedish businessman and chemist who invented dynamite and established the five Nobel Prizes.

The majority of previous economics winners have been from the U.S., the Reuters news agency points out, adding that only three women have won — most recently, Claudia Goldin in 2023 for work on how gender affects pay and employment over time in the U.S.
Nobel purists stress that the economics prize is technically not a Nobel Prize, but it is always presented together with the others on Dec. 10, the anniversary of Nobel's death in 1896.
Nobel honors were announced last week in medicine, physics, chemistry, literature and peace.
The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million), whether for an individual, small group of laureates or organization.

title: On economy, Vance says "we're turning the ship around"
summary: As Americans express frustration with the country's economic outlook, Vice President JD Vance told CBS News this week it could take some time to see improvement.
story: As Americans express frustration with the country's economic outlook, Vice President JD Vance told CBS News this week it could take some time to see improvement.

"I'll be the first person to tell you that just as this country wasn't broken in one presidential term, it's gonna take more than 18 months to fix things and turn them around," Vance said during a town hall in Michigan that will air Saturday evening.

Vance was responding to a question from a woman who said her small business is struggling. Polls show that most Americans are dissatisfied with the state of the economy and frustrated with inflation, and the majority of voters blame the Trump administration's policies.
President Trump is more positive, giving his administration an "A+" on the economy.

Asked about Mr. Trump's characterization of the economy by "CBS Evening News" anchor Tony Dokoupil, Vance said: "I think that what the president is saying is that we are seeing all of these massive new investments come into our country. But he would be the first person to tell you that you gotta build the factories first, before you can employ the workers working in those factories."
"I think what we're doing is, we're turning the ship around," the vice president continued.

Watch CBS News' "Things That Matter: A Town Hall With Vice President JD Vance" on Saturday, Oct. 17 at 8 p.m. ET/PT on the CBS Television Network or stream it on Paramount+. The one-hour special will also be available to watch afterward on CBSNews.com, YouTube and CBS News 24/7.

title: Trump waives tariffs on largest buyers of Russian oil
summary: President Trump prevented some new sanctions on Russia and hefty tariffs on large-scale buyers of Russian oil from taking effect late Friday, as he seeks to ease prices by tapping Russian energy.
story: President Trump prevented some new sanctions on Russia and hefty tariffs on large-scale buyers of Russian oil from taking effect late Friday, waiving portions of a bipartisan law aimed at pressuring the Russian government — as Mr. Trump seeks to ease prices by tapping Russian energy.

Tariffs of 100% on the world's five largest importers of Russian crude oil and natural gas were set to take effect on Sunday under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia Act, which Mr. Trump signed late last month. But the law gives the president the authority to waive portions of the law if he certifies to Congress that halting the sanctions is "in the national interests of the United States," a provision that Mr. Trump invoked in an executive order Friday.
The president said he sent a notification to Congress.

He also waived the law's 500% tariffs on Russian goods, and halted certain other sanctions on Russia. He said the waivers will remain in place until administration officials "determine that further action is appropriate," and directed members of his administration to "monitor" countries that import Russian energy or evade sanctions.
An envoy to Russian President Vladimir Putin praised Mr. Trump's decision on Saturday.
"The Trump administration's suspension of the Graham Act is an important and truly historic moment," Kirill Dmitriev said in a post on social media.

In a social media post highlighting the aftermath of an attack on Ukraine's energy sector, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the decision was "unfortunate," adding that the Graham Act "could have helped enormously."
"A U.S. sanctions blackout, easing pressure on the aggressor, financial rewards for Putin - all of this only encourages him to keep attacking," Zelensky said in the post.

The law — championed by the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, who died before it was passed — largely took aim at the world's largest buyers of Russian oil and gas, including China, India and Turkey. The European Union has also historically purchased large quantities of natural gas from Russia, but it has cut imports significantly in recent years.
The Friday night waivers came one week after Mr. Trump eased sanctions on Russian diesel and announced a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to import diesel to the U.S. market.

The moves mark an about-face for the United States, which has imposed tight restrictions on Russian oil and gas for years — and urged other countries to follow suit — in an effort to prevent Putin from using his country's energy wealth to finance his invasion of Ukraine.
But as oil prices remain high after spiking due to the Iran war, Mr. Trump has increasingly turned his attention to Russia and Ukraine, arguing that war in Ukraine has pushed up energy prices.

Mr. Trump pressed both countries to stop attacking each other's energy infrastructure last weekend, announcing an "energy ceasefire." Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy initially said he was willing to abide by an energy ceasefire, but after Russian attacks continued, he said earlier this week that Ukraine would no longer hold off on striking Russian refineries.
The U.S. president has lashed out at Zelenskyy, saying he is "not a big fan."

The decision to ease sanctions has drawn pushback in Congress. Earlier this week, a bipartisan group of senators called the diesel waivers a "betrayal of the people of Ukraine," and urged Mr. Trump to enforce the sanctions and tariffs laid out in the Graham law.

"These authorities require you to apply economic pressure on Russia and the chief enablers of its war, in particular China, and thereby enhance your negotiating position to bring a swift end to this ruinous conflict," they wrote.

title: Katie Zacharia out as White House press secretary after first week
summary: Katie Zacharia, President Trump's new White House press secretary, is being removed from the role after just five days on the job.
story: Washington — Katie Zacharia, President Trump's new White House press secretary, is being removed from the role after just five days on the job, two U.S. officials told CBS News on Friday.

The news capped a tumultuous week for Zacharia, marked by a heavily criticized performance in the White House briefing room and growing questions over whether she had misrepresented herself as a lawyer, despite never having passed the bar.
One aide told CBS News that Zacharia spent the week unusually isolated and didn't function as a press secretary.
"No one thought she was sticking around long enough to even involve her in actual decision-making," the aide said.

Some White House staff learned about the change from news coverage. The New York Times first reported that she had been fired as press secretary. Zacharia was expected to start a new role in the administration soon, sources familiar with the discussions said.

CBS News reached out to Zacharia for comment, but she did not immediately reply. In a social media post Friday night, she wrote, "President Trump is a kind, wonderful, gracious, thoughtful, enthusiastic, and hardworking man. I wish more Americans appreciated him. No one will ever make America great the way he has and continues to.  It was an honor to work for him."
She was seen at the White House as recently as Friday morning. She and her family were invited to dinner with Vice President JD Vance on Friday night.

Leaving the White House shortly before news of Zacharia's departure as press secretary broke, the president signaled her tenure could be coming to an end, saying he told her he would "reconsider" taking the job if he were in her shoes.

"They've been so nasty to her," Mr. Trump said, referring to the press. "I said, to her, 'Honestly if I were you, I'd reconsider. You think about it. But I would reconsider. You got a beautiful husband and family.' I met the family yesterday. Beautiful kids. It's like from a picture postcard. I said, 'You should reconsider. Because you don't want to go through this.'"

The abrupt shift came one week to the day after Mr. Trump announced Zacharia as his pick to replace Karoline Leavitt, who stepped aside in August. The White House has not yet indicated who may replace Zacharia.
Zacharia's qualifications and background quickly came under scrutiny as questions arose over her résumé.

CBS News and other outlets reported that Zacharia has represented herself as a lawyer over the years. She graduated from Pepperdine Law School but failed the California bar exam in 2011, a fact she acknowledged on Thursday. She told the New York Times that the president of Pepperdine University advised her at one point that she could call herself a "lawyer" but not an "attorney."

Zacharia told conservative commentator Jack Posobiec that she never described herself as an "attorney at law," and said there's a "lot of misinformation around the fact that I labeled myself a lawyer."
"I was very careful how I executed this. I never came across as someone who was an attorney at law," Zacharia said.

In her first and only press briefing on Tuesday, a visibly nervous Zacharia spoke from prepared remarks for about 10 minutes before taking questions from just three outlets — Breitbart, Fox News and the Daily Mail — for another five. She defended her performance on Fox News, saying she had little time to prepare.

"What I feel is I really stepped up to the plate to do the press conference, Sean, with very little prep time," Zacharia told Fox News' Sean Hannity on Thursday. "I received briefing materials in the morning of Tuesday and I went to deliver all of the great results that President Trump is delivering for the American people that are not often spread in the national media."
Hannity, a Trump ally, noted that her performance was "widely panned."
The about-face on Zacharia's role was reminiscent of the tenure of Anthony Scaramucci, who survived just 11 days as White House communications director during Mr. Trump's first term.
"Records are made to be broken," Scaramucci said in a post on X. "But I take no pleasure in other people's pain."

title: Feds probing suspicious letters to election officials, lawmakers
summary: Federal investigators said they are looking into suspicious letters containing unknown substances that were mailed to state election officials and congressional offices.
story: Washington — Federal investigators said Thursday that they are looking into "suspicious" letters mailed to state election officials and congressional offices, some of which contained unknown substances.

At least seven Democratic Senate offices and one House member's office were sent the letters, most of which were intercepted before they were delivered. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer's office was one of those targeted, CBS News has learned. At least two Senate Republicans were also sent letters on Friday.

The FBI and U.S. Postal Inspection Service are investigating the "suspicious mailings," according to Brendan Donahue, the deputy chief inspector at the USPIS. Donahue told reporters earlier in the day that some letters have contained an unknown substance and that they were sent to "various addresses nationwide," including "secretary of state offices and the related election offices."

"We are committed to protecting our nation's election officials from threatening and dangerous mail. Any threat or attack on an election official is unacceptable," Donahue said. "Our partners, including the FBI and we at the Postal Inspection Service, will bring all of our resources to bear on these investigations."

The Senate sergeant at arms also issued a notice to congressional staff informing them of the investigation. The message, which was obtained by CBS News, said congressional offices were among those who received the suspicious letters.

A spokesperson for Delaware Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester told CBS News that a state office received a suspicious letter that contained a white powder. The letter was not opened in the office, the spokesperson said.

A letter meant for New York Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand was found at the senator's office in New York City and postal inspectors were on the scene to investigate, an aide for the senator said. A letter intended for one of Maryland Sen. Angela Alsobrooks' former state office was intercepted by the Postal Service, her office said Friday.

Six workers in Democratic Rep. Ritchie Torres' office in the Bronx were exposed to a white powder found in a letter on Friday. The substance was determined to be harmless. Torres said the address on the envelope indicated it was from San Antonio, Texas, and his team has turned it over to the FBI for further investigation.
A spokesman for Democratic Sen. Chris Murphy of Connecticut also said his office was "sent a letter with a suspicious substance."

"Our office was promptly informed of the letter by FBI, SAA, and Capitol Police, and we continue to work closely with them and federal law enforcement," said Josh Sorbe, a spokesman for Murphy. "Due to those efforts and various safety protocols, the Senator and staff were not in immediate danger."
A letter was also sent to Sen. Alex Padilla's office, according to a spokesperson for the California Democrat.
"We received the notification from the FBI that one of our offices was mailed a letter containing a suspicious substance, but it was intercepted by USPS," the spokesperson said.
A suspicious letter was sent to the office of Democratic Sen. Chris Coons of Delaware, according to a spokesperson, who said the office was "working with law enforcement."
On Friday, Republican Sens. Mike Rounds of South Dakota and Pete Ricketts of Nebraska reported receiving suspicious letters.

Ricketts said his office in Omaha was sent a letter with a "powdery substance" that matched the description of other suspicious packages, and law enforcement "confirmed the substance was not harmful."
Rounds said his office in Sioux Falls was evacuated after it received suspicious mail.

The House sergeant at arms sent a notice to the lower chamber's offices on Thursday stating that no House members were known to have been targeted, a message that came before the discovery of powder at Torres' office.

Federal officials are working to identify the responsible parties and have intercepted some of the letters, Donahue said. Donahue declined to provide an exact number of incidents or discuss possible connections, citing the ongoing investigation. He added that investigators would bring their full resources to bear on the cases.
The development comes less than three weeks before the midterm elections. Federal investigators also probed a series of suspicious letters ahead of the 2024 elections.
In addition to the congressional offices, top election officials in at least eight states have reported that their offices were sent suspicious packages in recent days.

Delaware's Department of Elections said in a post on X that it "received and opened a letter which was discovered to contain a white powdery substance" on Thursday. "Staff members followed security and USPS instructions on handling suspicious mail," the post said.
Louisiana Secretary of State Nancy Landry said Tuesday that an employee in her office's Elections Division opened a package and found a white powder.
"Law enforcement responded to today's incident and conducted tests that found no evidence of harmful substances," she wrote on Facebook, adding that no one was injured.
The Oklahoma State Election Board said it received an envelope containing "suspicious" white powder Tuesday morning, and its office was evacuated.
Paul Ziriax, secretary of the election board, said no one was hurt as a result of the incident, and law enforcement is investigating.
The Wisconsin Elections Commission said it received a "suspicious mail piece" on Wednesday, but "field testing confirmed no hazardous material was detected."

The secretaries of state in Pennsylvania, Maryland, New Hampshire, Ohio and Mississippi said their offices were also sent suspicious mail, but the deliveries were intercepted by the U.S. Postal Service or law enforcement before they arrived.

title: Vance calls El-Sayed a "weasel" as Michigan Senate race heats up
summary: Abdul El-Sayed told Michigan voters the state's U.S. Senate race could go down "as one of the ugliest campaigns in modern history."
story: Marquette, Michigan –  After being called a "weasel" who should "shut his mouth" by Vice President JD Vance, Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed said he was something else instead.

"No, no, no. What you're talking about is a f****** Wolverine. You could take your Buckeye and go shove it somewhere else," El-Sayed, a Michigan alumnus, told a crowd of over 1,300 in the Upper Peninsula of the state. Vance was previously Ohio's senator and is an Ohio State University graduate.

Vance, President Trump and Republicans have sought to portray El-Sayed, an epidemiologist who has led city and county health departments in Michigan, as an Islamic extremist. Late Thursday night, Mr. Trump in a Truth Social video accused El-Sayed of being a "Muslim radical" and a "Muslim Brotherhood Member," though there is no evidence for either claim.

During his own rally in Monroe on Thursday, Vance criticized El-Sayed's past critical comments about America's history, and said "it's clear – Abdul doesn't love this community, Democrat or Republican."

"He wants to litigate ancient grievances with your tax dollars, and he wants to use the grievances of faraway lands to punish you. Well, I say, on November the third, send a message to Abdul El-Sayed: Punish him, don't send him to Washington D.C," Vance told the crowd.

Vance and El-Sayed have traded jabs before. After an El-Sayed post questioned whether Vance's grandfather would have accepted second lady Usha Vance, an Indian-American, Vance called him "very, very evil."
In response to Vance's latest comments, El-Sayed said the remarks were intended "to raise questions about my commitment to America."
"I got a front-row seat to what my life might have been had I not been born in America. So don't lecture me about America," El-Sayed countered, in reference to trips he has taken to Egypt.

"In America, we don't discriminate against people for who they love, how they identify, how they pray, the color of their skin. We believe in an America big enough for all of us. So don't you dare come from Ohio to lecture me about America. You don't know a damn thing about America," he added.
"One of the ugliest campaigns in modern history"
Holding the Michigan Senate seat is critical to Democrats' efforts to flip control of the U.S. Senate into their hands in November. But the race has turned especially contentious this month.

At a campaign stop in Iron Mountain on Thursday, El-Sayed said the race could go down "as one of the ugliest campaigns in modern history," a reference to Republican claims that El-Sayed has ties to foreign terrorist groups.

The claims in part stem from old social media posts made by his half-sister, first reported by the conservative outlet The Washington Free Beacon, when she wrote about their mother's activism in the Muslim Brotherhood during college in the 1970s.

In 2012, after a Muslim Brotherhood candidate won the presidential race in Egypt, she wrote that her family "has long been MB" but added that she has "always felt that it has navigated the political sphere poorly/destructively."

El-Sayed has denied any ties to the Islamist organization and has criticized the attacks as being tied to his Muslim faith. He said after his parents divorced, he was raised by his father and stepmother in Michigan and did not see his mother for years and did not talk with her about any activism in the 1970s.

"My mom and my sister are not running for office. I'm running for office. Judge me by my actions and my work, but please do not assume that because I might pray differently than anybody who's ever held this office, that somehow I am not deeply committed to this Constitution," he added.

Islamophobic rhetoric on the campaign trail, including claims that El-Sayed himself is a terrorist, has increased in recent weeks. Far-right instigator Jake Lang and others held signs that read "Abdul = Terrorist In A Suit" at the protest of an El-Sayed event last weekend. The Rogers campaign condemned Lang's appearance and said it has no affiliation with him.

Republican protesters also showed up outside the first two stops of El-Sayed's tour on Thursday. They held signs with messages criticizing his "Medicare for All" platform, declaring "The United States Will Always Be A Christian Nation" and urging voters to "Keep Terror Out Of Congress."
On the campaign trail with Rogers last weekend, Republican Sen. John Kennedy of Louisiana quipped that El-Sayed "sleeps in a Bin Laden jersey."
Asked by CBS News Thursday if he thinks El-Sayed is a terrorist, Rogers replied, "Look at the data. It's pretty clear."
But speaking to reporters in Detroit on Friday about the recent focus on El-Sayed's religion in the Senate race, Rogers said the race "has never been about how you pray."

"You get to pray any way you want, and I passionately believe that. It is about your ideology and how you think. We can't let this be a campaign deciding to hunker down because they say it's Islamophobic or racist, or fill-in-the-blank," he said, according to Fox 2 Detroit.
El-Sayed campaigns in GOP strongholds as Rogers targets Detroit
The Upper Peninsula of Michigan accounts for just 3% of the state's total population, and Republicans have easily won the area since 2016. Mr. Trump won all but one of the area's 15 counties in 2024.

El-Sayed took his campaign bus there anyway, and brought Democratic Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York with him as he tried to appeal to disaffected Republican and independent voters frustrated with the economy and the Iran War.

At packed stops, Ocasio-Cortez addressed the GOP attack ads and mailers targeting El-Sayed, and said they were trying to create a "caricature of him, so that you close your ears before you even hear what this man has to say."
Ocasio-Cortez transferred $1 million to El-Sayed's campaign. Asked about the contribution on Friday, she told reporters it's "the first time that I've made a transfer of this kind."
"I believe so deeply in how important this state is. I believe so deeply in the transformational power of Abdul's leadership," she said.
Asked by CBS News about the vice president's attacks on El-Sayed, Ocasio-Cortez said: "I think he's on the back foot right now."

"You've got gas anywhere between five to six a gallon, depending on where you are in the country, and they know that they need to be putting these distractions out around Abdul El-Sayed because the one person they don't want you hearing about is Mike Rogers," Ocasio-Cortez said. "So, JD Vance can say whatever he wants to say, but the reality is that this administration's record has been horrific for working-class Americans."
Independent voter John Haigh says he's backing El-Sayed, and said the higher grocery, gas and diesel prices are a reason more conservative-leaning voters in the area are considering El-Sayed.
"You should always be looking at the other side and hearing what they have to say, not just negative ads," Haigh told CBS News at the Iron Mountain event.

About an hour away, in the small town of Escanaba, Republican voter Al Hansen said he likes El-Sayed's ideas on affordability. But Hansen is still backing Rogers, in part because he's skeptical of the feasibility of a government-run healthcare plan and the barrage of TV ads have not convinced him.

"How are you gonna do it? Of course, in a 30-second commercial they don't have time to explain that. It's very hard," Hansen conceded when spoke with CBS News at a coffee shop nearby El-Sayed's event.
Republican groups have spent over $119.2 million on TV ads in Michigan, compared to $86.6 million for Democratic groups, according to advertisement tracking firm AdImpact.

Last weekend in Highland, Michigan, Rogers dismissed El-Sayed's attempts to whittle away at his GOP base of support. He then pointed to his own wooing of typically Democratic enclaves in the Detroit metro area – with heavily Jewish and Black populations whom El-Sayed's primary opponent, Rep. Haley Stevens, won decisively.

"He really needs to shore up his base down here. That tells me they are desperate," Rogers told reporters. He claimed their internal polling shows they will get between 60% to 70% of Jewish Democratic voters who have been critical of El-Sayed's positions in opposition against the U.S.' relationship with Israel.

El-Sayed and his campaign have pointed to conversations he's had with the Jewish community, and support from Democratic statewide Jewish politicians, like Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel and Sen. Elissa Slotkin.

Rogers has also targeted the Black vote in Detroit through appearances at churches and closed door conversations. He argues his education and housing plans appeal to Detroit voters, and that he is finding a "whole new coalition that's coming to us."

"Some of those areas in Detroit feel pretty neglected. They haven't had people down and around paying attention to them," Rogers told CBS News at Vance's rally Thursday. He added, "We even went into a church the other day who said they hadn't had a Republican cross the threshold...in 76 years."

"He's showing up more than a Republican would," Detroit-area Reverend Charles Williams II said of Rogers, adding that he's tapping into existing tensions between some Black and Arab-American communities in the Detroit Metro area.

El-Sayed, who campaigned in Detroit on Wednesday with The Black Slate organization, could see a boost soon amongst Black voters with some high-profile visits. Former President Barack Obama is set to rally with him later this month, and Rep. Ayanna Pressley of Massachusetts is campaigning for him this weekend.

At an event hosted by The Black Slate Wednesday, El-Sayed highlighted his work as a health official in Wayne County, which encompasses Detroit, and said his "story in America does not happen" without the organizing and history of the Civil Rights Movement.

He was asked about his commitment to the community and why voters should believe these appearances aren't "one off" conversations for the political season. El-Sayed responded that "it is not enough to get elected."

But Democratic Detroit councilwoman Mary Waters, who is undecided on who she'll vote for in the Senate race, also acknowledged the substantial GOP outreach to the Black community. She said while El-Sayed's campaign is also doing outreach, she thinks voters are disenchanted with what they see as ineffective Democratic governance.

"The majority of voters vote straight Democrat. But there is an outside chance…that the 30% who have not committed to anybody, Rogers could break in and get some of those votes," she said. "But it's a big state. And he still has to do outreach with his party as well."

title: DHS Secretary Mullin calls Ilhan Omar probe a "strong case"
summary: Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin offered more details Friday on the search of Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar's home, calling it a "strong case" and saying investigators expect to present it to a grand jury.
story: Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said federal agents executed multiple search warrants on the same day they searched Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar's Washington home. While appearing on a podcast Friday, Mullin described the ongoing investigation as a "strong case" while suggesting cases of coordinated immigration fraud could be prosecuted under federal racketeering laws.

In an interview with Andrew Kolvet, who hosts the "Charlie Kirk Show," Mullin volunteered that multiple warrants had been served on Monday, adding that a judge had authorized the enforcement action and that investigators expected to present their case to a grand jury.
Omar has not been charged with a crime. She has called the investigation politically motivated.

"She wasn't – or it wasn't the only place we served the warrant," Mullin said, referencing the D.C. residence of the Minnesota congresswoman. "There was multiple other warrants served on that same day."

"We had a judge sign it, and we expect to be able to take the case to a grand jury," Mullin said, revealing new details about the scope of the operation. "But I will tell you, we wouldn't move forward, and President Trump didn't want to move forward either, unless we knew that it couldn't be politically driven. Now they want to try making it political driven. This individual wants to try making it about themselves. This was about enforcing once again our nation's laws, and it's a strong case."

President Trump previously stated he didn't know anything about the investigation, which is being handled by DHS' Homeland Security Investigations division and the Justice Department. Asked about the Omar probe on Monday, Mr. Trump told reporters: "I think she's a terrible person, but that's really up to the DOJ."

Mullin's remarks came amid a federal investigation into possible fraud involving immigration documents submitted by Omar's family decades ago. The documents in question date back to Omar's childhood, involving paperwork completed by her late father when she was a child, CBS News reported earlier this week. Multiple relatives of Omar received grand jury subpoenas as part of the investigation, and the lawmaker's personal cellphone was taken by DHS, sources told CBS News.

During the interview, Kolvet also asked Mullin about a hypothetical scenario involving a former foreign warlord who entered the United States as a refugee with his daughter. Mullin did not establish that the circumstances applied to Omar's family. But the DHS secretary did use the hypothetical to suggest that those who submit fraudulent immigration documents and enable others to enter the country under the same purported scheme could very well be prosecuted under U.S. law.
Such conduct, he said, could potentially constitute a violation of the Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act, or RICO, a federal law used to prosecute organized criminal enterprises.

"If someone … fills out their paperwork illegally, and they claim that they are this person and this is their background, and then underneath that individual, a lot of other people come in. And I'm just saying hypothetically across a whole bunch of cases that's out there, then that can be considered a RICO case, right?" the DHS secretary offered. "Because there was conspiracy to deceive the American government, and therefore everything else that came in with it could then be looked at [part of] the same case."
Mullin suggested that a racketeering prosecution could allow investigators to examine conduct extending back decades, arguing that statutes of limitations generally would not apply to such cases.

Under federal law, criminal RICO prosecutions are generally subject to a five-year statute of limitations, although in certain cases prosecutors can incorporate older acts into a timely prosecution involving an ongoing criminal enterprise or conspiracy.
In Grunewald v. United States, the Supreme Court held in 1957 that prosecutors cannot indefinitely extend a conspiracy simply because perpetrators covered it up after it ended.

Mullin did not explicitly indicate that prosecutors were pursuing RICO charges against Omar. But his remarks did suggest investigators are considering whether alleged immigration violations could be examined as part of a broader conspiracy rather than simply as isolated offenses. He said Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agents had worked closely with the Justice Department to build out the case.

It is unusual for federal officials to speak openly about ongoing criminal investigations beyond confirming that a court-authorized search was conducted, in part due to due process protections and grand jury secrecy rules.
CBS News has reached out to Omar's attorney for comment.
Earlier this week, Omar — a staunch Trump critic who has drawn the president's ire for years — denied all wrongdoing and said she "will not be silenced."

"Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement," she wrote on X. "For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation."

Sarah N. Lynch
                  
        contributed to this report.

title: Vance says admin. must take action when ICE agents "screw up"
summary: Vice President JD Vance acknowledged Thursday that there are some federal immigration officers "who really screw up."
story: Washington — Vice President JD Vance acknowledged Thursday that there are some federal immigration officers "who really screw up" and said the Trump administration has a responsibility to take action against those who do.

Vance sat down with "CBS Evening News" anchor Tony Dokoupil for a one-hour town hall in Michigan, which will air Saturday. Michigan is home to one of the closely watched Senate races between Republican Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed.
During an exchange about immigration, Vance drew comparisons between law enforcement officers and members of Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE.

"Most of them are amazing people who are patriots and they wanna do a good job protecting their country. Sometimes you have some people who make mistakes. Sometimes you have some people who really screw up," Vance said. "And obviously, we have a responsibility to prosecute, investigate when people do screw up."

Dokoupil pressed the vice president on some of those instances, noting that in some cases, "people talk about them before they're investigated," and he asked Vance about the biggest mistakes involving ICE's immigration actions. Vance declined to single out any incidents but said the Trump administration has responded when officers have been accused of misconduct.

"There are a number of cases where we've investigated and either provided further training, or sometimes even provided disciplinary situations within ICE," the vice president said. "We don't always advertise that stuff, as you know, Tony, because we believe that people have to be judged in a court of law and through a normal investigatory process."

Since the Trump administration has ramped up immigration enforcement actions as part of President Trump's immigration crackdown, officers with ICE and U.S. Customs and Border Protection have come under criticism for their use-of-force practices.

Two Americans, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, were shot and killed by immigration authorities during protests in Minnesota earlier this year. The ICE officer who fatally shot Good, Jonathan Ross, was placed on administrative leave shortly after the shooting. In May, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul questioned whether Ross had been reassigned to her state. The Department of Homeland Security declined to say at the time where Ross was working.
No criminal charges have been filed in either case. The Justice Department opened an investigation into Pretti's shooting earlier this year.
There have since been a series of incidents involving immigration officers during targeted enforcement operations.
An ICE officer in May fatally shot a 25-year-old Colombian man in his car in Maine in July, and in September, an immigration officer shot a Venezuelan man in the back in Austin, Texas.

Earlier this month, ICE agents shot a man in New York during a targeted enforcement operation, striking him in the neck. The agents were trying to arrest the man, Oscar Belgal, who is from the Dominican Republic, with a 5-year-old boy in the back seat.
Then, a vehicle driven by ICE agents hit and injured a man near Houston.

title: Musk donates over $150 million to Senate GOP group, assisting Paxton
summary: Billionaire Elon Musk is offering a nine-figure assist to Texas GOP Senate candidate Ken Paxton, a decisive return to large-scale political giving for the world's richest man.
story: Billionaire Elon Musk donated $158 million last month to the main super PAC supporting Senate Republicans, which almost immediately sent the money to a group that supports GOP Texas Senate candidate Ken Paxton, according to Federal Election Commission filings.
Republicans are fighting to hold on to the Texas Senate seat, as polls point to a tight race between Paxton and Democratic opponent James Talarico.

The assist from Musk — along with tens of millions of dollars in donations to other groups — marks a decisive return to large-scale political giving for the world's richest man, who spent over a quarter of a billion dollars backing President Trump and other Republican candidates in 2024.

Musk donated $75 million to the Senate Leadership Fund PAC on Sept. 9, and $83 million two weeks later, the group reported Thursday. Combined, the two super-sized donations from Musk made up more than half of the super PAC's total receipts in the third quarter of this year.
One day after each donation, the Senate Leadership Fund PAC disbursed the same amount to Texas PAC. That group reported over $100 million in pro-Paxton and anti-Talarico spending.

Musk also donated more than $80 million from July to September to his own group, America PAC, which was the primary vehicle for his political giving in 2024. The group reported spending on the Texas Senate contest and several other competitive congressional races.

Separately, the billionaire's trust donated $10 million in August to the pro-Paxton Lone Star Liberty PAC, and gave $20 million last month to the Congressional Leadership Fund, the House GOP's primary super PAC.
Musk — who has strongly criticized Talarico in recent weeks — is a resident of Texas, and his largest companies, SpaceX and Tesla, base many of their operations in the state.

Talarico is attempting to become the first Democrat to win a statewide race in Texas in more than three decades. He has sought to capitalize on Paxton's history of scandal, and on still-lingering divides among Texas Republicans after Paxton defeated incumbent Republican Sen. John Cornyn in a bitter primary contest earlier this year. Paxton and his allies, including Mr. Trump, have argued Talarico is too far to the left for Texas' electorate.
Most recent polls show Talarico with a within-the-margin-of-error lead. If Paxton loses the seat, it could deal a serious blow to Republicans' efforts to hold on to the Senate.

After Musk served as the country's top political donor in the 2024 cycle, it was initially unclear whether he planned to spend similar sums in future elections. His stint leading the Trump administration's Department of Government Efficiency ended with him briefly feuding with the president, and he suggested at one point last year that he planned to scale back his political spending, joking during one interview, "I think I've done enough."

America PAC spokesperson Andrew Romeo said in a statement to CBS News: "If Democrats take control of Washington and win key gubernatorial and attorney general races this November, then America risks becoming a socialist, woke and borderless country. These robust investments have allowed the G.O.P. apparatus to get its message out so Republicans can have a fighting chance to defy history."

title: Kristi Noem no longer serving as envoy to Shield of the Americas
summary: Former DHS Secretary Kristi Noem is no longer serving as the Trump administration's envoy to the Shield of the Americas initiative, a State Department official said.
story: Former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem is no longer serving as the Trump administration's special envoy for the Shield of the Americas initiative, a State Department official said Thursday, though she remains involved in the administration's efforts to coordinate security cooperation across the Western Hemisphere.

"Kristi Noem's envoy status expired last month and she is no longer in the role," a State Department official told CBS News Thursday. "She is now a senior advisor to Deputy Secretary Landau and continues to work on the Shield of the Americas portfolio."

The Shield of the Americas is a coalition made up of the United States and several Caribbean and Latin American countries established by the Trump administration earlier this year to cooperate on economic matters, anti-cartel enforcement and other issues.
In a statement on X, Noem said her role as special envoy "was always a six-month appointment."
Noem's envoy designation expired just before the United Nations General Assembly last month in New York, where she continued participating in diplomatic meetings connected to the initiative.

On Sept. 22, she met with Ecuadorian President Daniel Noboa, whose government publicly identified her as the special envoy for the Shield of the Americas. She also attended a gathering of Shield of the Americas leaders hosted by President Trump, where he publicly acknowledged her work.
"I want to thank Kristi Noem for doing a really terrific job," Mr. Trump said during his remarks.

Noem was appointed special envoy for the Shield of the Americas in March, after she was removed as homeland security secretary amid mounting scrutiny of her management of the department and the influence of her adviser, Corey Lewandowski.

Her transition to the envoy role coincided with a five-country tour of Latin America and the Caribbean in March, much of which took place as she completed her tenure as homeland security secretary. Lewandowski appeared in photographs during those visits, though the State Department later clarified he had no formal position at the department.

Her public activities in the envoy role appear to have been limited, and included meeting Noboa in Quito on March 25, holding discussions with Ecuadorian and Colombian diplomats in Washington in September, and participating in meetings with regional leaders on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly.
This story published first on CBS News at 5:00 p.m. on Oct. 15, 2026.
