title: Hayden Panettiere’s final moments revealed in frantic 911 call from boyfriend’s brother
summary: The newly released 911 call captures Zach Hickerson performing CPR on Hayden Panettiere as Brian Hickerson administered Narcan inside a South Carolina apartment.
story: The Greenville County Coroner released the cause of death for 36-year-old actress Hayden Panettiere, ruling it a tragic accident from the toxic effects of fentanyl and other substances. Fox News chief correspondent Jonathan Hunt reports from Los Angeles on her sudden death in South Carolina.

Hayden Panettiere’s final moments were captured in a frantic 911 call as the brother of her on-and-off boyfriend desperately tried to revive the actress after finding her unconscious at a South Carolina apartment Aug. 16.
"​​Oh, God, oh, my God — you do like CPR or something?" Zach Hickerson asked the dispatcher in the newly released audio obtained by ABC News and CBS News.
The seven-minute call reveals Hickerson performing CPR on Panettiere while Brian Hickerson administered Narcan.

In a statement to TMZ shortly after Panettiere’s death, Zach said he called 911 after he and Brian tried to wake up the actress.

His behavior soon became too much to handle, and it was clear to those around him that his health and wellbeing were at risk.

"The last scene we shot was with Charlie and Melanie Lynsky," Lorre wrote. "He couldn’t remember any of his lines and had to use the furniture to keep himself upright. Melanie was terrified. It was clear to everyone that this man, whom we’d all grown to love, was in trouble. I had no choice but to shut down the show."
Lorre wrote that after refusing to get help for his drug problem and later trashing him on television, Warner Bros. decided they no longer wanted Sheen on their lot, and he was let go.
Fox News Digital reached out to representatives for Charlie Sheen for comment.
JULIA LOUIS-DREYFUS REVEALS ‘TONS’ OF FRICTION BEHIND THE SCENES OF ‘SEINFELD’
Casting controversy
Lorre shared that he had to fight for Melissa McCarthy to be the lead in "Mike & Molly." (Cliff Lipson/CBS via Getty Images)
During his career as a television writer and show creator, Lorre encountered pushback from studio executives many times when it came to choosing actors to star in his shows.

In his memoir, Lorre explained the casting decisions behind some of the most popular shows from the past few decades, noting executives initially didn't want to cast Jon Cryer on "Two and a Half Men," or Nayyar on "The Big Bang Theory."

Despite the success of these actors in their respective roles, studio executives challenged him once again when it came time to cast the female lead in "Mike & Molly."

"The casting of Molly was, like with Jon Cryer, a tortuous journey," he said. "Once again, my brilliant casting director, Nikki Valko, brought in a comic genius. Melissa McCarthy. And once again, CBS hated her. Believe it or not, they wanted a hot young woman to play a woman struggling with her weight. It was even suggested by one exec—a female exec—that I consider casting a more attractive actress and put her in a fat suit."
Lorre recalled feeling smart when McCarthy starred in "Bridesmaids." (Frederick M. Brown/Getty Images)

Lorre explained that at this point he had learned his lesson and did not take no for an answer, insisting that McCarthy be given the role, "end of discussion," adding that "when 'Bridesmaids' came out, I felt pretty god-damn smart."

Scientology
Lorre revealed he was once a member of the Church of Scientology. (Michael Tullberg/Getty Images)
When discussing his life prior to making it big as a TV writer, Lorre revealed he was once a part of the Church of Scientology.

He recalled going to the Church of Scientology in Columbus, Ohio, after being invited by the sax player at a bar. He wrote that he "had no idea what Scientology was," but since he had nothing to do and his car was in a junkyard, he decided to go, and was quickly taken with the "pretty girls" there.

Lorre explained that after taking a communication class, he had an out-of-body experience, and sought out the Church of Scientology when he was in Los Angeles. There, he found himself presented with a one billion year contract to join Scientology's Sea Org.

Which means contractually, I owe the Church of Scientology a billion years of labor minus two days."
Age gap regrets
Lorre admitted entering into an age-gap marriage was not the best decision. (Allen Berezovsky/Getty Images)

title: Prince Harry, Meghan Markle accused of staging 'royal theatre' as King Charles faces new dilemma: expert
summary: Royal experts say the Sussexes' Nottingham charity visit risks defying Queen Elizabeth II's rule against a "half in, half out" arrangement.
story: Hugo Vickers, author of "Queen Elizabeth II: A Personal History," details how the Duke and Duchess of Sussexs exit and Oprah interview added strain during the late monarch's final years.
Prince Harry and Meghan Markle are being accused of playing royals on their own terms — and sidestepping the late Queen Elizabeth II's wishes in the process.

On Oct. 15, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex visited Nottingham for their first joint public appearance since returning to the U.K., Fox News Digital confirmed. The city holds special significance for the couple, as it was the first place they visited after announcing their engagement in November 2017.

Kinsey Schofield, host of the YouTube show "Kinsey Schofield Unfiltered," told Fox News Digital that, based on her sources, "there is frustration" inside Buckingham Palace as Harry and Meghan prepare to visit several charities in a manner resembling an official royal engagement.
KING CHARLES DRAWS ‘LINE IN THE SAND’ WITH PRINCE HARRY, MEGHAN MARKLE AFTER COUPLE CAUGHT OFF GUARD: EXPERT
Meghan, Duchess of Sussex during a visit with Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex to Nottingham on Oct. 15, 2026, in Nottingham, England.  (Samir Hussein/WireImage)

Prince Harry and Meghan Markle attend the Terrence Higgins Trust World AIDS Day charity fair at Nottingham Contemporary on Dec. 1, 2017 in Nottingham, England. The couple returned to the city on Oct. 15, 2026. (Chris Jackson/Getty Images)

"Harry and Meghan are no longer working members of the royal family," Schofield said. "King Charles recently reminded his government that the Sussexes are private citizens. The Sussexes appear increasingly determined to recreate the optics of royal life without the responsibilities that come with it. … The charitable visits, the appearances, the photographers. It’s royal theatre without royal authority."

Meghan, Duchess of Sussex and Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex at Himmah Hub, which provides meals and a welcoming space for people experiencing financial hardship or isolation, during a visit to Nottingham on Oct. 15, 2026, in Nottingham, England. (Mark Cuthbert/Getty Images)

"Royal engagements aren't just photo-ops," Schofield said. "There's diplomacy involved. There's soft power. Working royals represent the sovereign, strengthen relationships and serve the interests of the country. Harry and Meghan appear more interested in faking the image of royalty than embracing its purpose. They can imitate the engagement, but they can't replicate the authority or constitutional significance."
Prince Harry and Meghan Markle gesture during a visit to Nottingham Academy in Nottingham, central England, on Dec. 1, 2017. (POOL/AFP via Getty Images)
"They are pushing to reclaim the spotlight they left behind," British broadcaster Helena Chard told Fox News Digital. "It's definitely a reboot — a pseudo royal reboot."
WATCH: PRINCE HARRY, MEGHAN MARKLE CAUSED QUEEN STRESS IN FINAL YEARS: AUTHOR

In January 2020, Queen Elizabeth II drew a firm line at the Sandringham Summit: There would be no "half in, half out" role for the Sussexes. They couldn't remain working members of the royal family while pursuing independent, income-generating ventures. The couple stepped back from royal duties that year, citing intrusive coverage by the British press and a lack of support from the palace.

From left: Queen Elizabeth II, Meghan, Duchess of Sussex and Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex, watch a flypast marking the centenary of the Royal Air Force from the balcony of Buckingham Palace in London on July 10, 2018. (Getty Images)

"Following conversations with the duke, the queen has written confirming that in stepping away from the work of the royal family it is not possible to continue with the responsibilities and duties that come with a life of public service," Buckingham Palace said in a statement on Feb. 19, 2021.

Meghan, Duchess of Sussex and Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex during a visit to Himmah Hub during their visit to Nottingham on Oct. 15, 2026, in Nottingham, England. (Annabel Lee-Ellis - Pool/Getty Images)
In response, the couple issued a statement of their own, saying: "We can all live a life of service. Service is universal."
Prince Harry and Meghan Markle returned to the U.K. six years after leaving for California. (Getty Images)

In Nottingham, the couple focused on charitable work. They visited a food bank, where Meghan reconnected with some of the women she supported at the Hubb Community Kitchen in London. As a working royal, Meghan helped produce "Together: Our Community Cookbook," which featured recipes from women associated with the kitchen.
Prince Harry is seen here during a visit to Himmah Hub on Oct. 15, 2026, in Nottingham, England. ( Annabel Lee-Ellis - Pool/Getty Images)
They also visited the Community Recording Studio, which helps young people affected by violence, and spent time at Epic Partners, which supports young people through mentoring and sports.

Meghan, Duchess of Sussex visits the Hubb Community Kitchen in London on Nov. 21, 2018, to celebrate the success of their cookbook. The kitchen was set up by women affected by the Grenfell Tower fire, and the duchess wrote a foreword to the cookbook to help raise funds for the victims. (POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

Although Harry and Meghan are free to support charities as private citizens, their visits are not official royal engagements, as they no longer represent the monarch. However, royal commentators argue that the couple's public appearances risk blurring that distinction.
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE
Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex, arrives for a visit to the Community Recording Studio in St. Anns on Sept. 9, 2025, in Nottingham, England. (Getty Images)

"The Sussexes have not been given permission to behave like working royals, and yet they seem to have gone ahead with their own plans to recapture the spotlight in the U.K.," Christopher Andersen, author of "Kate!," told Fox News Digital. "These are worthy causes that the couple was supporting previously, so that obviously takes some of the sting out of it."
Prince Harry and Meghan Markle visit the Terrence Higgins Trust World AIDS Day charity fair at Nottingham Contemporary in Nottingham, England, on Dec. 1, 2017. (Getty Images)

Several royal experts told Fox News Digital that the couple's public appearances put King Charles in an increasingly uncomfortable position. While Harry and Meghan are no longer working royals, their titles, global profile and carefully choreographed public appearances can still look strikingly similar to official royal duties, even though they do not carry the authority of the crown. This, they argued, leaves the monarch to decide how firmly to enforce the boundary his late mother drew.
Fox News may be compensated for or earn a commission if you buy through our referral links.
"Kate!: The Courage, Grace, and Power of the Woman Who Will Be Queen" by Christopher Andersen is available now. (Gallery Books)
"King Charles faces a severe problem because Harry and Meghan appear determined to ignore the late queen's instructions," Schofield said.

King Charles III meets guests during a reception to celebrate the Commonwealth Diaspora ahead of the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in Antigua and Barbuda at St. James's Palace in London on Oct. 14, 2026. (Getty Images)

"They’ve retained their titles and international recognition, allowing them to stage appearances that resemble official engagements, despite no longer representing the crown. The king has demonstrated throughout his life that he can be decisive when protecting his interests and the institution. The question is whether he’s prepared to demonstrate that same strength when it comes to his youngest son."

Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex during a visit to Himmah Hub during their visit to Nottingham on Oct.15, 2026, in Nottingham, England.  ( Annabel Lee-Ellis - Pool/Getty Images)

"Queen Elizabeth was unequivocal," Schofield said. "You can't be half in, half out. If Harry and Meghan are determined to recreate that arrangement through the back door, Charles may eventually have to remind them why the front door was closed."
Queen Elizabeth II, England's longest-reigning monarch, died in 2022. She was 96. (Toby Melville - WPA Pool/Getty Images)

Andersen noted that the king is "weary of having to deal with all this drama" and of being "a sort of referee between his sons." However, Andersen said, the king may ultimately have little choice but to act if the Sussexes continue to blur the line between private citizens and working royals.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex, sits in the stands during the Gallagher PREM 2026/2027 match between Leicester Tigers and Gloucester Rugby at Mattioli Woods Welford Road Stadium on Oct. 9, 2026, in Leicester, England. (Getty Images)

"Anything that looks like an official royal engagement will definitely be interpreted as defying the monarch’s wishes, pure and simple," Andersen warned. "The queen’s decree was that members of the royal family are either all in or all out. And the king is determined to fulfill his mother’s wishes."
Meghan, Duchess of Sussex and Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex visit Epic Partners during their visit to Nottingham on Oct. 15, 2026, in Nottingham, England.  ( Joe Giddens - Pool/Getty Images)
Fox News Digital reached out to Buckingham Palace and Archewell for comment.

Meghan, Duchess of Sussex visits the Hubb Community Kitchen to see how funds raised by the 'Together: Our Community' Cookbook are making a difference at Al Manaar in North Kensington, London, England, on Nov. 21, 2018. (Samir Hussein/WireImage)
A source told People magazine that the Sussexes are "both excited to focus more on their work and the projects that matter to them."
Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex, poses for a selfie with well-wishers after a visit to Community Recording Studio in Nottingham, central England, on Sept. 9, 2025. (POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

The outlet reported that while the Sussexes reunited with King Charles and Queen Camilla in July, they are not believed to have seen the king in person since moving back to Britain. According to People, Harry and his father have remained in contact by phone. Harry and his older brother, Prince William, reportedly haven't spoken in years. A palace insider told the outlet that the rift between the brothers has only been "magnified" by Harry's return to the U.K.
Meghan, Duchess of Sussex and Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex visit Epic Partners during their visit to Nottingham on Oct. 15, 2026, in Nottingham, England. (Joe Giddens - Pool/Getty Images)

Royal broadcaster Ian Pelham Turner told Fox News Digital that, as private citizens, Harry and Meghan have the freedom to pursue their own projects without requiring the blessing of the king or the Prince of Wales.
Prince William, Prince of Wales, attends Earthshot's "Cricket On The Mall" on Oct. 13, 2026, in London. (Getty Images)

"There are suspicions that Harry and Meghan are trying to create an alternative royal family," he said. "Their first joint event together has raised eyebrows in some royal circles. But as they are now private citizens, 'The Firm' have very little, if any, power over them. This, in some ways, could be a blessing for Harry and Meghan and a curse for those in royal circles."

Meghan Markle visits Nottingham Contemporary on Dec. 1, 2017, in Nottingham, England. The visit came shortly after she and Prince Harry announced their engagement on Nov. 27, 2017. (Samir Hussein/WireImage)
Schofield said the Sussexes can't control how the palace will react, particularly if people within the palace believe the couple's plans disrespect the late queen.
"What should concern the king is the growing frustration among royal supporters who want to see him take a more assertive approach towards his youngest son and daughter-in-law," Schofield said.

Britain's King Charles III reacts to the heat during a visit to the humid climate of the "Giants of the Galapagos" enclosure at ZSL London Zoo to celebrate the zoo's 200th anniversary in central London on July 9, 2026. (Richard Pohle / POOL / AFP via Getty Images)

"King Charles may believe that silence is the most dignified response, but there comes a point when restraint risks being mistaken for weakness. The monarchy doesn’t need to compete with Harry and Meghan for publicity, but it does need to protect the integrity of royal service and the distinction between working royals and private citizens."

King Charles III inspects the Balaklava Company, 5th Battalion, The Royal Regiment of Scotland, at the gates of Balmoral, on Aug. 18, 2026. (PA Images via Getty Images)

"After years of telling the world how miserable royal life made them, they’re desperately returning to the very formula they abandoned," Schofield reflected. "Hollywood was supposed to offer them something bigger and better. Instead, they appear to be discovering that the royal connection was their greatest asset all along."

title: Canadian singer Joni Mitchell officially becomes American citizen after 62-year journey
summary: Joni Mitchell shared a photo and video from her naturalization ceremony, becoming a U.S. citizen at 82 while retaining Canadian citizenship.
story: Country music superstar Chris Janson joins 'Fox & Friends' at Liberty House in Jersey City, N.J., for the America 250 celebration. Janson articulates his profound patriotism, stating he's 'never been shy' about loving the flag, troops and freedom.
Joni Mitchell has officially become an American citizen at age 82, more than six decades after she first moved to the United States.
The music icon, who hails from Canada, announced the news on Instagram, sharing a photo of herself beaming while holding an American flag along with a video from her naturalization ceremony.
"A journey that began 62 years ago," Mitchell wrote in the caption of her post.
Joni Mitchell has become a U.S. citizen after 62 years in America. (Joni Mitchell Instagram)
ART GARFUNKEL JOINS GROWING LIST OF CELEBRITIES CONSIDERING A MOVE ABROAD OVER TRUMP PRESIDENCY

Mitchell wore a red and navy blue floral cardigan that had an American flag pin along with a red beaded necklace, a red beret and black pants with black boots while posing in between an American flag and a Department of Homeland Security flag.
In the video Mitchell uploaded, she was seated in the front row at the ceremony as the speaker announced, "And Joni Mitchell, Canada" to cheers and applause from the audience.
According to KSL, Mitchell will also retain her Canadian citizenship because the U.S. and Canada legally permit dual citizenship.
The legendary singer-songwriter was born Roberta Joan Anderson in Fort Macleod, Alberta, to Royal Canadian Air Force flight Lt. William Andrew Anderson and teacher Myrtle Marguerite.

Mitchell's family lived on several bases during World War II before eventually settling in Saskatoon, which the singer has often referred to as her hometown. She went on to attend the Alberta College of Art in Calgary before dropping out and relocating to Toronto, where she played gigs at coffee houses and folk clubs.

The "Both Sides Now" songstress moved to the United States in 1965 at age 21 after marrying American folk singer Chuck Mitchell. The former couple, who lived in Detroit, Michigan, performed together as a folk duo before divorcing in 1967.
The legendary singer-songwriter was born in Canada and moved to the U.S. in 1965. (Getty Images)
After their divorce, Mitchell left Detroit and moved to New York City, where she became part of the Greenwich Village folk scene and performed along the East Coast.

By 1968, Mitchell moved to Los Angeles, settling in Laurel Canyon, which was becoming a hub for singer-songwriters including David Crosby, Graham Nash and others. In the mid-1970s, Mitchell moved to LA's Bel Air neighborhood, where she lived in a historic 1920s home for decades.
Mitchell built her legendary music career while living in California, where she recorded many of her most acclaimed albums, including "Blue," "Court and Spark" and "Ladies of the Canyon."
Mitchell has won 11 Grammy Awards and was inducted into both the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame and the Songwriters Hall of Fame in 1997.
Mitchell lived in Detroit before moving to New York City and then Los Angeles. (Redferns)
She was also recognized with the Kennedy Center Honors in 2021 and received the prestigious Library of Congress Gershwin Prize for Popular Song in 2023.
The musician lives in Santa Barbara, California.
Mitchell is an outspoken critic of President Donald Trump and expressed frustration that she couldn't vote in U.S. elections because she was Canadian.
CHRIS ROBINSON, BRUCE SPRINGSTEEN FACE BACKLASH AS 'AMERICANS HAVE HAD ENOUGH' OF BEING LECTURED: EXPERT
She has won 11 Grammy Awards.  (Getty Images)
During a performance at the Hollywood Bowl in LA in October 2024, Mitchell slammed Trump while performing her 1985 song "Dog Eat Dog," according to Billboard.
After singing a lyric about wealthy financiers, she added, "Like Donald Trump!"
Following her performance of the song, Mitchell responded to an audience member who shouted an anti-Trump remark.
"'F--- Donald Trump.' I love that song," she said, apparently referencing rapper YG's 2016 protest song "FDT (F--- Donald Trump)" featuring the late rapper and activist Nipsey Hussle.
Mitchell is an outspoken critic of President Donald Trump.  (Alex Wong/Getty Images)
She then encouraged Americans to participate in the 2024 U.S. presidential election, in which Trump ran against Democratic nominee former Vice President Kamala Harris.
"Everybody get out and vote. This is an important one. I wish I could vote . I'm Canadian. I'm one of those lousy immigrants," Mitchell said.
Months before becoming an American citizen, Mitchell criticized the political climate in the U.S. while accepting a lifetime achievement award at Canada's Juno Awards in March.
The 2012 Kennedy Honors recipient slammed Trump at a concert in 2024. (Getty Images)
At the ceremony, Mitchell praised Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, saying, "I'm so glad to be back in Canada. This man is a blessing. You guys are so fortunate."

She also appeared to take a swipe at the Trump administration while contrasting Canada with the U.S.
"I'm living in the states, and you know what's happening there," she said.
After Mitchell's comments at the Juno Awards, the White House issued a dismissive response.

When asked about her remarks, White House spokesperson Davis Ingle told The Independent, "Who the hell is Joni Mitchell?"

title: John Stamos says Beach Boys legend Mike Love is facing 'serious health challenges'
summary: John Stamos revealed Mike Love is facing serious health challenges, but the Beach Boys legend insisted on performing at the Ryman over the weekend.
story: ‘Full House’ star John Stamos told Fox News Digital he ‘made sure’ Mike Love performed at the Ryman amid health challenges.
John Stamos performed with the Beach Boys on Sunday at the Ryman Auditorium in Nashville.
Before the show, the actor was overcome with emotion talking about Beach Boys legend Mike Love, who is facing "serious health challenges."
Stamos, 63, shared a carousel of images on social media with his "musical hero and mentor" before admitting he was "struggling" to put his feelings into words.
ROD STEWART CONFIRMS FINAL TOUR AFTER HEART PROCEDURE AND HEALTH SCARES

"My beloved friend, father figure, musical hero and mentor, Mike Love, is facing serious health challenges," he wrote. "We hope he’ll be doing what he loves for years to come, but we don’t know what the future holds. We have tonight."
At Tuesday's Hot Cuisine fundraiser for the Scleroderma Research Foundation (SRF), Stamos told Fox News Digital it was his mission to get Love to the Ryman Auditorium for a performance of a lifetime.
John Stamos shared an emotional update about Beach Boys legend Mike Love before the Nashville performance. (John Lamparski)

"Our goal was to get him up at the Ryman this weekend. He wanted it," Stamos said. "I've been spending a lot of time with him, you know, quiet time. We've been listening to music. … Doo-wop. He loves Doo-Wop.
"And I said, ‘You gotta tell me, do you really think you can do these shows this weekend?’ He said, ‘Yes, and I really want to.’ I said, 'We'll make it happen.'

"Everybody told him not to — doctors, his family — but it was something he wanted to do. He's made all my dreams come true and all my wishes. So, I had to fulfill his wish, and we made sure that he got there and did a good job."

SRF presented John Stamos with the Bob Saget Legacy Award, recognizing his steadfast support for scleroderma research and his commitment to following in Bob’s footsteps by shining a spotlight on scleroderma and raising funds toward a cure.
Love's representatives did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. It's unclear what health struggles Love faces.
Stamos and Love's son, Brian Love, delivered speeches prior to the show.
"One thing about him is he's stubborn, and he's steadfast, and he did not want to miss the Ryman. I mean, for good reason," Brian said, via Variety.

"Look at this place. So, we are happy. We're going to be positive. We're gonna sing along. But I still remember something he told me when I was a child, and it stuck with me. I said, ‘Dad, why do you do so many shows?’ I mean, we are talking about a guy who's done over 100 concerts a year well up into his 80s."

"That's just incredible, right? So, he told me, ‘Well, if you don’t do as many concerts, you don't see as many towns, and then that means less people get to hear the amazing Beach Boys personally.' So, he's always cared for the small towns, the fairs. … This is obviously a much more well-known, beautiful venue. But he cares about the listener, and I think it's such an honor to be part of that. And we've gotta live in the moment."

Stamos said, "All we have is tonight really, and I think it's going to be very, very special. Mike, he insisted on being here. … He's done over 7,000 live shows. And tonight'll be 7,422, I think exactly. I think that's where we're at. He's counting. … We love you, and have the greatest night ever, and God bless you all."
After the curtains opened, Love was already seated on stage, the outlet reported.
He sang in his seat along with his bandmates but did not do his lead vocals.

During the performance, the Beach Boys legend addressed concerns about his health, saying, "Obviously, I’ve been going through some health issues for quite a while. But I didn’t want to miss being at the Ryman with y’all."
Variety reported that Love was helped up by Brian and Stamos at the end of the show as the song "We Are The Champions" by Queen played.
JON BON JOVI ABRUPTLY ENDS MADISON SQUARE GARDEN SHOW AFTER HEALTH SETBACK
In his social media post, Stamos acknowledged that Love "is a fighter," and despite "doctors, family and friends urging him to focus on his health, he insists on being on stage."

"He says he needs his band, the audience, his friends and drummer surrounding him to lift him up," Stamos wrote. "I’ve played with Mike for 41 years. I never imagined how deeply it would affect me to see someone larger than life face something so human and fragile."
Love and Stamos performing on the Palomino Stage on the final day of Stagecoach Country Music Festival at the Empire Polo Club in Indio. (Allen J. Schaben/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)
The Beach Boys have been touring in support of the 60th anniversary of their groundbreaking 11th studio album, "Pet Sounds."
Stamos noted that "the Mike Love we see tonight may not be exactly the Mike we’ve always known. But he’s still every bit the Mike we love."

John Stamos has performed with the Beach Boys for more than four decades. (Vinnie Zuffante)
"Forty-one years of stages, airplanes, hotel rooms, laughter and moments nobody else saw. He married Caitlin and me. He’s shared experiences with my family, and now my son."
The "Full House" star noted that Love didn't only give him a spot in the band. He "gave me a place in his life."

The Beach Boys (L-R) — Carl Wilson, Bruce Johnston, Brian Wilson, Mike Love and Al Jardine — pose for a portrait session May 1, 1987, in Los Angeles. (Harry Langdon/Getty Images)

title: Ethan Hawke blasts Hollywood's 'greedy bastards,' predicts massive rebellion against powerful elites
summary: Ethan Hawke predicts massive rebellion in music and live theater against Hollywood's "greedy bastards" who he says control the entertainment industry.
story: Ethan Hawke celebrates Willie Nelson’s 90th birthday and tells Fox News Digital ‘a lot of people disagree, but a lot of people can agree about Willie Nelson’
Ethan Hawke isn't holding back when it comes to the powerful forces he believes are controlling the entertainment industry.

During a new interview with GQ, the Oscar-nominated actor took aim at wealthy power players, blasting "greedy bastards" who think they control every aspect of Hollywood and predicting a major rebellion against the industry.

"I believe in rebellion. And I think people are going to wake up and punch back and there’s going to be massive movements in music and massive movements in live theater and massive movements of people getting together," Hawke said.
FROM ‘SCREAM’ TO STREAM: JAMIE KENNEDY REVEALS HOW HOLLYWOOD LOST ITS WAY AND WHY HE WON'T GIVE UP ON LA
Ethan Hawke spoke about the "greedy bastards" who believe they control Hollywood. (Getty Images)

"So don’t worry that the money and the greedy bastards that think they control everybody, they always lose in the end," he continued. "And they’re all going in the grave eventually. They think they’re winning, but they’re losing because their lives are worthless."
Hawke also expressed frustration with the financial pressures shaping Hollywood, arguing that the projects actors care about most often come with the smallest paychecks.
TRUMP, SCHIFF FORGE UNLIKELY ALLIANCE AS HOLLYWOOD BLEEDS JOBS
"There's a direct correlation. I find that the more you love a project, the less you get paid," he said. "If you want to beat the algorithm, it's very difficult to do that and be paid."
Hawke found fame at a young age. (Matt Winkelmeyer/Getty Images)
This isn't the first time Hawke has spoken about the pitfalls of Hollywood.
ROBERT DOWNEY JR. SLAMS MODERN CELEBRITY CULTURE AS 'ABSOLUTE HORSES---'
Last year, the actor called celebrity a "poison" for a young actor's brain.
During an appearance on "The Joe Rogan Experience," Hawke got candid about his start in Hollywood as a young man and reflected on the psychological effect of becoming famous at a young age.

"I think celebrity is like a tiny drop of mercury. Or it's poison. It's poison for your brain," the actor said. "To be a professional actor at a young age, it's dangerous in extremely insidious ways that are very, very hard to perceive when it's happening," Hawke said.

Rogan compared the experience of becoming famous as a child to concrete. If concrete is made incorrectly, with the wrong amount of water or cement, that's it, he explained. Rogan added that once it dries there is no way to repair or fix it.
Ethan Hawke at the 2026 BAFTAs on Feb. 22. (Getty Images)
DISNEY ALUM CHRISTY CARLSON ROMANO RIPS HOLLYWOOD FOR FAILING CHILD STARS AFTER HAYDEN PANETTIERE’S DEATH

"That analogy works for all walks of life. Really. If you have something really traumatic happen in childhood, it's very hard to recover. It's a tremendous amount of work to recover. And I agree with you, like I think celebrity is like a tiny drop of mercury. Or it's a poison. It's a poison for your brain," Hawke said.
During his GQ interview, Hawke expressed the same sentiment.

"I wouldn’t be the first person to say that there’s an aspect of celebrity that is like a disease," he said. "And you can handle little bits of it, but too much of it — we can see what happened to Elvis and we can see Michael Jackson. It’s a form of isolation. It’s like being put in a zoo, and zoo animals go nuts. So do human beings."

"And it seems like a kind of nice isolation because people are giving you money, and they’re telling you you’re wonderful, but nobody’s being real with you," he continued. "And that makes people insane. And they start scratching, trying to find some real life. And sometimes people do that with drugs, some people do that with acting out or getting in fights or whatever the ways that people do it."
Hawke once referred to celebrity as a "poison." (Gareth Cattermole/Getty Images for BFI)
Last year, fellow actor Dakota Johnson also ripped into Hollywood, calling the industry an absolute "mess."
During her appearance on the show "Hot Ones," Johnson was asked why "Hollywood is risk-averse."

"I think it’s hard when creative decisions are made by a committee, and it’s hard when creative decisions are made by people who don’t even really watch movies or know anything about them … that tends to be what’s occurring a lot," Johnson shared with host Sean Evans.
Johnson, who has grown up in the business as the daughter of actors Melanie Griffith and Don Johnson, is no stranger to the inner workings of Hollywood.
The "Fifty Shades of Grey" actress’ comments come as studios continue to create sequels and remakes, with original storytelling often sidelined.
Actress Dakota Johnson called Hollywood an absolute "mess." (Photo by Christopher Polk/CBS via Getty Images)

"When something does well … studios want to keep that going so they remake the same things," she claimed. "But humans don’t want that. They want fresh. They want to feel new things, experience new things, see new things."
She added, "So I don’t know, I guess it’s all just a bit of a mess right now, isn’t it?"

title: Leonardo DiCaprio's 'dad bod' puts spotlight on dangerous belly fat — and how to lose it
summary: Leonardo DiCaprio's beach photos sparked a 'dad bod' debate, as a trainer warns that excess belly fat and visceral fat carry serious health risks.
story: Marfred Suazo, a New York City-based personal trainer known as Fonz the Trainer, spoke with Fox News Digital about the potential risks associated with excess abdominal fat and ways to reduce it.
Recent beach photos of actor Leonardo DiCaprio have reignited the "dad bod" debate — and raised questions about whether carrying a little extra weight around the middle can pose hidden health risks.
The popular term generally describes a softer physique with extra weight around the midsection.

While appearance alone isn’t an indicator of health, excess abdominal fat — particularly visceral fat surrounding the organs — has been linked to an increased risk of heart disease, diabetes and other medical conditions, according to Cleveland Clinic.
YOUR WAISTLINE COULD REVEAL A HIDDEN HEART RISK YOUR BMI MISSES, MAJOR STUDY FINDS
Marfred Suazo, a New York City-based personal trainer known as Fonz the Trainer, spoke with Fox News Digital about the potential risks associated with excess abdominal fat and ways to reduce it.
Suazo, who has not trained DiCaprio, defines a dad bod as a "loss of structure," an increase in waist circumference and a loss of muscle mass.
Leonardo DiCaprio, 51, soaks up the Hawaiian sunshine as he enjoys a beach day at the luxurious Four Seasons Resort Lanai. The photos have reignited the "dad bod" debate. (BACKGRID)
"Maybe you're losing structure in your day-to-day eating … moving a lot less, taking fewer steps per day," he said of potential causes.
"And typically you're eating and drinking more than you're moving. And the body just starts showcasing that stuff."
BEST FOODS FOR REDUCING DANGEROUS BELLY FAT AND PROTECTING HEART HEALTH
An expanding waistline can be an important indicator of health risk.

According to the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases, men with a waist circumference greater than 40 inches have a higher risk of developing health problems, including type 2 diabetes and heart disease.

Marfred Suazo, a New York City-based personal trainer known as Fonz the Trainer, spoke with Fox News Digital about the potential risks associated with excess abdominal fat and ways to reduce it. (Fox News Digital)
Visceral fat — which lies deep within the abdomen and surrounds internal organs — has also been linked to a higher risk of cardiovascular disease, Cleveland Clinic states.
"We want to try to mitigate these things as best as possible before they become an issue," Suazo said.
Getting rid of a dad bod
Reversing a "dad bod" starts with getting nutrition in check, according to Suazo.
That includes understanding daily calorie intake and getting an appropriate balance of protein, carbohydrates and fats.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

He recommends pairing that strategy with full-body strength training two to three times per week, focusing on compound movements such as squats, stiff-leg deadlifts, back rows, push-ups and chest presses.

Also among his favorite exercises are pull-ups. "It’s a tremendous exercise that targets the stomach, the biceps and the back," he said, noting that working larger muscle groups can help build overall strength.
An expanding waistline can be an important indicator of health risk, experts say. (Getty Images)
Suazo also recommends incorporating cardio into a well-rounded routine that includes nutrition, strength training and cardiovascular exercise.

Federal physical activity guidelines recommend that adults get at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity or 75 minutes of vigorous activity each week, along with muscle-strengthening exercise on at least two days.

The trainer noted, however, that exercising the abdominal muscles alone won't eliminate belly fat.
"When it comes to belly fat and any fat on the body, we can target our exercises through isolated movements … but we can only reveal it through a loss of body fat throughout the whole body," he said.

"When it comes to belly fat and any fat on the body, we can target our exercises through isolated movements … but we can only reveal it through a loss of body fat throughout the whole body," the trainer said. (BACKGRID)
Suazo said people who improve their nutrition may begin noticing changes within several weeks, although results can vary based on factors including diet, activity level and starting body composition.

"Upon four weeks of dialing in your nutrition, you will see a tremendous change in the body," he said.
Nutritional improvements can also boost energy and confidence, the trainer noted, which may help people become more consistent in the gym.

Better nutrition can also support sleep and exercise recovery, he said.
Combining those dietary changes with a smart exercise routine and cardio can create a "recipe for success," according to Suazo.

title: Brain-infecting fungus that can kill 7 in 10 patients is on the rise across America
summary: Cladophialophora bantiana, a neurotropic black mold with a 60%-70% fatality rate, surged nearly fourfold in U.S. detections between 2023 and 2025.
story: Dr. Jeffrey Kahn, chief of pediatric infectious diseases at UT Southwestern and Children's Health in Dallas, Texas, says Naegleria fowleri is rare, but nearly 100% fatal.
A rare fungal infection that can strike healthy people is rising across the U.S., prompting calls from public health officials for heightened awareness and national tracking.

Cladophialophora bantiana (C. bantiana) is a black yeast-like mold that can infect the brain and contains a dark pigment called melanin, according to a new report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
Data from a microbiology laboratory at the University of Washington shows that detection of the fungus nearly quadrupled between 2023 and 2025.
LOUISIANA GIRL, 8, DIES AFTER CONTRACTING SUSPECTED BRAIN-EATING AMOEBA LINKED TO LAKE SWIM

Between January 2009 and July 2026, researchers identified 48 confirmed cases and one probable case of C. bantiana in tissue samples from 21 states and the District of Columbia. The median patient age was 68 years old.
Unlike many fungal infections that mainly affect people with weakened immune systems, about half of C. bantiana infections occur in otherwise healthy people.
Cladophialophora bantiana (C. bantiana) is a black yeast-like mold that can infect the brain and contains a dark pigment called melanin, according to a CDC report. (iStock)
Researchers believe the mold enters the body when it is inhaled or through a skin wound, then travels through the bloodstream to the brain.

The CDC report states that 88% of cases were detected in brain tissue samples and 12% were identified in lung tissue, supporting the theory that respiratory inhalation is one of the main transmission mechanisms.
DEADLY ‘FOX TAPEWORM’ LINKED TO LETHAL DISEASE DETECTED IN WEST COAST WILDLIFE
The fungus causes a severe infection associated with a 60% to 70% fatality rate, even with aggressive medical intervention, according to a systematic review published in Medical Mycology.

The pathogen has historically been rare, with the University of Washington laboratory identifying only one to five cases per year between 2009 and 2023. However, the CDC says annual cases surged to eight in 2024 and reached 14 in 2025.
Public health officials are urging clinicians to consider fungal pathogens when evaluating brain abscesses and calling for national case reporting to better track the surge. (AP Photo/Jeff Amy, File)
To make sure the increase wasn’t simply due to more testing, researchers compared the number of infections with the total number of brain tissue samples tested for fungi.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
They found that detections rose from 8.4 cases per 1,000 specimens during 2017–2023 to 26 cases per 1,000 specimens in 2025.
"Reasons for the apparent increase are unknown," the CDC report stated, calling for systematic national reporting mechanisms to better track the pathogen.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Cases were reported across a wide geographic range, with the highest counts originating in California (six), Florida (five), Texas (five) and Pennsylvania (four).
Standard tests like spinal taps may miss the fungus, meaning doctors sometimes need to take a tissue sample through surgery to confirm the diagnosis. (iStock)
Because C. bantiana typically manifests as a brain abscess without clear external signs of infection, experts say early diagnosis is challenging.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

In one documented fatal case at the University of Washington Medical Center, spinal fluid PCR tests returned negative results both one month prior to and at the time of a brain biopsy, highlighting the difficulty of detecting the mold.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Public health experts advise clinicians to consider C. bantiana when evaluating patients who have signs of a brain abscess.
Treatment typically involves surgery to remove the infected tissue, along with multiple antifungal medications.

title: Pope Leo XIV seen for first time since lung cancer surgery amid major recovery milestone
summary: The Vatican released first photos of Pope Leo XIV celebrating mass at Gemelli Hospital, days after surgeons removed a lung lobe due to adenocarcinoma.
story: Dr. Lary Robinson, an oncologist at Moffitt Cancer Center in Tampa, Florida, reacts to the pope's diagnosis and how lung cancer can occur in never-smokers.
Pope Leo XIV is up and moving after having part of his lung removed.

After undergoing thoracic surgery Tuesday, during which surgeons removed the lower lobe of the pope’s right lung, examination of the tissue confirmed a diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, or lung cancer, according to the Vatican.
The pope, 71, has spent four days recovering at Gemelli Hospital in Rome, Italy, after the successful procedure.

Pope Leo plans to make his first public appearance since the procedure on Sunday during the noon Angelus, which he normally leads.
NEVER SMOKED A CIGARETTE? YOU COULD STILL BE AT HIGHER RISK FOR LUNG CANCER

title: Pope Leo's lung tumor raises questions about cancer risk for nonsmokers
summary: An oncologist says Pope Leo XIV has a roughly 90% chance of cure if the lung cancer is stage 1, but pathology results will determine next steps.
story: Dr. Lary Robinson, an oncologist at Moffitt Cancer Center in Tampa, Florida, reacts to the pope's diagnosis and how lung cancer can occur in never-smokers.
Pope Leo XIV has been diagnosed with lung cancer after a scheduled surgery, the Vatican announced Tuesday.
After undergoing thoracic surgery, where surgeons removed the lower lobe of the pope’s right lung, examination of the tissue confirmed the diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma.
The diagnosis had been suspected based on testing conducted before the procedure, according to the Holy See Press Office.
POPE LEO DIAGNOSED WITH LUNG CANCER AFTER SURGEONS REMOVE PART OF RIGHT LUNG, VATICAN SAYS
The pope reportedly does not smoke and does not have a known history of smoking. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention indicates that most lung cancer deaths (80%) are caused by smoking.

Lung adenocarcinoma is the most common type of lung cancer, representing about 40% of all lung cancers in the U.S., according to the Lung Cancer Foundation of America. It is also the most common type among non-smokers.
NEVER SMOKED A CIGARETTE? YOU COULD STILL BE AT HIGHER RISK FOR LUNG CANCER

In an interview with Fox News Digital, Lary Robinson, M.D., an oncologist at Moffitt Cancer Center in Tampa, Florida, shared his surprise regarding the pope’s health status, as the lung nodule was "felt to be malignant."

About 80% of lung cancers occur in people who smoke or have smoked, said Robinson, who has not treated the pope. However, he noted that lung cancer also occurs among never-smokers — including an estimated 10% of male patients and 25% of female patients.
Newly elected Pope Leo XIV, Cardinal Robert F. Prevost of the U.S., appears on the balcony of St. Peter's Basilica at the Vatican, on May 8, 2025. (Dylan Martinez/Reuters)

"But [the pope] had surgery and had a lobectomy, so this is usually only done with people who have localized disease, and presumably he had localized disease. And hopefully that's a stage 1 cancer," the doctor added.

If the pope’s cancer is stage 1, there is a "high chance" of cure — about 90%, depending on the size of the tumor, the oncologist said. The fact that he went straight to surgery suggests there was likely no evidence that the cancer had spread.
HEALTHY DIETS SPARK LUNG CANCER RISK IN NON-SMOKERS AS PESTICIDES LOOM
"We'll have to wait for the pathology to determine … whether he had a stage 1 cancer and whether he needs any additional treatment afterward," Robinson said.
"Size matters in lung nodules and lung cancer – the larger the cancer, the worse outlook it is, because it's more likely to be advanced and have spread."
Not all lung cancer cases are caused by smoking, according to experts. (iStock)
Risk factors for never-smokers
Not all lung cancer cases are caused by smoking. Other factors like family history and genetic predisposition can play a role, experts say.

Recent research discovered that a rare genetic mutation in the gene EGFR T790M increased lung cancer risk by 25 times compared with people who did not have the mutation, according to findings published in the journal Science.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Among people who had never smoked, carriers of the mutation had about 62 times the odds of lung cancer compared with never-smokers who were not carriers.
Family history and environmental exposures can increase lung cancer risk. (iStock)
Robinson added that other types of smoking, like pipes and cigars, can increase the risk of lung cancer, as well as heavy use of marijuana.
Another risk factor is exposure to environmental toxins, such as diesel exhaust and radon, according to the oncologist.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"Unfortunately, probably over half of the people who are never-smokers with lung cancer come into stage 4 disease," Robinson said. "And that's higher than people who are smokers or former smokers, so they start out at a worse stage in general."
Symptoms and screening

In most cases, early-stage lung cancer will not come with any symptoms, according to Robinson. In those who do have symptoms, however, the most common are related to the lungs, including a persistent cough, shortness of breath or coughing up blood.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Unexplained weight loss can result from any form of cancer, the oncologist noted. Neurological symptoms, like persistent headaches, may also warrant seeing a doctor.
The most common symptoms are related to the lungs, including a persistent cough, shortness of breath or coughing up blood. (iStock)
Lung cancer is rare in younger adults, which is why annual CT screening is generally recommended starting at age 50 for those at high risk, the doctor said.
People considered at high risk include current smokers with at least a 20 pack-year history, as well as former smokers who quit within the past 15 years.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"Only about 15% of the people who are eligible get screened, unfortunately," Robinson said.

"I'm hoping that within four or five years, a screening CT scan will only be confirmatory after they have a positive blood test done at your doctor's office." That approach could make screening easier and potentially help detect more lung cancers, according to the doctor.
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Experimental skin cream linked to 2-year drop in biological age in early study
summary: Rubedo Life Sciences says its skin cream RLS-1496 cleared senescent cells, boosted collagen 10% and reduced skin age in a four-week trial study.
story: Fox News correspondent Alexandria Hoff reports on viral beauty and longevity trends gaining popularity through social media influencers on ‘Special Report.’
An experimental skin cream altered molecular markers associated with aging and inflammation in an early human trial, according to preliminary data released by its developer this week.
Rubedo Life Sciences, a biotechnology company based in Mountain View, California, tested its investigational treatment, RLS-1496, in patients with eczema and other skin conditions.

In an analysis of 11 paired skin samples from patients with atopic dermatitis, researchers reported that four weeks of treatment was associated with an average 2.1-year decrease in measured epigenetic skin age, an estimate based on age-related changes in DNA.
3 COMMON FACTORS MAY BE SECRETLY SPEEDING UP THE AGING PROCESS, EXPERT SAYS
Rubedo CEO Dr. Frederick Beddingfield said the "significant" early findings warrant further investigation.

"This is one of the few drugs developed for aging in general and with AI to show positive data in humans in multiple indications and to show a reduction in skin age," Beddingfield told Fox News Digital.
An early human trial found that a novel topical treatment, RLS-1496, reduced measured epigenetic skin age by an average of 2.1 years after four weeks of daily use. (iStock)
He believes the early results will translate into "clinical improvements with longer-term treatment."
The latest skin-aging findings have been presented at a scientific conference but have not yet been published as a full peer-reviewed study.
SCIENTISTS UNVEIL 'LIVING BANDAGE' THAT COULD DRAMATICALLY SPEED WOUND HEALING
RLS-1496 is designed to target senescent cells, aging or damaged cells that have stopped dividing but can release substances that promote inflammation.
The drug targets a protein called GPX4, which helps cells respond to stress. Researchers are studying whether blocking it can clear away damaged, aging cells while helping healthier cells survive.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Beddingfield described the approach as targeting cellular aging rather than simply treating its outward effects.
"It's a bit like 'what does not kill you makes you stronger' for those surviving cells," he added.
Tissue analysis from the study showed a 10% increase in structural collagen alongside decreased inflammatory markers circulating in the blood. (iStock)

Skin samples showed a 10% increase in a type of collagen that helps support the skin, according to the company. Blood tests also showed lower levels of several markers linked to inflammation, although it is not yet clear what those changes mean for patients' health.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

The preliminary findings come with several limitations. The skin-aging analysis included just 11 paired samples and measured biological signs of aging in the skin rather than whether the skin actually looked younger or functioned better.

Treatment lasted only four weeks, so it is not known whether the changes will persist. The studies were sponsored by Rubedo, and the latest skin-aging findings have not yet been published as a full peer-reviewed study.
"Our next trial will treat for several months," Beddingfield said.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

The treatment is also being tested for other skin issues. In a separate early-stage study of 22 patients with actinic keratosis, rough, precancerous skin patches caused by sun exposure, the company reported a 49% average reduction in lesions after 28 days of treatment.
The open-label study compared treated forearms with untreated forearms rather than a placebo cream.
While FDA prescription approval is projected to take three to four years, non-prescription cosmetic formulations utilizing similar mechanisms could hit the market within a year. (iStock)
The cream caused minimal skin irritation, and the drug was detected in the blood of very few participants, according to the company.

"With topical application, we have seen very little risk," Beddingfield said. "Local irritation is rarely seen and generally mild when it occurs, and no one has discontinued treatment to date. Very few subjects show any drug in their blood after skin application."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Rubedo is also beginning an early-stage trial of RLS-1496 for androgenetic alopecia, or pattern hair loss.
Beddingfield estimated that potential FDA approval remains three to four years away, pending larger clinical trials.

title: Weight-loss drugs may fight 7 serious health problems before the pounds even come off
summary: GLP-1 medications like semaglutide and tirzepatide may be repairing joints, calming inflammation, and protecting vital organs before any weight loss occurs.
story: Sai Yendamuri, M.D., a thoracic surgeon at Roswell Park Comprehensive Cancer Center in Buffalo, New York, speaks to Fox News Digital about whether weight-loss drugs could reduce cancer risk.
GLP-1 medications may provide health benefits that extend beyond weight loss, according to a growing body of research.
From reducing cardiovascular risks to potentially easing joint pain and inflammation, studies suggest these drugs may affect multiple systems throughout the body.
Here are seven potential benefits beyond shedding pounds.
POPULAR WEIGHT-LOSS STRATEGY SHOWS SURPRISING POTENTIAL FOR CHRONIC PAIN RELIEF
No. 1: Protecting heart health
Research suggests semaglutide — the active ingredient in Ozempic and Wegovy — may provide cardiovascular benefits beyond those associated with weight loss.

A major study published in The Lancet found that semaglutide reduced the risk of heart attacks, strokes and cardiovascular death among people with existing cardiovascular disease and overweight or obesity. The benefits were observed across different body weights and were not fully explained by weight loss.
Semaglutide has been shown to reduce cardiovascular risks, with benefits that appear to extend beyond weight loss. (iStock)
No. 2: Reducing joint pain and improving mobility
GLP-1 medications have been linked to reduced joint pain, although researchers are still investigating how much of the benefit comes from weight loss versus other effects.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

The STEP 9 clinical trial, published in the New England Journal of Medicine, found that semaglutide significantly reduced knee osteoarthritis pain and improved physical function among adults with obesity.
Research suggests GLP-1 medications may help reduce knee osteoarthritis pain, although their ability to repair damaged cartilage has not been established. (iStock)
No. 3: Promoting kidney health
GLP-1 medications may help protect kidney function through several mechanisms, including improvements in blood sugar, blood pressure and inflammation.
GLP-1 BOOM COULD RESHAPE RESTAURANT BARS AS DINERS CUT BACK ON ALCOHOL

In the landmark FLOW trial, published in the New England Journal of Medicine, semaglutide reduced the risk of major kidney-related complications and cardiovascular death by 24% among patients with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease.
No. 4: Reducing liver inflammation and scarring
MASH, or metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis, is a more severe form of fatty liver disease involving inflammation and liver cell damage.
Research suggests GLP-1 medications may help improve liver health, although the extent to which these benefits occur independently of weight loss remains under investigation.
Clinical trials have found that semaglutide can slow the progression of kidney disease in certain patients. (iStock)

A clinical trial published in the New England Journal of Medicine found that semaglutide improved liver tissue findings among patients with MASH, including reductions in inflammation and liver scarring.
Researchers found that 62.9% of semaglutide recipients experienced resolution of MASH without worsening liver fibrosis, compared with 34.3% receiving placebo.
No. 5: Reducing respiratory flare-ups
Real-world research presented at the European Respiratory Society Congress has linked GLP-1 medications to fewer asthma attacks and COPD flare-ups.
Researchers believe the drugs' potential anti-inflammatory effects may play a role, although additional studies are needed to determine whether the medications directly improve respiratory health.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
No. 6: Supporting mental health and curbing addiction
The brain contains GLP-1 receptors in regions involved in regulating appetite, emotions, motivation and responses to rewards.
Emerging research suggests semaglutide may have potential benefits for mental health and addiction.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

An observational study published on the preprint server medRxiv linked semaglutide use to lower rates of substance-related and mood disorders. However, the findings have not been peer-reviewed and do not establish that the medication caused the reductions.
Preliminary research has linked semaglutide use to lower rates of certain substance-related and mood disorders, although further studies are needed. (iStock)
No. 7: Soothing severe skin conditions
GLP-1-based medications are also being investigated for their potential benefits in inflammatory skin conditions, including psoriasis.

A clinical trial published in JAMA Dermatology found that adding tirzepatide to an existing psoriasis treatment improved skin clearance among adults with moderate to severe psoriasis and overweight or obesity.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Researchers are continuing to investigate whether these benefits result from weight loss, reduced inflammation or a combination of factors.
The effects of GLP-1 medications can vary by drug and individual, and patients should consult a healthcare provider about potential risks and benefits.

title: Man claims he went blind after taking Ozempic, shares warning for other users
summary: Todd Engel claims Ozempic caused his total vision loss from NAION and has filed a lawsuit against Novo Nordisk over inadequate drug warnings.
story: Todd Engel, 63, was first prescribed Ozempic in 2023 to help manage his diabetes. Approximately four months later, he was diagnosed with NAION (nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy).
A Maryland man claims that a popular weight-loss drug caused his total vision loss, leaving him legally blind.

Todd Engel, 63, was first prescribed Ozempic in 2023 to help manage his diabetes. The GLP-1 medication, which is approved to treat type 2 diabetes, is also commonly prescribed off-label for weight loss.
Approximately four months after starting the medication, Engel was diagnosed with nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION).
POPULAR WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS FACE NUMEROUS LAWSUITS OVER RARE ‘EYE STROKE’ LINKED TO VISION LOSS
The condition, in which reduced blood flow damages the optic nerve, can cause sudden and permanent vision loss.
A Maryland man, Todd Engel, claims that a popular weight-loss drug caused his total vision loss, leaving him legally blind. (Engel family)

"I first noticed it on New Year's Eve, 2024. I had just gotten out of the shower, was getting ready to go to work. And I said to Shelley, ‘I can't see in my right eye. It's totally black. It's totally dark in my right eye,’" Engel told Fox News Digital during an on-camera interview.
"I was horrified. I was very, very upset that I couldn't see."
DOCTORS REVEAL HIDDEN DANGER FOR SOME OZEMPIC, WEGOVY USERS WITH BRAIN DISORDERS
Engel was referred for further testing, including at Johns Hopkins’ Wilmer Eye Institute. He was told he had suffered an "eye stroke," another term used for NAION.
"The blood work came back in the normal range for me. My blood pressure was fine. They said, ‘You can go back to work,’" he said.
"I didn't go blind — I had my vision taken from me, which was catastrophic to me and to my family."
Engel continued taking Ozempic because, according to the family's account, neither he nor his doctors knew of a possible association between semaglutide and NAION.
About 10 months later, vision loss suddenly occurred in his left eye.
"At that point in time, losing sight in both eyes, there was a tremendous amount of concern," he said.
RAPID WEIGHT LOSS ON POPULAR DRUGS COULD ‘STARVE’ THE BRAIN, EXPERT WARNS
Doctors told Engel there was no medication or surgical procedure that could restore his vision.
Shelley Engel said that medical testing did not identify another common factor beyond Ozempic. Her husband immediately stopped taking the drug after losing vision in his second eye.
At the time of his vision loss, Engel was working for Howard County Highways as a heavy equipment operator and truck driver. (The Engel family)
"I didn't go blind — I had my vision taken from me, which was catastrophic to me and to my family," he said.

Engel has filed a lawsuit against Novo Nordisk, the Denmark-based manufacturer of Ozempic, alleging that the company failed to adequately warn patients and doctors about the potential risk of vision loss.
WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS LINKED TO 'OZEMPIC EARS' AND OTHER COSMETIC COMPLAINTS, SURGEONS SAY
He is among hundreds of patients currently pursuing legal action against makers of GLP-1 medications, including Ozempic and Wegovy, over claims that the drugs caused NAION.

The lawsuits allege that manufacturers failed to provide sufficient warnings about the potential risks, although a causal relationship between the medications and the condition has not been definitively established.
Life after vision loss
At the time of his vision loss, Engel was working for Howard County Highways as a heavy equipment operator and truck driver.
He had worked in the field for about 40 years and held a commercial driver's license for nearly as long.
Beyond losing his career, Engel said even ordinary activities he once took for granted have become difficult. (The Engel family)
"I was extremely mechanically inclined with my hands and in my mind. I can't do that anymore, which is extremely upsetting to me," he said.
"People want to be able to retire on their own accord when they want to, not when a medical catastrophic injury such as this ... takes away your livelihood."
PEOPLE ON WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS REPORT FINGERNAILS FALLING OFF AS RESEARCHERS UNCOVER SURPRISING LINK
Beyond losing his career, Engel said even ordinary activities he once took for granted have become difficult.
An avid reader before his vision loss, Engel said he can no longer read newspapers, magazines or books. Inside his home, he has learned to count steps to help navigate familiar spaces.
7 EVERYDAY MISTAKES COULD BE QUIETLY DAMAGING YOUR VISION, EYE DOCTOR WARNS
"I know that coming in from our parking lot, there are 10 steps ... nine going down into our basement, 13 going up into our bedroom."
Engel said he now uses a white cane to navigate outside his home and relies on his family for help with everyday activities. His four grandchildren often guide him during family gatherings.

Engel is among hundreds of patients currently pursuing legal action against makers of GLP-1 medications, including Ozempic and Wegovy, over claims that the drugs caused NAION. (Michael Siluk/UCG/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)
"They will take me by my hand and talk to me: ‘Pops, three steps straight. Then we're gonna turn right,’" he said.
"For me personally, it's embarrassing. I'm 64 years old. I shouldn't need ... my grandchildren or my wife to help me get from point A to point B."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
His wife, Shelley Engel, said her husband's vision loss has affected the entire family.
"It has completely changed every aspect of our lives," she said. "There is not one piece of our lives that hasn't changed or been touched by this throughout our whole family."

"It has completely changed every aspect of our lives," Engel's wife said. "There is not one piece of our lives that hasn't changed or been touched by this throughout our whole family." (The Engel family)
For Engel, some of the most painful losses involve the things he can no longer do with the people closest to him.
"I will never be able to see my wife's beautiful face again, be able to see children and grandchildren, be able to play ball with them," he said. "And that is very, very upsetting to me."
"I wake up in the dark, I go to sleep in the darkness."
A warning to others
Engel said that if he had been warned about a possible link between Ozempic and vision loss, he would not have taken the drug.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"Had I known, had my doctor had any inkling that this could have happened ... I'm sure he would have asked me and I would have said absolutely not," he said. "I will deal with the diabetes ... I refuse to jeopardize my eyes."

Novo Nordisk has disputed that the medication causes NAION, stating that the available evidence does not establish a causal relationship between semaglutide and the eye condition. (LISELOTTE SABROE/Scanpix Denmark/AFP via Getty Images)
The Engels said they are speaking publicly in hopes of preventing others from experiencing the same outcome.
"Do the research for yourselves to make sure that my catastrophic injuries do not happen to you or anybody else," Engel said. "If we can help one person, then that's a pleasure to Shelley and I."
‘It's about information’
The family's attorney, Jonathan Orent, said the legal team is seeking a warning on the U.S. Ozempic label similar to information provided to patients and doctors in Europe.
Orent is co-lead counsel in nationwide litigation involving GLP-1 drugs, including lawsuits alleging vision loss linked to Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro and Zepbound.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"It's amazing what just a simple warning can do," he told Fox News Digital. "That's really what this case is about. It's about information."
Company response

Novo Nordisk, the Denmark-based company that makes Ozempic, has disputed that the medication causes NAION, stating that the available evidence does not establish a causal relationship between semaglutide and the eye condition.
"Novo believes the personal injury lawsuits filed in the U.S. are without merit and we are defending them in court."

"A causal relationship between GLP-1RAs, including semaglutide, and NAION cannot be confirmed based on the totality of data," Liz Skrbkova, head of U.S. Media and Stakeholder Relations for Novo Nordisk, told Fox News Digital.
The company pointed to an analysis of its randomized, placebo-controlled clinical trials that found very few confirmed cases of NAION and no increased incidence among patients taking semaglutide.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Novo said it continues to monitor NAION as part of its routine drug-safety surveillance.
"Novo believes the personal injury lawsuits filed in the U.S. are without merit, and we are defending them in court," Skrbkova said.
Melissa Rudy is senior health editor and a member of the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to melissa.rudy@fox.com.

title: 10 health conditions may be linked to Alzheimer's years before diagnosis
summary: Depression, vertigo, headaches and stroke were among conditions linked to early-onset Alzheimer's disease years before diagnosis, a Finnish study suggests.
story: Dr. Jeremy Koppel explains the breakthrough blood test for Alzheimer's disease, detailing how it identifies abnormal protein accumulation. He clarifies the test's current role in diagnosing symptomatic individuals.
Certain medical conditions may signal early-onset Alzheimer’s disease several years before diagnosis, a new Finnish study suggests.
Researchers found that depression, vertigo, headaches and other conditions were more common during the five years preceding diagnosis, potentially offering clues for earlier detection.

The researchers analyzed medical records from 407 people with early-onset Alzheimer’s disease and 4,035 people of similar age and sex without the diagnosis, focusing on the 15 years prior to diagnosis.
SUBTLE CHANGE IN HOW YOU SPEAK COULD BE EARLY SIGN OF DEMENTIA RISK, NEW RESEARCH SUGGESTS
The average age at diagnosis was 60. Early-onset disease is diagnosed in people under 65.
The findings were published in the journal Alzheimer’s & Dementia.
Certain medical conditions may signal early-onset Alzheimer’s disease several years before diagnosis, a new study suggests. (iStock)
The following conditions were found to be significantly more prevalent among those who were ultimately diagnosed with early-onset Alzheimer’s.
Vertigo (5.9% of those with diagnosis, vs. 2.1% of those who were not diagnosed)
Depression (5.7% vs. 2.3%)
Headache (4.9% vs. 1.6%)
Stroke (4.4% vs. 2.0%)
Alcohol-related disorders (3.4% vs. 1.4%)
Brain disorders (2.9% vs. 0.9%)
Thyroid disorders (2.5% vs. 0.8%)
Epilepsy (2.2% vs. 0.7%)
Delirium (1.5% vs. 0.1%)
Ear, nose, and throat disorders (5.2% vs. 2.9%)
Researchers found that depression, vertigo, headaches and other conditions were more common during the five years preceding diagnosis. (iStock)
Differences in medical conditions were most pronounced in the five years before an early-onset Alzheimer's diagnosis, the study showed.
3 THINGS TO AVOID IN MIDDLE AGE COULD MEAN 13 MORE YEARS WITHOUT DEMENTIA, STUDY FINDS

The researchers also found that healthcare visits increased substantially among early-onset Alzheimer’s patients immediately before and during the time of diagnosis, which may indicate emerging symptoms.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"It is well-known that the neuropathological changes associated with Alzheimer’s disease begin at least 15 to 20 years before clinical cognitive symptoms appear," Suvi-Johanna Krüger, M.D., Ph.D., study co-author and clinical lecturer at University of Oulu, said in a press release.
"Most previous studies have focused on late-onset Alzheimer’s disease, and considerably less is known about early-onset Alzheimer’s disease."

The researchers analyzed medical records from 407 people with early-onset Alzheimer’s disease and 4,035 people of similar age and sex without the diagnosis, focusing on the 15 years prior to diagnosis. (AP Photo/Evan Vucci, File)
Study limitations
Because the study was observational, it only establishes associations and cannot demonstrate that these conditions can reliably predict Alzheimer's disease.
"Our study cannot determine whether these conditions cause early-onset Alzheimer’s disease or whether they are consequences of the underlying disease process," Krüger noted.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"Some conditions may represent risk factors, while others may reflect early symptoms or changes occurring during the prodromal phase of the disease."
It is also possible that genetics, lifestyle and socioeconomic factors played a role in the patients’ outcomes.
"Early diagnosis is important because more treatment and support options are available in the early stages of the disease."
Also, the researchers could not independently verify all medical diagnoses or assess the severity of the patients’ disease. Additionally, the findings may not apply to populations outside Finland.

Larger studies looking at disease biomarkers, genetics and clinical assessments could help determine whether there is a casual relationship between the medical conditions and Alzheimer’s incidence and whether these medical patterns could be used to improve early detection.

For people experiencing any persistent medical symptoms, including issues with memory or cognition, experts say it’s important to see a healthcare provider.

"Early diagnosis is important because more treatment and support options are available in the early stages of the disease," Krüger advised.
"Early diagnosis also gives individuals and their families more time to plan for the future and access appropriate support services."
