title: Selma Blair's lawyer cites missed medication, head injury after in-flight arrest: What doctors say
summary: Selma Blair's attorney claims she missed doses of a powerful MS medication, triggering severe neurological symptoms before her in-flight arrest.
story: Dr. Lee Murray, a board-certified neurologist practicing in Jackson, Tennessee, shared the potential health effects that could occur if a multiple sclerosis patient skips doses of necessary medications.
Selma Blair’s recent in-flight arrest has raised questions about the potential effects when a person with multiple sclerosis misses prescribed medication.

The actress, 54, was arraigned Monday on two counts of second-degree assault after allegedly attacking a police officer and nurse following an altercation with flight attendants aboard a Delta flight into New York City, The Associated Press reported.
In court, Blair’s attorney, Shawn Barnes, said that Blair had missed several doses of Nuedexta, "a powerful medication that controls severe neurological symptoms," according to multiple outlets.
SELMA BLAIR ACCUSED OF KICKING NURSE HOURS AFTER JFK PLANE ARREST

The attorney added that Blair hit her head during the flight, which departed from Los Angeles, and was in "a state of severe confusion and disorientation." He also suggested the altitude may have been a factor.
The incident was the result of a "medical emergency" and not criminal misconduct, he claimed.
Selma Blair’s recent in-flight arrest has raised questions about the potential effects when a person with multiple sclerosis misses prescribed medication. (Getty Images)
Blair was diagnosed with MS in 2018.
Fox News Digital reached out to Blair's representatives requesting comment.
What to know about MS medications
There are three primary treatment approaches for multiple sclerosis, according to Dr. Lee Murray, a board-certified neurologist practicing in Jackson, Tennessee, at West Tennessee Healthcare.
"The first-line treatments we utilize try to prevent recurrent inflammatory attacks," Murray, who has not treated Blair, told Fox News Digital.
'HELICOPTER BRAIN' COULD BE MAKING YOU FEEL SICK: HOW TO SPOT IT AND WHAT TO DO
These medications often involve IV infusions, but they can be in the form of pills or injections the patient gives themselves.
"These are oftentimes medications folks take for several years," Murray said. "The hope of that is to keep the MS suppressed, to keep [the patient] from having MS attacks."

Selma Blair exits Queens Criminal Court on Monday, Oct. 12, 2026. The actress was arrested Sunday after allegedly attacking crew members on board a Delta flight into New York City. (Rashid Umar Abbasi for Fox News)
When patients experience an MS relapse, doctors may prescribe high-dose steroids, either orally or intravenously, to reduce inflammation and help speed recovery, according to Cleveland Clinic.
Patients with multiple sclerosis often have other health issues, Murray noted.
"If an MS medication dosage is missed, the patient runs the risk of having an MS relapse."

"For instance, patients with MS may have bladder difficulties, or they’ll develop depression or neuropathic pain," he said. "And so we prescribe medications that don't treat the MS itself, but they deal with the symptoms related to MS."
Dr. Yoshua Quinones, board-certified internist with Medical Offices of Manhattan, reiterated that there are different classes of MS medications.
PARKINSON'S PATIENTS MAY PROTECT MEMORY AND MOVEMENT WITH ONE SIMPLE HABIT
"Disease-modifying therapy reduces relapses, new MRI lesions and long-term disability accumulation," Quinones, who also did not treat Blair, told Fox News Digital.
Other medications are used to treat acute relapses or manage symptoms such as fatigue, walking difficulties, spasticity and bladder problems.
Actress Selma Blair and her son Arthur Saint Bleick attend the 26th annual Race to Erase MS Gala at the Beverly Hilton hotel on May 10, 2019, in Beverly Hills. (Getty Images)
Disease-modifying therapies themselves fall into several categories, according to the doctor.

Immunomodulators help regulate the immune system, while anti-trafficking drugs prevent certain immune cells from reaching the brain and spinal cord. Cell-depleting therapies, which are generally considered highly effective treatments, target and remove specific immune cells.
Risks of skipping doses
It’s essential for patients to be compliant with their MS medications, according to Murray.

"If an MS medication dosage is missed, the patient runs the risk of having an MS relapse, which can result in acute or new changes neurologically," he said. "There's a host of different symptoms that can occur."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Potential effects of a relapse may include balance difficulties, vision loss, dizziness, bowel or bladder dysfunction, or weakness, numbness or tingling on one side.

In Blair's case, Murray said, "If the Nuedexta was being used to treat pseudobulbar palsy secondary to her MS, missed doses could result in uncontrolled crying or laughter and emotional lability (rapid or unpredictable changes in emotion or mood)."
"I have never seen a missed dose of Nuedexta cause physical aggression," he added.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

If a patient with multiple sclerosis has missed doses of medication and begins to develop new neurological deficits, they should seek medical attention to determine whether they are in an active MS flare, the neurologist advised.
"Recognizing that and being able to quickly get on high-dose steroids can reverse some of the symptoms the patient may be experiencing," he said.
It’s essential for patients to be compliant with their MS medications, according to a neurologist. (iStock)
Although steroids can speed recovery from an MS relapse, they have not been shown to improve long-term outcomes, according to the MS Society.
Quinones agreed that skipping medications will reduce disease control.

"Poor compliance will increase the risk of relapse and MS-related hospitalizations," he said. "For example, if you stop any anti-trafficking medication, it carries a high risk of rapid disease reactivation. Abrupt cessation of this class can even trigger a rebound worse than baseline."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Cell-depleting agents can act over months, so a single missed or delayed dose is less immediately impactful, Quinones added.
"A single dose of disease-modifying therapy is not catastrophic — however, if constantly missed, it can raise a relapse risk."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The risks of missing medication depend on the specific drug, how long treatment is interrupted and the patient's individual circumstances, according to doctors.
Fox News’ Tracy Wright contributed reporting.

title: Popular erectile dysfunction pill may deliver additional boost to aging men
summary: Tadalafil boosted muscle precursor cell survival in a lab study, but researchers say the active Cialis ingredient also delayed mature muscle development.
story: Jacob Zemer, a New York-based fitness coach who primarily trains clients ranging from 35 to 55 years old, said there are several reasons adults start losing muscle as they get older.
Researchers in Italy have discovered a potential association between the common erectile dysfunction drug Cialis (tadalafil) and muscle regeneration.
The study, published in the journal Molecular Biology Reports, tested the drug on mouse muscle cells in a laboratory.
Over a seven-day period, the researchers looked at how the drug affected muscle cell growth, survival and development.
VIAGRA COULD DO MORE THAN ADVERTISED AS STUDY REVEALS SURPRISING HEALTH SUPERPOWER
Tadalafil was found to increase the number of muscle precursor cells, which are involved in the early stages of muscle formation, and helped more of them survive.
The drug also showed signs of helping muscles repair themselves by encouraging growth and reducing cell death.
Researchers in Italy have discovered a potential association between the common erectile dysfunction drug Cialis (tadalafil) and muscle regeneration. (iStock)
Despite these positive outcomes, the research found that tadalafil delayed the development of fully mature muscle cells.
This suggests that the drug could create and maintain more cells involved in muscle regeneration but does not indicate an increase in muscle size and function in humans.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Because the study was conducted in mouse models, the results may differ when applied to humans, posing a limitation to the study findings.
The study lasted just seven days, so more research is needed to understand the drug's long-term effects, the researchers acknowledged.
"This research opens up exciting new possibilities for future therapeutic strategies in muscle recovery," a researcher commented. (iStock)

Study co-author Dr. Cristina Antinozzi, a researcher in the Endocrinology Unit at the University of Rome Foro Italico, said these findings represent an "encouraging look at how tadalafil might be repurposed to support muscle tissue repair and regeneration."
"That's a fascinating biological signal, but it's far from proving that Cialis builds muscle or improves recovery in people."

"While more work is needed, this research opens up exciting new possibilities for future therapeutic strategies in muscle recovery, though it also highlights the need to monitor how such mechanisms might be viewed or misused in sports and performance contexts," she told Fox News Digital.
Dr. Kien Vuu, a radiologist and founder of VuuMD Performance and Longevity in Los Angeles, who was not involved in the study, agreed that this is an "intriguing early finding."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"In mouse muscle cells studied in a laboratory, tadalafil — the active ingredient in Cialis — helped muscle precursor cells grow and survive, but also delayed their maturation into muscle fibers," he told Fox News Digital.
"That's a fascinating biological signal, but it's far from proving that Cialis builds muscle or improves recovery in people.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"Successful regeneration ultimately requires those cells to mature and form functional muscle tissue. This experiment didn't establish that outcome."
Vuu said this is "worth studying" from a longevity perspective because age-related muscle loss contributes "significantly" to frailty, metabolic dysfunction and loss of independence.
Resistance training, adequate protein and quality sleep remain the "most reliable ways" to protect muscle with age, an expert says. (iStock)

"However, this was a laboratory cell study, not a clinical trial," he said. "We need animal studies and eventually human trials examining actual muscle mass, strength, physical function and safety before drawing conclusions about clinical use."
Lifestyle practices such as resistance training, adequate protein and quality sleep remain the "most reliable ways" to protect muscle with age, Vuu added.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The expert noted that tadalafil also carries "meaningful risks," including dangerous blood pressure reductions when combined with nitrates.
"So, people should not take it for muscle-building based on these findings," he said.
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Doctors may be getting childhood obesity wrong, new research suggests
summary: A Lancet Commission definition of clinical obesity cuts pediatric rates sharply by requiring evidence of health complications beyond body mass index.
story: Murdoch Children's Research Insitute pediatrician Dr. Danielle Longmore discusses a new global childhood obesity definition from the Murdoch Children's Research Institute that looks beyond BMI. Longmore explains how the new definition considers critical health impacts.
A new global definition of childhood obesity is reframing how doctors evaluate youth health, looking past traditional body mass index (BMI) measurements to focus on actual physiological impacts.

According to research from the Murdoch Children's Research Institute in Australia, just 2.1% to 4.9% of children and adolescents qualify as clinically obese under the revised standard, compared to 7% to 10.8% under standard BMI calculations.
Dr. Danielle Longmore, a pediatrician at the Melbourne institute, outlined the shift during an appearance on "Fox & Friends."
YOUR WAISTLINE COULD REVEAL A HIDDEN HEART RISK YOUR BMI MISSES, MAJOR STUDY FINDS

"There's a push to really understand the impact of body fat on health," Longmore said. "BMI is really just measuring size. So, it doesn't really have a way of capturing whether somebody is well or unwell."
The traditional BMI measurement calculates a person's weight relative to their height.
While clinical obesity rates are substantially lower in youth, they surge with age, peaking at 52% among adults aged 65 to 74 as chronic conditions accumulate. (iStock)

The new definition, developed by an international panel of medical experts convened by the medical journal The Lancet, requires evidence of both excess body fat and related health problems or limitations in daily activities.
WEIGHT GAIN IN CERTAIN DECADE OF LIFE MAY BE MORE DANGEROUS, STUDY SUGGESTS
These indicators can range from elevated blood pressure and abnormal blood sugar to impaired mobility or poor sleep.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Longmore noted that many children defined as obese by BMI metrics are active, sleeping well, attending school and otherwise healthy.
The new diagnostic model formalizes what many pediatricians already practice by assessing blood pressure, blood sugar, sleep and physical mobility alongside size. (iStock)

"I think this definition just really clarifies what people have been doing in actual clinical practice," Longmore said, noting that physicians typically evaluate patients for underlying complications rather than relying strictly on scale weight.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
While clinical obesity appears to be significantly less prevalent in youth under the new model, the trajectory reverses dramatically later in life.
The study, which analyzed nearly 800,000 individuals across their lifespan, found that clinical obesity rates climbed through adulthood.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Among adults ages 65 to 74, the rate of clinical obesity reached 52%, as health problems linked to excess body fat became more common with age.
The findings come at a time when prescription weight loss medications, particularly GLP-1 receptor agonists, are gaining in popularity.
Many children categorized as obese by traditional BMI standards are fit, active and otherwise healthy, without secondary medical complications. (iStock)
However, Longmore cautioned that the study's dataset reflects pre-GLP-1 records, making the long-term impact of these treatments an open area for future study.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"This is really just the start of understanding what this new diagnostic entity means, and we really need more research," Longmore said, emphasizing that while the definition refines clinical diagnoses, early health interventions and lifestyle prevention remain critical for children at risk.
Khloe Quill is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital. She and the lifestyle team cover a range of story topics including food and drink, travel, and health.

title: Biggest waste of money in your home gym may surprise you, fitness expert says
summary: Fitness coach Jacob Zemer reveals the three home gym essentials — bands, dumbbells and a bench — that let you train every muscle group on a budget.
story: New York-based fitness coach Jacob Zemer spoke with Fox News Digital about the most worthwhile investments for working out at home — and which equipment may not deliver enough bang for the buck.
Americans are spending more on health and wellness, research shows — and for some home gym enthusiasts, the cost can quickly climb into the thousands.
A YouGov poll conducted in September 2026 found that 31% of Americans are spending more on health and wellness than a year ago, while 20% expect to spend more in the coming year.
Meanwhile, a 2026 poll by Garage Gym Experiment, an online community for home fitness enthusiasts, found that 44% of respondents expected to spend at least $1,000 on their home gyms this year.
FITNESS EXPERT REVEALS 6 THINGS PEOPLE OVER 35 SHOULD DO AFTER WORKOUTS TO STAY STRONG
But building an effective home gym doesn’t have to break the bank, according to New York-based fitness coach Jacob Zemer.
The biggest home gym money-waster may not be a particular piece of equipment, he said, but rather anything that takes up significant space and is difficult to set up or use consistently.
Building an effective home gym doesn’t have to break the bank, according to New York-based fitness coach Jacob Zemer, right. (Jacob Zemer)
Zemer spoke with Fox News Digital about the most worthwhile investments for working out at home — and which equipment may not deliver enough bang for the buck.
The 3 home gym essentials
"A lot of people think building a home gym requires an elaborate setup, and it doesn't," Zemer said.
If someone is building a home gym from scratch, the fitness pro recommends starting with a few affordable pieces and adding equipment over time.
10-MINUTE FITNESS HABIT CAN HELP ADULTS OVER 40 MAINTAIN MUSCLE AND STAY STRONG
"You can accomplish everything for every muscle group with just three items," he said.
Exercise bands are a good first investment, Zemer said, "just because they're so incredibly affordable."
They’re also very effective, he said, especially for those who are new to strength training.
Exercise bands are a good first investment, Zemer said, "just because they're so incredibly affordable." (Jacob Zemer)
"You can do everything you need to with just those pieces of equipment — and you can travel with them, bring them on a plane and to a hotel, which makes them very versatile," Zemer said.
When choosing dumbbells, it’s important to consider how much floor space they’ll take up — especially if the home gym is in a room with multiple purposes, according to Zemer.
"With adjustable dumbbells, you can have a very small floor print — however, they are a little bit more costly, and some of them are slightly fragile, so just be mindful of that," he advised.
4 SIMPLE HABITS CAN HELP SLOW MUSCLE LOSS AS YOU AGE, FITNESS EXPERT SAYS
Beginners should first focus on learning the proper form and choosing a weight that makes the final repetitions challenging, according to Zemer.
Progress doesn’t always mean moving to heavier dumbbells, he noted.
When choosing dumbbells, it’s important to consider how much floor space they’ll take up — especially if the home gym is in a room with multiple purposes, according to Zemer. (Jacob Zemer)
"Pushing yourself doesn’t mean adding 20 pounds — it could mean doing one more rep," Zemer said. "You need to progressively get stronger, because your body will adapt to the stimulus you’re using."
Once it becomes easy to complete a high number of repetitions, it may be time to increase the weight.
With some exercises, it can be limiting if you have to lie on the floor or stand, Zemer said.
"You can get quite an affordable bench online," he said. "I would look for one that both declines and inclines, maybe even perhaps sits completely upright. That will give you a lot of versatility."
For added versatility, Zemer suggests looking for a bench that both declines and inclines, and maybe even sits completely upright. (Jacob Zemer)
The biggest waste: equipment you won’t use
Before buying a piece of home gym equipment, Zemer recommends considering how much space it requires, how many exercises it supports and whether it will be easy to use consistently.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Equipment that is bulky or difficult to move, or requires too much setup, may end up becoming an expensive waste of money.
"The most important thing is that it’s quick and easy to set up, easy to grab and therefore more likely to be used," he said. "The more setup it requires, the less likely you will to be use it."
Before buying a piece of home gym equipment, Zemer recommends considering how much space it requires, how many exercises it supports and whether it will be easy to use consistently. (Jacob Zemer)

Zemer learned that lesson after buying lever arms, attachments that connect to a power rack and move up and down for exercises such as presses, rows and squats. Because the equipment was cumbersome to move, he eventually sold it secondhand.
"The secondhand market of gym equipment is brutal, so if you buy something, and you don't use it, the resale value is next to none," Zemer cautioned.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
He recommends prioritizing items that serve multiple purposes, rather than devices designed to target just one body part.
"I always look for equipment that can do multiple things," he said.
"A lot of people think building a home gym requires an elaborate setup, and it doesn't."
Do you need cardio equipment?
Cardio equipment is not essential for everyone, according to the trainer, especially for those who are mobile.
Many people can also raise their heart rate through activities such as walking, running or strength-training workouts performed at a faster pace, he said.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

For those who prefer a cardio machine, Zemer recommends choosing an option that is versatile and less likely to aggravate the knees or back, such as a stationary bike or ski erg (an indoor exercise machine that simulates the motion of cross-country skiing).
Melissa Rudy is senior health editor and a member of the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to melissa.rudy@fox.com.

title: Dementia risk more than quadruples among adults with common disorder
summary: Adults with ADHD had more than four times the risk of dementia or mild cognitive impairment, a University of Pittsburgh study of 187,000 people found.
story: Dr. Elizabeth Landsverk, a geriatric medicine and dementia expert, noted that people with ADHD can have more difficulty with organization, which could be one factor contributing to the higher risk of cognitive impairment.
A common neurodevelopmental disorder could be linked to dementia risk, a new study suggests.

Research led by the University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine, involving more than 187,000 adults aged 50 and older, found that ADHD (attention deficit hyperactivity disorder) was associated with a substantially increased risk of dementia or mild cognitive impairment (MCI).
The observational study looked at electronic health records and genetic information of participants who were enrolled in the U.S. National Institutes of Health All of Us Research Program.
7 NEW DEMENTIA RISK FACTORS REVEALED — INCLUDING ONE MILLIONS STRUGGLE WITH
Cognitive impairment was observed in 6.7% of participants with ADHD versus 3.4% without the disorder — nearly twice the rate.
After researchers adjusted for age, gender and other health conditions, those with ADHD had more than four times the risk.
A common neurodevelopmental disorder could be linked to dementia risk, a new study suggests. (iStock)
The findings — which were published Oct. 7 in JAMA Psychiatry — only show an association and cannot determine that ADHD increases dementia risk, the researchers acknowledged.

"This doesn’t prove that ADHD causes dementia, but seeing the same pattern show up independently in medical records and in people’s genes gives us greater confidence that the association is not simply an artifact of how ADHD gets diagnosed," said senior author Tharick A. Pascoal, associate professor of psychiatry and of neurology at Pitt, in a press release.
"Two different kinds of evidence are pointing in the same direction."
3 THINGS TO AVOID IN MIDDLE AGE COULD MEAN 13 MORE YEARS WITHOUT DEMENTIA, STUDY FINDS
Meanwhile, those with the highest genetic susceptibility to ADHD were found to have a 35% greater risk of dementia than those with the lowest susceptibility.

"Analyzing genetic information alongside years of health records allows us to identify patterns that might not be visible in a smaller or more traditional study," said Guilherme Bauer-Negrini, co-first author and postdoctoral associate in biomedical data science at Pitt, in the release.
"It goes back to nature versus nurture — particularly if we're starting at age 50, as opposed to starting at 20."
"With this kind of data, we can start to investigate what may be driving this association and whether any of those factors could be modified to support healthier cognitive aging."
Understanding the link

Dr. Elizabeth Landsverk, a geriatric medicine and dementia expert with over 20 years of experience treating patients with Alzheimer’s and cognitive decline, noted that people with ADHD can have more difficulty with organization, which could contribute to the higher risk of cognitive impairment, although neurological differences may also play a role.

"It might [be] that keeping on top of health issues and getting to the doctor is more difficult for them," Landsverk, a California-based doctor who is not involved in the study, told Fox News Digital.
Cognitive impairment was observed in 6.7% of participants with ADHD versus 3.4% without the disorder — nearly twice the rate. (iStock)
The study also found that people with ADHD had a 20% higher incidence of utilizing health resources, she pointed out.

"Having just signed up for Medicare, I know that it's really complicated — if you have trouble with focusing and getting things done, you may not be able to get the resources that you need," Landsverk said. "You may not be able to go to the doctor. You may not get your blood pressure taken care of. So there's probably a correlation."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"It goes back to nature versus nurture — particularly if we're starting at age 50, as opposed to starting at 20."
ADHD vs dementia
It can be challenging to distinguish between ADHD and cognitive decline, as some of the symptoms may overlap, according to Landsverk.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"I imagine it can look similar," she said. "You know, you don't remember why you went into a room. You don't know where your keys are, you don't remember the name of an actress."
It is cause for concern if the individual struggles to take care of day-to-day tasks, the expert noted.
The findings only show an association and cannot determine that ADHD increases dementia risk, the researchers acknowledged. (Getty Images)

"You can't pay your bills, you can't get your medications right, you can't get to your appointments, you tell people that you're going to do stuff and then you don't — that's when you need to get checked."
Changes in judgment, mood or social behavior may be more suggestive of dementia than ADHD, Landsverk noted.
Reducing the risk
Although the study found an association between ADHD and cognitive impairment, Landsverk emphasized that some lifestyle behaviors can help people reduce their overall dementia risk.

She pointed to maintaining a healthy weight, avoiding smoking and excessive alcohol, and staying physically active as important modifiable factors, along with controlling blood pressure, cholesterol and diabetes.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"There's a lot we can do," Landsverk said, recommending a largely plant-based diet and at least 30 minutes of daily exercise.
Physical activity can also help improve mood and focus, she added.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Anyone experiencing persistent problems with memory, focus, organization or managing everyday tasks should consider seeing an expert for an evaluation, Landsverk advised.

title: 'Helicopter brain' could be making you feel sick: How to spot it and what to do
summary: Doomscrolling is linked to higher anxiety and psychological distress, but a neurologist says it may also trigger what he calls "helicopter brain."
story: Board-certified neurologist Dr. Steven Resnick discusses how overstimulation can lead to the "helicopter brain" effect, which can manifest as physical symptoms, and shares how to reverse it.

A new analysis of 44 studies has linked "doomscrolling" to higher levels of anxiety and psychological distress — but for some, information overload may also contribute to a phenomenon one neurologist calls "helicopter brain."

The research, published in Frontiers in Psychology, found associations between excessive consumption of negative online content and poorer mental health, although it did not establish a cause-and-effect relationship.

Board-certified neurologist Dr. Steven Resnick uses the term "helicopter brain" to describe a nervous system that remains constantly on high alert, much like a "helicopter parent" who constantly hovers over a child to protect them from harm.
FUNCTIONAL MEDICINE EXPERT WARNS EVERYDAY HABITS MAY ACCELERATE CELLULAR AGING

"Imagine your own helicopter — that is your nervous system," Resnick, chief of the Division of Neurology and medical director of the Comprehensive Stroke Center at Mount Sinai Medical Center in Miami Beach, Florida, told Fox News Digital. "Your nervous system’s job is to protect you from harm."
Information overload may also contribute to a phenomenon one neurologist calls "helicopter brain." (iStock)
Information overload, overstimulation and uncertainty can keep the brain on high alert, activating the autonomic nervous system, the neurologist said.
"The brain is scanning for danger," Resnick said. "When it scans for danger, then you have that autonomic nervous system pushing the accelerator."
NEARLY 3 IN 4 AMERICANS ARE BATTLING THE SAME EXHAUSTING HEALTH PROBLEM, CDC REVEALS

The neurologist, who also hosts "The Healthy Mind" podcast, said he often sees patients experiencing symptoms they struggle to explain, including headaches, gastrointestinal issues, fatigue, sleep problems, tingling and dizziness.
In some cases, patients undergo evaluations by multiple specialists before identifying a potential explanation.
"The brain is scanning for danger," the neurologist said. "When it scans for danger, then you have that autonomic nervous system pushing the accelerator." (iStock)
"They end up going to see a neurologist, who sends them to the gastroenterologist, who sends them to the cardiologist, then the rheumatologist," he said.
"They don't understand what they're feeling is actually authentic, it's real — it's the nervous system that is actually activated."
THINK YOUR CORTISOL IS TOO HIGH? EXPERT REVEALS THE TRUTH BEHIND VIRAL WELLNESS CRAZE
Although constant information overload can contribute to this heightened state of alertness, Resnick said the same patterns can emerge in response to everyday stressors and deeply ingrained habits.
The neurologist outlined the following five strategies for recognizing these patterns, calming the nervous system and developing healthier responses to stress.
No. 1: Recognize what you’re feeling
When seeing patients, Resnick said his first step is to listen to them, to ensure that he understands what they’re feeling.

"I hear patients say, ‘I'm scared, I'm fearful, I'm concerned, I'm worried,’ and then you start to realize what their nervous system is telling you," he told Fox News Digital. "I would never have done that by just fixing the problem right away."
When seeing patients, Resnick said his first step is to listen to them, to ensure that he understands what they’re feeling. (iStock)
The nervous system can begin to calm when patients feel truly heard, safe, secure and connected, the neurologist said.
"The solution can be done later," Resnick said. "And we have to stop using the word ‘fixing,’ because a lot of things cannot be fixed — but over time, you can start feeling better."
No. 2: Name the pattern
Recognizing recurring patterns — in thoughts, behaviors and reactions — is an important first step toward changing them, Resnick said.
"Mindfulness is not just about meditation; it's about noticing," he said.

That could mean recognizing the same conflict happening repeatedly with a co-worker, lying awake each night with racing thoughts, or turning to food or cigarettes during periods of stress, according to Resnick.
THIS ONE QUESTION MAY REVEAL WHETHER YOUR BODY IS GETTING THE REST IT NEEDS, STUDY FINDS
When those behaviors repeat, people can begin operating on "autopilot," he said.

"The brain wants to resort to what is familiar, what is safe and what is known," Resnick said. "It keeps going back to that because the brain understands it, retrieves it and does the same thing over and over again."
Breaking that cycle requires recognizing the pattern and making a conscious effort to respond differently, he added.
No. 3: Catch the trigger
Next, the neurologist said it’s important to "catch the cue," or trigger, that kick-starts the pattern.
"It's a stimulus," he said. "It's something that is very sneaky. It goes under your level of consciousness."
"It could be your boss' face. It could be a telephone. It could be a chair or a couch in a room. It could be a smell or a feeling."
The neurologist said it’s important to "catch the cue," or trigger, that kick-starts the pattern. (iStock)
That cue can trigger an almost automatic behavior, Resnick said, such as procrastinating, eating, reaching for a drink or lashing out.
If the behavior provides pleasure or helps someone avoid an uncomfortable feeling or situation, the brain can become more likely to repeat it.
Even worrying can become part of that cycle. If the feared outcome doesn’t happen, Resnick said, the brain may interpret the worry as protective, reinforcing the habit.
ONE TYPE OF SLEEP LINKED TO DRAMATICALLY LOWER RISK OF DEMENTIA, PARKINSON'S AND 81 OTHER DISEASES
Breaking the pattern starts with identifying the specific cues that set it in motion, according to the neurologist.

Rather than viewing anxiety or overthinking as something that happens "all the time," Resnick encourages patients to pinpoint a specific episode, consider what triggered it and recognize the behavior and potential reward that followed.
No. 4: Reward the new habit
The next step is replacing the unwanted behavior with a healthier habit that provides a noticeable reward, Resnick said.
"Give your new habit a reward you can feel," he advised.
DIETITIAN REVEALS SIMPLE EATING STRATEGY FOR BETTER SLEEP — AND ONE HABIT TO AVOID

That reward does not have to be significant. After an early-morning workout, for example, it might be a sense of accomplishment or an improved mood. A healthy shake after the workout could provide another small reward.
"Give your new habit a reward you can feel."
"Even checkboxing something on a piece of paper feels good," Resnick said.
These immediate, positive reinforcements can help the brain begin associating the healthier behavior with something rewarding.
"Rewards are very important," the neurologist said. "Even the small ones are important."
No. 5: Float instead of fight
Finally, when anxiety or panic strikes, Resnick recommends taking a counterintuitive approach: "Float instead of fight."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
In many cases, he said, people are not only afraid of a particular situation, but of the anxious feelings that may result.
Someone with claustrophobia, for example, may fear getting an MRI because they anticipate the physical sensations of anxiety that could arise inside the machine.
A person with claustrophobia may dread getting an MRI because they expect to experience anxiety-related physical sensations while inside the machine. (iStock)
"Don’t fight it," Resnick advised. "You want to allow it. You want to feel it."
Avoiding a situation can reinforce the brain’s perception that it poses a threat, he said, while safely experiencing it can help create a new association.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"After you have that experience where you felt safe, and you went toward it, then your brain and body … pair it as being safe," Resnick said.
The goal, he added, is "to teach the brain safety through your body and through your brain and mind."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
While these strategies may help people better manage stress and anxiety, Resnick emphasized the importance of recognizing the patterns behind the symptoms.
People experiencing persistent or unexplained physical symptoms should seek medical evaluation to rule out underlying health conditions.

title: New belly fat injection cuts dangerous fat surrounding organs by 12% in early human trial
summary: CBL-514 injection triggers apoptosis only in fat cells to reduce visceral fat by 12% in early trials, with implications for insulin resistance.
story: HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. cautions that the nature of GLP drugs means there might be unknown side effects in a ‘Saturday in America’ town hall.
Early human trials of an experimental injection called CBL-514 have shown the potential for reducing deadly visceral fat.
Visceral fat, which sits deep inside the abdomen wrapped around internal organs, affects metabolism and influences insulin resistance. It can impact the development of type 2 diabetes.
Research published in March by the American Heart Association found that visceral fat had a stronger association with the risk of heart failure than body mass index (BMI).
YOUR WAISTLINE COULD REVEAL A HIDDEN HEART RISK YOUR BMI MISSES, MAJOR STUDY FINDS

The trials tested whether the injection could diminish visceral fat deposits. They were conducted by Dr. W. Timothy Garvey of the University of Alabama at Birmingham and Yu-Fang Ling of Caliway Biopharmaceuticals in New Taipei City, Taiwan.
Previous phase 2 trials had already shown that the drug could reduce subcutaneous fat, the layer of fat directly beneath the skin.
An experimental injection called CBL-514 has been shown to reduce visceral fat in early human trials. (iStock)
MRI scans from two phase 2 trials exhibited a decrease in visceral fat in participants who received the CBL-514 drug, while the visceral fat increased in those who received a placebo drug.
Participants who were given CBL-514 received injections into their lower abdomen every three weeks for up to 12 weeks, with doses of up to 600 milligrams.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER
The number of injections given to participants depended on the thickness of their abdominal fat.
As the fat layer decreased in volume, the number of injections also decreased.
The amount of injections that participants received depended upon the thickness of their abdominal fat. (iStock)
The CBL-514 injection selectively sparks apoptosis — a process that causes cells to self-destruct — but only in fat cells, leaving nearby cells unharmed.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

Four weeks after the final treatment, the average volume of fat had lowered by 12.01% in the group given CBL-514, while it had increased by 5.68% in the group that received a placebo, SciTechDaily reported.
Participants who were given CBL-514 received injections into their lower abdomen every three weeks for up to 12 weeks — with doses of up to 600 milligrams. (iStock)
The potential cosmetic effects, such as a flatter stomach due to subcutaneous fat loss, are appealing to patients, Garvey acknowledged.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

What’s even more important, he noted, however, is the decrease in body weight, improved blood pressure and cholesterol, and the loss of visceral fat that the injection can cause — as these factors impact overall health.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Liposuction, a common surgical cosmetic procedure, cannot remove visceral fat, and thus cannot reduce the health risks caused by a high amount of visceral fat.
Sadie Chafe is a writer on the Lifestyle team at Fox News Digital.

title: Hidden clues could help predict a woman’s breast cancer risk years in advance
summary: An AI tool developed at NYU Langone Health analyzes years of 3D mammograms to predict breast cancer risk up to five years before a diagnosis.
story: AI technology is transforming breast cancer screening by assisting doctors in identifying women at higher risk years before cancer develops. Mount Sinai's Breast Surgery Director and author of 'The Breast Advice' Dr. Elisa Port highlights how AI uncovers hidden tumors and slashes false positive results, especially for women with dense breasts. This advancement aims to increase screening adherence among the 30-40% who currently don't get regular mammograms.
An artificial intelligence (AI) tool could help doctors predict a woman's risk of developing breast cancer years in advance, according to new research.

In a new study, published in the American Journal of Roentgenology, researchers at NYU Langone Health and its Perlmutter Cancer Center tested an AI model designed to estimate a woman's risk of developing breast cancer within five years.
The tool looks at several years of a woman's 3D mammograms to track changes in breast tissue over time, rather than looking only at the latest scan, according to the researchers.
NEW ALZHEIMER'S BLOOD TEST PREDICTS WHO IS LIKELY TO DEVELOP DEMENTIA IN 5 TO 10 YEARS
The model was developed using more than 313,000 mammograms from more than 161,000 women, according to the study.
An artificial intelligence (AI) tool could help doctors predict a woman's risk of developing breast cancer years in advance. (iStock)

Connie Lehman, a Massachusetts-based breast imaging specialist and professor of radiology at Harvard Medical School who was not involved in the study, told Fox News Digital that AI could help identify women whose increased risk might otherwise go unnoticed.

"For decades, as a doctor and breast imaging specialist, I have cared for women who were shocked by a breast cancer diagnosis," Lehman said. "Again and again, I heard: 'How can this be? No one in my family has had breast cancer.'"
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER
Traditional risk assessments can consider factors such as family history and genetic mutations, while AI can look for additional clues within a woman's breast tissue, according to Lehman.
The tool looks at several years of a woman's 3D mammograms to track changes in breast tissue over time. (iStock)
"A mammogram can tell us more than whether cancer is visible today — it can also provide information about a woman's risk of developing cancer in the years ahead," she said.
That information could eventually help doctors tailor breast cancer screening to a woman's individual risk, Lehman said.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES

Women identified as being at increased risk could discuss additional screening, such as MRI, with their health care providers, while women at average risk may continue with routine mammograms, according to Lehman.
The technology could also analyze mammograms a woman has already had, meaning the added risk information would not require another imaging exam or additional radiation, she noted.
Traditional risk assessments can consider factors such as family history and genetic mutations, while AI can look for additional clues in a woman's breast tissue, experts say. (iStock)
Lehman cautioned that an AI risk score is not a cancer diagnosis and cannot predict with certainty whether a woman will develop the disease.

"A higher score can prompt a conversation with your health care provider about additional screening and risk-reduction options," she said. "A lower score does not eliminate risk or replace regular mammography."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
The NYU model remains a research tool and is not FDA-authorized for clinical use, according to Lehman.
The researchers also noted that more testing is needed. The study used mammograms from NYU Langone hospitals and imaging equipment from one manufacturer.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The team plans to test the model using data from other medical centers and different 3D mammography systems, according to NYU Langone.
Fox News Digital reached out to the researchers for comment.

title: Silent inflammation could be damaging your body — and 5 habits may help keep it in check
summary: Jim LaValle reveals how the gut-immune-brain interface drives chronic inflammation, and why stress, blood sugar and environmental toxins play key roles.
story: Clinical pharmacist Jim LaValle breaks down how diet, stress, medications, blood sugar, environmental exposures and even overtraining may contribute to inflammation — and why the gut-brain connection matters.

Inflammation is a natural immune response that helps protect the body from injury and infection, but when it becomes chronic, it can pose a health threat, according to the National Institutes of Health.
Over time, chronic inflammation can contribute to rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, inflammatory bowel disease and cardiovascular disease.
Keeping the condition in check can help protect healthy tissues and support overall health, experts say.
POPULAR WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS MAY HELP PROTECT AGAINST A DEADLY DISEASE, DOCTOR SAYS
Jim LaValle, a clinical pharmacist and metabolic medicine expert based in Texas, told Fox News Digital that inflammation can be influenced by a variety of factors beyond injury or infection.
Inflammation is a natural immune response that helps protect the body from injury and infection, but chronic inflammation can damage healthy tissues and contribute to serious diseases. (iStock)

LaValle first pointed to the gut-immune-brain connection — the communication between gut microbes, the immune system and the central nervous system — as one pathway that can influence the body's inflammatory response.
Beyond gut health, he said several everyday lifestyle factors can play a role in preventing chronic inflammation.
DOCTORS SAY 8 FORGOTTEN HABITS COULD HELP FIGHT STRESS, OBESITY AND CHRONIC DISEASE
No. 1: Manage stress
Managing stress and anxiety can help support the gut-brain connection and keep inflammation in check, according to LaValle.
He pointed to cortisol, a hormone released in response to stress, which he said can "wreak havoc on your chemistry" when levels remain elevated.
Stress can "wreak havoc on your chemistry," the expert warned. (iStock)
Chronic stress can also affect the intestinal barrier, potentially allowing substances that would normally remain inside the gut to pass through more easily, LaValle said.
This increased intestinal permeability is sometimes called "leaky gut."
ZERO SUGAR, MORE PROBLEMS? STUDY REVEALS SURPRISING GUT HEALTH EFFECTS
"So, it turns out that if I'm stressed out a lot, I can be more prone to irritable bowel," LaValle said, as stress can trigger or worsen digestive symptoms in some people.
No. 2: Watch for food triggers
Diets high in sugar, fat and ultraprocessed foods can also affect gut health.
Paying attention to which foods trigger certain symptoms may help identify potential food sensitivities or intolerances, LaValle noted.
Paying attention to what kinds of food trigger certain reactions or sensitivities may help signal what is causing inflammation in the body. (iStock)
Symptoms such as bloating, rashes or discomfort after eating certain foods may signal a food-related reaction, although they can have other causes.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Certain medications, including antibiotics, may also alter the gut microbiome, but their effects vary depending on the drug and the individual, the expert said.
No. 3: Keep blood sugar in check
Maintaining healthy blood sugar levels is another important factor in managing inflammation, according to LaValle.
Maintaining healthy blood sugar levels is another important factor in managing inflammation. (iStock)
LaValle noted that conditions such as diabetes and insulin resistance are often associated with chronic inflammation.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Research suggests that GLP-1 medications, commonly prescribed for type 2 diabetes and obesity, may have anti-inflammatory effects, while scientists are investigating other potential benefits beyond weight loss and blood sugar control.
No. 4: Be aware of environmental exposures
The "exposome," or the environmental exposures people experience throughout their lives, can influence inflammation and the risk of chronic disease, according to the National Institutes of Health.
Microplastics could trigger inflammation signaling, according to the expert. (iStock)

LaValle pointed to emerging research on how environmental exposures — including "forever chemicals," microplastics, metals and pesticides — may affect weight, blood sugar regulation and other aspects of health.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"A lot of us don't think about that kind of impact on our health and how that could trigger inflammation signaling," he added.
No. 5: Don’t over-train
Regular exercise supports overall health, but intense workouts without adequate recovery time can put additional stress on the body, LaValle cautioned.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"You’re not getting a good enough recovery," he said. "You’re training hard. And, in fact, you might be training hard every day to lower that cortisol, but you're not getting good recovery. And that could lead to silent inflammatory signaling as well."
Anyone who is concerned about chronic inflammation or is experiencing persistent symptoms should consult a doctor to determine the underlying cause and appropriate treatment.
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: From handyman to House history: HVAC mogul Joe Strada pushes trade schools, business mindset in Florida race
summary: From humbling beginnings, Joe Strada built a half-billion dollar a year HVAC business; now he wants to bring his hard work, no-nonsense approach to Washington DC.
story: Florida congressional hopeful Joe Strada explains how he built a half-billion-dollar business, why he entered politics and what matters more to him than money.
If Republican Joe Strada wins Florida's eleventh congressional district in three weeks, he will likely be the wealthiest individual to ever hold a seat in the US House of Representatives.
It's an impressive trajectory for a man from humble beginnings who got his start fixing equipment in a bowling alley, but always had a zest for learning, building, and working with his hands.

Strada, whose HVAC, electrical and plumbing company employs roughly 4,000 people across 13 states, told Fox News Digital that his journey from handyman to wealthy entrepreneur embodies the American Dream but that neither his fortune nor his business success defines him.
Interview with Joe Strada
PULLING BILLIONS FROM HARVARD TO FUND TRADE SCHOOLS? HERE’S WHAT PEOPLE ARE SAYING ABOUT TRUMP’S LATEST MOVE

"How about that? Just the kid, a handyman in a bowling alley, fixing things that break…and now I'm blessed to have a business that's in 13 states, thousands of people that work for me. It's been a blessing and, I'm able to live the American dream.

"But it's difficult. It was difficult with the headwinds and the rules and regulations that come out of Washington, D.C. And it was very challenging …It should be difficult, but not this challenging."
Strada wants everyone to be able to benefit from the American capitalist system that brought him great success:

"You know, as a business owner, I realized and recognized all the problems that Washington, D.C. is causing. All the rules and regulations that are impacting families, small business owners all across the country. And I finally said, we need a different type of person in Washington, DC.

"We have enough lobbyists, politicians and attorneys there. It's time to have a business-minded person that knows how to fix things that could go to Washington, and solve problems for the real, you know, real problems for the American people."
Strada is on a nationwide mission to pitch young people on the value of the trades, and suggests it's a worthy alternative to racking up massive student loans:

WASHINGTON, DC - JUNE 30: Student loan borrowers demand President Biden use "Plan B" to cancel student debt Immediately at a rally outside the Supreme Court of the United States on June 30, 2023, in Washington, DC. (Photo by Paul Morigi/Getty Images for We The 45 Million) (Getty Images)

"The word of trade is really starting to spread now. Trades people, young people just want to be successful. Sometimes they don't know there's an opportunity in the trades. You come to my company, you don't know how to spell AC, you don't know what end of the screwdriver to hold, but you're paid the very first day. We train you. We give you a career that will support yourself and your family the rest of your life.

"You don't have a $250,000 student debt, and you're able to be successful… And my objective, not just with my company, it's across the country. I'm working with trade schools and high schools everywhere. I'm talking to young people all over our country to come into the trades because it's a great opportunity to live your version of the American dream."
As Strada's HVAC company was growing throughout the country, a labor shortage prompted a serious challenge, and a major shift in business strategy:

"The most difficult challenge was we had the opportunity to grow, and we didn't have enough labor. So I had to develop a program to teach people the trade. So we could grow, and we've been fortunate: we're in 13 states now and 4,000 people that work with us. We never would have done that if we didn't develop our own training program.
"I couldn't wait for the government to come and solve my problem. I'm a business guy who solves problems and I had to go develop a training program for young people."
Strada argues that people on government assistance should also take a serious look at the trades, suggesting we have a large untapped labor pool within our own borders:

CIUDAD JUAREZ, MEXICO - MARCH 15: Two men scale the cyclone fence installed by the Texas National Guard as hundreds of migrants queue up along the border wall dividing Mexico and the United States, awaiting processing by the Border Patrol in hopes of receiving asylum on March 15, 2024, in Ciudad Juarez, Mexico.  (David Peinado/Anadolu via Getty Images)

"The border had to be closed, and we did a great job keeping all the criminals out of our country. And as far as getting more workers, we have Americans that want to work. We have plenty of people sitting at home getting a government paycheck. Let's get them to work.
"Some of them are just lazy and don't want to work, others just need the opportunity and the push to say, 'this is easy, let's get into a trade, let's learn a business.'
TRUMP-BACKED GOP CANDIDATE WHO OUSTED SCANDAL-PLAGUED INCUMBENT WARNS AGAINST 'NEVER-ENDING WAR' WITH IRAN
"I've have plenty of people that turned out to be an entrepreneur. They've opened their own business, and I'm very happy and gratified when I'm helping people."
Hard work is at the foundation of Strada's success, and he argues an inherent part of that economic success is bringing others along:

"You know, most people think when you're successful, it was handed to you. I got to tell you, David, I'm proud of the hard work my father did, but it was tough growing up. We were fortunate, we had a swimming pool, but it was mainly, a lot of times it was green because we couldn't afford chlorine. It was the best Marco Polo pool in the neighborhood.

"I started with nothing. It's just hard work. The passion and drive to want to be successful, to achieve goals. And it's always about everybody wins. My employees have to win. My customers have to win, the company has to win and that's the position I like to be in is to be able to help sit at a table, moderate those kinds of things and execute those results."
Ultimately, Strada downplays the importance of money, and emphasizes character, while revealing that his greatest motivation in life was born from a family tragedy:

"I wake up every day the same person I was when I was 12 years old that I am today. I've been blessed to be wealthy. I worked hard. I don't apologize for it…But you know, money is just a number. My perspective is everybody puts their head on the pillow at the end of the night. And when you put your head on your pillow, what do you stand for? What's the character of who you are?
The US Capitol in Washington, DC, US, on Thursday, Jan. 29, 2026.  (Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"How much money you have…How many zeros you have and where the decimal point is on your bank account? None of that matters. What kind of character are you? I strive every day to do the right thing. For my God, my son in heaven who looks down at me, I want to make him proud. Every decision I make is to make him proud of me, and I do the best I can every single day."
Strada's son, Joe Strada, was an innocent bystander killed by a stray bullet in Lake Mary, FL, during a gunfight outside a shopping center in 2018.
Finally, Strada promises to be a powerful voice for tradeschools if he is elected to Congress next month.

"Well, first of all, I would love to have my name on the SAVE Act and put it into law. That's the first thing. I also think our trade schools are so important: to treat our trade school just like we have our Ivy League colleges.
CLICK HERE TO GET THE FOX NEWS APP

"We're funding our Ivy league colleges billions and billions of dollars and we're graduating unhirable people that, some of them, hate America. I think the trade schools need more support from our government and treat them just like the universities."
Strada will face off in the general election against Democrat James Pericola, a Clinton administration official.
David Unsworth reports on Latin America. You can follow David Unsworth on Twitter @LatinAmerUpdate

title: Ilhan Omar should be jailed, deported if citizenship fraud proven, Top House Republican says
summary: House Majority Whip Tom Emmer says Ilhan Omar should serve jail time and be deported if the federal investigation proves she lied on paperwork.
story: House Majority Whip Tom Emmer, R-Minn., spoke with Fox News Digital about the federal probe into Rep. Ilhan Omar and what he says should happen if it finds she lied to get citizenship.

EXCLUSIVE: The highest-ranking House lawmaker from Rep. Ilhan Omar's home state is calling for the embattled progressive to be jailed and deported if it is found that she or her father lied on federal paperwork to get her U.S. citizenship.

Omar, D-Minn., is under federal investigation over allegations that she or her father lied about her birth year on immigration paperwork in order to obtain her citizenship when her family fled Somalia in the late 1990s. She and other Democrats, including House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., have denounced the probe as political persecution of one of President Donald Trump's detractors weeks before a critical election.

But Majority Whip Tom Emmer, R-Minn., the No. 3 leader in the House of Representatives, told Fox News Digital that "there have been rumors for years" about Omar and, if proven true, she should face consequences.

"I would say first she should probably serve time in the gray bar motel and then get the hell out of here. She should go back to where she came from" if the allegations are proven to be true, Emmer said. "If it's determined that she lied to gain citizenship, then absolutely, she should go back to the front of the line."
REP ILHAN OMAR'S IMMIGRATION HISTORY FACES NEW SCRUTINY AS FEDERAL INVESTIGATORS SUBPOENA RELATIVES

House Majority Whip Tom Emmer, R-Minn., called for Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., to face consequences if the federal probe into her immigration proves wrongdoing. Omar has criticized the probe as political. (Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images; Graeme Sloan/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Omar is a member of the House "Squad," a far-left clique that includes Reps. Rashida Tlaib, D-Mich., and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y.
FEDERAL AGENTS RAID ILHAN OMAR’S DC HOME AMID IMMIGRATION FRAUD INVESTIGATION
Federal agents raided Omar's Washington, D.C., home earlier this week and took her cellphone and other possessions.
The allegations stem from her father becoming a U.S. citizen in 2000. Omar was believed to be 17 at the time, and as a minor was automatically qualified for citizenship under U.S. law along with him.
HOMAN CONFIRMS 'CRIMINAL' INVESTIGATION INVOLVING ILHAN OMAR, SAYS HE KNOWS 'THINGS ARE GOING ON’
But recently, it’s been alleged that she was actually 18 and would have needed to go through the process herself at that point.
Federal agents with Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) raided the Washington, D.C., home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., early Monday morning. (Andrew Murray/Fox News Digital)

"I’m ok. Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement. For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation," Omar posted on X after the raid. "I will not be silenced."
DEMOCRATS' FURY OVER ILHAN OMAR RAID DRAWS STINGING GOP REMINDER ABOUT RAID FROM THE PAST: ‘SET THE PRECEDENT’
Omar’s allies and other critics of the probe have called it an unprecedented action with less than three weeks before Election Day on Nov. 3.

Jeffries and his top deputies said in a joint statement that the raid was "deeply disturbing and raises serious questions about the continued corrupt weaponization of the federal government against Donald Trump’s adversaries."
Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., is seeking another term in Minnesota’s heavily Democratic 5th Congressional District. (Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call Inc. via Getty Images)

Emmer argued it was not political. He said that the existence of a judicially authorized search warrant, which the Department of Justice (DOJ) said was being acted on, meant there was a reasonable basis to believe the allegations could be true.

"That judge had to determine that there was probable cause that a federal crime has been committed. And I'll tell you what, as long as it was Ilhan Omar, it was going to be scrutinized to the very detail," Emmer said. "So the fact that they issued the warrant in the first place and then executed it, I mean maybe after all these years, someone is finally going to hold Ilhan Omar accountable."
Fox News Digital reached out to Omar’s congressional office for comment.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Fox News Digital's Peter D'Abrosca contributed to this report.
Elizabeth Elkind is a politics reporter for Fox News Digital leading coverage of the House of Representatives. Previous digital bylines seen at Daily Mail and CBS News.

title: Your bumper sticker could help Flock cameras track where you go — new bill aims to stop it
summary: Rep. Pat Harrigan's bill would require warrants for ALPR searches, delete records within 24 hours and ban tracking political or religious stickers.
story: Rep. Pat Harrigan, R-N.C., told Fox News Digital his bill would strengthen privacy protections and limit how law enforcement can use automated license plate readers.

FIRST ON FOX: Americans are sounding the alarm over privacy concerns surrounding Flock cameras and other automated license plate readers (ALPRs) that can snap photos of cars and track locations, and one GOP lawmaker is moving to close the gaps.

Rep. Pat Harrigan, R-N.C., introduced a bill Thursday that would ban ALPR searches targeting political or religious messages on vehicles, require warrants for most searches, mandate that records be deleted within 24 hours and prohibit vendors from selling or sharing location data.

"When you consider that these systems track everything that you do, where you work, where your kids go to school, where you even go to church, I think it's pretty easy to understand why people are concerned," Harrigan told Fox News Digital. "So that's an extraordinary amount of information about somebody that the government has that has never committed a crime."
POWERFUL CRIME-FIGHTING SURVEILLANCE GROWTH SPURS LAWMAKERS TO ISSUE WARNING: 'ORWELLIAN'
Rep. Pat Harrigan’s new bill would tighten restrictions on automated license plate readers, including Flock cameras, amid growing privacy concerns. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

Flock cameras and other ALPRs have drawn widespread debate. Law enforcement uses them in criminal investigations to collect searchable license plate, location and other vehicle data that allow officers to search by location and identify vehicles matching a suspect’s vehicle description.

Critics believe they raise constitutional concerns by tracking drivers without consent, while supporters say they are needed for crime prevention. President Donald Trump has voiced support for Flock cameras, telling reporters on Sept. 13 that he "sort of" likes them because of their use by law enforcement despite some people calling them "an infringement."

Harrigan's bill would impose restrictions on all ALPR systems, including prohibiting government agencies from categorizing vehicles by "expressive attributes" like political or religious bumper stickers, flags or decals.
HAWLEY RIPS FLOCK’S SPRAWLING SURVEILLANCE WEB AS TEXAS CITIES CUT CAMERAS OVER PRIVACY AND DATA FEARS

Rep. Pat Harrigan, R-N.C., conducts a news conference at the Republican National Committee after a meeting of the House Republican Conference on Tuesday, March 25, 2025. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

"At the end of the day, they have nothing to do with whether you committed a crime or not," Harrigan said. "As all of this data comes in and is vacuumed in by the government, it becomes searchable, particularly with the new technologies that we have surrounding artificial intelligence."

That means messages ranging from "Back the Blue" to "Jesus Saves" or "Black Lives Matter" could not be turned into searchable data. The bill would also block ALPR searches targeting political or religious activity, civil immigration violations, parking or non-moving traffic violations, debts and other civil penalties.
As ALPR technology expands, Flock Safety says its systems can detect bumper stickers but cannot identify their type, "like a political party or a house of worship."

However, its AI-powered FreeForm search allows users to search vehicle characteristics "in plain terms," raising questions about how bumper stickers and other markings could be used to identify vehicles. The company said safeguards are designed to block searches for vehicles based on political or religious bumper stickers and symbols.

The bill would require law enforcement to have a probable cause warrant in most searches, with exceptions for immediate threats to someone’s life or safety. Records would have to be deleted within 24 hours, with exceptions for warrants, emergencies and court orders.

It would also require agencies to log ALPR searches, publish annual reports and undergo audits. States without qualifying protections could lose 10% of certain federal criminal justice funding. Additionally, vendors would be prohibited from selling ALPR data or using it to train artificial intelligence (AI) models.

And for Americans worried about their Fourth Amendment rights, the bill would offer legal protections, allowing people to sue over illegal searches for at least $1,000 per violation and keep illegally obtained evidence out of court.
TEXAS GOV. GREG ABBOTT MOVES TO CUT STATE FUNDING FOR AI-POWERED FLOCK CAMERAS AMID PRIVACY CONCERNS
A Flock surveillance camera, which reads and records the license plate number and details of passing vehicles. (Jim West/UCG/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)

In August, The Washington Post found that at least 50 officers had been accused or charged with misusing license plate readers. Some reportedly used them to spy on romantic partners, exes or other women, with Flock’s system used in 46 cases.
Harrigan said the bill would not stop the technology from being used as an investigative tool and would instead place limits on how far law enforcement can go.

"Simultaneously, when we have technology that can benefit humanity and our experience here as Americans and make America safer, we should leverage that. But we have to strike the right balance," he said.
He said he believes lawmakers can get behind the bill "regardless of your political philosophy."

"Protecting Americans from criminals and protecting their constitutional rights, to me, those are two core responsibilities of government," he said. "And I think that that's something that members on both sides of the aisle can get behind."
