title: Why verified social media accounts can still lead you into a scam
summary: Microsoft's X account was hijacked to promote a crypto pump-and-dump scheme, exposing its more than 13 million followers to a scam campaign.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

We have all developed little shortcuts for deciding whether something online looks legitimate. You check the account name. You recognize the company logo. Then you spot that verification badge and your guard comes down a little. That can be exactly what scammers are counting on.

Microsoft’s official X account became the latest reminder after attackers gained unauthorized access and used the account in an apparent cryptocurrency pump-and-dump scheme. The account has more than 13 million followers, giving whoever controlled it access to a huge audience and the credibility that comes with Microsoft’s name.
Here is what happened, why compromised verified accounts can be so convincing and what you should check before trusting the next surprising post that shows up in your feed.
Join us for a free CyberGuy LIVE class.

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson shares practical ways to stay safer, smarter and more confident with technology. Explore classes on stopping spam, phone security, financial protection and using AI to get better health care . Each class is free, easy to follow and comes with a free printable checklist .
See the classes and register at CyberGuyLive.com
6 CRYPTO SCAM SCRIPTS CRIMINALS USE TO STEAL YOUR MONEY
Microsoft’s name and logo carry enormous trust, which is exactly why a compromised official account can make a scam look convincing. (Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
How Microsoft's X account got pulled into a crypto scheme

BleepingComputer reported that Microsoft's @Microsoft account followed and reposted content from another X account that appeared to be Clippy-themed. That account was promoting a cryptocurrency called $Clippy. Microsoft tells CyberGuy that two unauthorized posts appeared during the period when its account was compromised. According to the company, the first was a quote repost of content from what appeared to be a Clippy-themed account and referenced bringing back Microsoft Office's old animated paperclip character. The second appeared to be an apology related to the earlier activity. Microsoft says neither post originated from the company.

A Microsoft spokesperson provided CyberGuy with the following statement: "We have confirmed unauthorized access to our account on X, including posts that did not originate from Microsoft. The account has been secured, the unauthorized posts have been removed, and we are continuing to investigate the circumstances."
Why a verified account can make a scam much harder to spot

If an account you have never heard of suddenly tells you Microsoft launched a Clippy cryptocurrency, you might keep scrolling. When Microsoft’s actual account appears to amplify that same message, it becomes much easier to hesitate. You may assume someone at the company approved the post. You might click a link because you recognize the account. Someone interested in crypto could move even faster because they are worried about missing an opportunity.

That is the advantage attackers get when they compromise a well-known account. They inherit trust that has already been built for them. We recently saw the same basic weakness after hackers hijacked HBO Max’s verified Reddit account. Researchers found that attackers used the compromised account to push 108 malicious ads over roughly 48 hours. Because those ads appeared under a familiar verified account, they had an extra layer of credibility.
THOUSANDS OF HACKED SITES TRICK YOU INTO INSTALLING MALWARE
Microsoft said it did not authorize or endorse the $Clippy cryptocurrency token after unauthorized access to its X account.
Microsoft has dealt with a similar account takeover before

This is also not Microsoft’s first encounter with a crypto scam involving one of its X accounts. In June 2024, scammers hijacked Microsoft India’s X account and used it to impersonate Keith Gill, better known online as Roaring Kitty. The attackers then promoted what appeared to be a GameStop cryptocurrency presale.

People who followed the link and connected their cryptocurrency wallets risked having their assets stolen through wallet-draining malware. That example shows how quickly a social media takeover can turn into something much more expensive. A post may only be the beginning. The real danger often waits behind the link.
Even the SEC’s official X account was hijacked

One of the clearest examples happened in January 2024 when attackers took over the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission’s official X account. The compromised account falsely announced that the SEC had approved spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds. According to the Justice Department, Bitcoin jumped by more than $1,000 following the false post. After the SEC regained control and corrected the announcement, Bitcoin fell by more than $2,000.

Investigators later determined that attackers gained control through a SIM swap involving the phone number associated with the SEC account. Eric Council Jr. pleaded guilty in February 2025 to conspiracy charges related to the attack and was sentenced in May 2025 to 14 months in prison. That case gives us a good example of how much influence one compromised account can have. An official-looking post can spread quickly before the real organization has time to warn everyone that something has gone wrong.
A verification badge cannot guarantee who controls the account right now

A verification badge can still be useful. It may help confirm that an account belongs to the person, company or organization it claims to represent. What it cannot tell you is whether that same organization still controls the account at the exact moment you are reading a post.

Hackers can steal credentials through phishing or take advantage of other account takeover techniques. SIM swapping has also been used to intercept password reset codes and defeat some forms of two-factor authentication. CyberGuy has covered this problem before on X, where hackers have taken over verified accounts and then changed them to impersonate cryptocurrency projects. The account may look established because it is. The person controlling it may have changed.
The Microsoft account takeover shows why even posts tied to major companies should be verified before you click, invest or connect a crypto wallet. (David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
7 ways to protect yourself from scams posted by trusted accounts

You do not need to assume every surprising post is the work of a hacker. Still, when an account suddenly asks you to spend money or connect something valuable, a few extra checks can save you from a painful mistake.

If a company announces a cryptocurrency, giveaway or major investment opportunity on social media, go directly to the company’s website. Look for the same announcement in its newsroom or another official channel. If the only place you can find it is one social media post, wait before acting.

If an account that normally talks about software suddenly starts pushing an obscure crypto token, treat that change as a warning sign. Scroll through its recent posts and check whether the promotion fits anything the company has announced elsewhere.

Connecting a cryptocurrency wallet can expose you to malicious approvals that allow attackers to move assets. Navigate directly to a service you already trust instead. Never enter your recovery phrase or private key into a site because a social media post tells you to.

Strong antivirus software can help warn you about phishing sites, malicious downloads and other threats that may be waiting behind a suspicious link. Security software adds another layer of protection, but it should never replace slowing down and checking where a link came from. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android & iOS devices at Cyberguy.com

Scammers love deadlines. You may be told a token is launching right now or that an offer disappears in a few minutes. That pressure is designed to get you moving before you verify what you are seeing. Give yourself time to check another source.

Even when the post comes from a legitimate account, the link inside it may lead somewhere dangerous. Look carefully at the web address before entering a password, payment information or crypto credentials. Small changes in a domain name can lead you to an entirely different site.

Use a unique password for important accounts and turn on two-factor authentication (2FA). A password manager can help you create and store strong, unique passwords so you are less likely to reuse them across accounts. An authenticator app or passkey can provide stronger protection than relying only on texted security codes. Also check your account’s active sessions periodically and sign out any devices you do not recognize.
What to do if you already clicked
What you should do next depends on how far you got before realizing something looked suspicious.

Clicked the link only: Close the page. If a file downloaded automatically or you were prompted to install something, run a security scan with strong antivirus software.Entered a password: Go directly to the real website or app and change it immediately. Update that password anywhere else you reused it, then turn on two-factor authentication (2FA). Consider using a password manager to create and store strong, unique passwords for each account.Connected a crypto wallet: Review your token approvals and revoke anything you do not recognize. Revoking suspicious approvals can help prevent additional unauthorized transfers, but it cannot recover funds that have already been stolen.Exposed a recovery phrase or private key: Treat the wallet as compromised and move any remaining assets to a new secure wallet.
Clicked the link only: Close the page. If a file downloaded automatically or you were prompted to install something, run a security scan with strong antivirus software.

Entered a password: Go directly to the real website or app and change it immediately. Update that password anywhere else you reused it, then turn on two-factor authentication (2FA). Consider using a password manager to create and store strong, unique passwords for each account.

Connected a crypto wallet: Review your token approvals and revoke anything you do not recognize. Revoking suspicious approvals can help prevent additional unauthorized transfers, but it cannot recover funds that have already been stolen.
Exposed a recovery phrase or private key: Treat the wallet as compromised and move any remaining assets to a new secure wallet.
Kurt’s key takeaways

The Microsoft attack is a good reminder of how quickly the signals we rely on can turn against us. We tell people to check the account name, look for the real profile and be cautious with impersonators. In this case, attackers briefly had control of the account people were supposed to trust. I would still use verification as one clue, but I would never let a checkmark do the thinking for me when money, passwords or a crypto wallet are involved. If a company suddenly posts something that feels out of character, verify it somewhere else before you act. Go to the company’s website, check another official channel and give yourself a minute before clicking. That extra pause can be the difference between spotting a scam and paying for one.

title: Detective suspected in girl’s murder may have killed others, former investigator fears
summary: A fingerprint on an 8-year-old's communion purse finally identified Chicago cop Thomas McInerney as Gloria Kowalewicz's killer after 65 years, police say.
story: Chicago cop Thomas F. McInerney Jr. has been identified as the man who abducted, shot and killed Gloria Kowalewicz on Nov. 12, 1960.
More than 65 years of searching for a killer has ended: Chicago police say they now know who shot an 8-year-old girl walking to mass.
He was part of the force.
Chicago cop Thomas F. McInerney Jr. has been identified as the man who abducted, shot and killed Gloria Kowalewicz on Nov. 12, 1960.
Thomas F. McInerney Jr. joined the Chicago Police Department not long before killing Gloria Kowalewicz. (Chicago Police Department)
FORMER CHICAGO POLICE DETECTIVE LINKED BY DNA TO 8-YEAR-OLD GIRL'S COLD-CASE MURDER, POLICE SAY
At the time, McInerney was a recent addition to the agency, a violent crimes detective with the Chicago Police Department. He died in 2006.
But evidence pointing to him as the killer lived on. And recent improvements in technology finally brought answers.
DNA TECHNOLOGY LEADS TO ARREST IN 1988 KILLING OF ORLANDO WOMAN AFTER NEARLY FOUR DECADES
Just before 8 a.m. on the morning of her death, Kowalewicz began walking a few blocks from her home to St. Mary of Mt. Carmel Church. She never arrived.
About four hours later, her body was found in a ditch in a forest preserve southwest of Chicago. Her killer left evidence scattered at the scene of the crime and along a highway back to Chicago.
Investigators found a bullet, Kowalewicz’s coat, her shoes, and her little, white communion purse that held her prayer book. But the killer was never identified.
Gloria Kowalewicz was abducted and killed in Chicago on Nov. 12, 1960. (Findagrave.com)

But recently, investigators pursued more clues using updated technology. Ultimately, it was a fingerprint lifted off the strap of her purse that led investigators to McInerney after more than six decades.
DNA BREAKTHROUGH LEADS TO ARREST IN GRISLY 33-YEAR-OLD COLD CASE INVESTIGATORS NEVER GAVE UP ON
Rogue cop
As part of the investigation, Chicago police formed a task force. They knocked on hundreds of doors and interviewed more than 1,300 people in the hopes of finding the girl's killer.
More than a dozen people were questioned under a polygraph. The man responsible continued to blend inside the department.

"It's not that law enforcement was incompetent at the time—they just didn't have the sophisticated investigative tools," said Michael Gould, a founding member of the New York Police Department’s K-9 unit.
Using K-9 teams to track the scent of the killer could have been a more effective strategy, Gould told Fox News Digital.
Chicago cop Thomas F. McInerney Jr. has been identified as the man who abducted, shot and killed Gloria Kowalewicz on Nov. 12, 1960. (Findagrave.com)
But using dogs to investigate crimes wasn’t widely adopted until the mid ‘80s, Gould said. Now, they’re routinely used and have "cracked a lot of missing person cases."
"Dogs could have tracked where the person lived and what direction he fled."
"They give us X-ray vision. They allow us to see things—evidence—that's invisible to the naked eye. And that's what the primary locating tool should be for law enforcement, police K-9."
KILLER EX-COP EXECUTED FOR CHILD'S SLAYING AS SHERIFF SAYS HE’S SURE SAME MONSTER MURDERED ANOTHER GIRL

The DNA and fingerprint evidence was preserved for decades until, finally, technology advanced enough to bring answers.

The Chicago Police Department said DNA evidence and a preserved fingerprint helped investigators identify the killer of 8-year-old Gloria Kowalewicz more than 65 years after her murder. (Talia Sprague/Chicago Tribune/Tribune News Service via Getty Images)

It’s rare for law enforcement to maintain records and keep evidence that long, Gould said.
He expects the DNA connection may lead to solving more cold cases.
"My prediction there are going to be other victims [linked to McInerney]. I don't think this was a sole act."

"This, in my view, would have been a planned and intentional act. It's rare that this happens once in a serial murderer's life," he said. "They don't do it one time. In fact, it usually escalates when they're successful."

title: Serial killer's ex-wife slept beside murderer for 8 years, never suspected his deadly double life
summary: Bonnie Lou Gower reveals the haunting warning signs she missed while sharing a bed with serial killer Richard Evonitz for over eight years.
story: The two-part special, ‘The Amazon Review Killer,’ is now streaming on Fox Nation.
This story discusses suicide. If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or 1-800-273-TALK (8255).
For years, Bonnie Lou Gower shared a bed with a man she thought she knew better than anyone. She had no idea the man sleeping beside her was capable of murder.
Her husband, Richard "Marc" Evonitz, was leading a double life, one that would ultimately expose him as a serial killer who preyed on young girls.
His victims included a 16-year-old who lost her life while Evonitz was still married to Gower.
SERIAL KILLER SURVIVOR WHO ESCAPED 18-HOUR CAPTIVITY REVEALS INSTINCT SHE WISHES SHE NEVER IGNORED
Richard Evonitz and Bonnie Lou Gower were married from August 1988 to January 1997. (Investigation Discovery)
Decades after Evonitz’s crimes came to light, Gower is revisiting the warning signs she didn't recognize — alongside the young woman who survived him.

In Investigation Discovery’s true crime docuseries "The Serial Killer Connection," Gower meets with Kara Robinson Chamberlain, who endured 18 hours of captivity and torture before escaping Evonitz, as they investigate whether he may be linked to other unsolved cases.
For Gower, one question has followed her since learning the truth about the man she married.
Bonnie Lou Gower has since remarried. She's now the mother of two children. (Investigation Discovery)
"When I initially learned about [his crimes] and I told people, honestly their first response is, ‘Well, obviously you knew. How could you not have known?’" Gower told Fox News Digital.

"That was my very first question to the FBI. ‘How could I not know this? How could I not know I was sleeping next to somebody for eight and a half years that was doing this?’ And of course, they assured me that there’s no way I could have known."
Looking back, Gower admitted there were things she didn’t question at the time.

Bonnie Lou Gower and Richard Evonitz are seen here in the 1990s. Gower told Fox News Digital that whenever she traveled to visit her family, Evonitz insisted on staying home. (Investigation Discovery)
Whenever she left town to visit family, Evonitz insisted on staying behind, claiming he had to work. Only later did Gower discover that he had actually taken time off while she was away.
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X
"One of the reasons he never came with me was because he said he was working," said Gower.
Richard Evonitz is seen here in South Carolina, circa 1988. (Investigation Discovery)

"And then, I come to find out, he had actually taken off work on the days that I was out of town. But at the time, I wasn’t at all concerned about leaving him behind. I was just going and visiting my family. It definitely makes you look at everybody and everything now, whether you can trust someone’s words or actions."

Gower met Evonitz, who was eight years her senior, in South Carolina. He was the older brother of one of her friends and would come home whenever he was on leave from the U.S. Navy. She quickly developed a crush on him as she got to know him and, at age 16, Evonitz asked her out on a date.
They married in August 1988 when she was 17 and he was 25.
After marrying, Bonnie Lou Gower and Richard Evonitz moved from South Carolina to Maine, where Evonitz was stationed at the time. (Investigation Discovery)

"You think you know who you are when you’re 17, but I really don’t think I did," said Gower. "I don’t think I had a handle on that. And I was relatively sheltered. I was very naïve, very trusting, taking everything at face value. I think he knew that."

During the marriage, there were moments when Gower suspected Evonitz was being unfaithful. Whenever she questioned him, Evonitz told her it was all in her head. She believed him. But as the relationship progressed, Evonitz began isolating her from friends and family as they moved around the country, from Maine to San Diego to Virginia.
SIGN UP TO GET THE TRUE CRIME NEWSLETTER
Bonnie Lou Gower initially believed Richard Evonitz was having an affair. He assured Gower it was all in her head. (Investigation Discovery)

"No one ever thinks that their significant other is going to be a serial killer," Chamberlain told Fox News Digital. "I think worst case, and this is something that she expressed to me, he was having an affair. No one ever thinks your spouse is out murdering someone."
"He kept that part of himself very tightly controlled and didn’t show it to the people he was closest to."
In "The Serial Killer Connection," a three-part docuseries, Bonnie Lou Gower and Kara Robinson Chamberlain retrace Richard Evonitz's past. (Investigation Discovery)

The marriage began to unravel after Evonitz left the Navy. Gower said financial pressures fueled growing tensions between the couple, while Evonitz became prone to mood swings and what she described as "rages." He also frequently criticized her weight. Behind closed doors, Gower was also uncomfortable with his interest in bondage, according to the docuseries.

In June 2002, Bonnie Lou Gower (seen here with Richard Evonitz in the '90s) discovered that her ex-husband was a murderer who had killed at least three young girls and kidnapped a fourth. The FBI showed up at her doorstep in California and informed her of her ex's secret double life. (Investigation Discovery)

Even as the marriage reached its breaking point, Gower said she still didn’t see Evonitz as someone capable of hurting her. Walking away, she said, was a decision that came after years of mounting unhappiness.
When Gower made the decision to leave the marriage, Gower said her fear was for him, not herself.
"I was concerned for his safety when he said he was going to take the gun and kill himself," Gower recalled. "I never feared for my own life."
SEND US A TIP
According to the FBI, Richard Evonitz fled to Sarasota, Florida, where he took his life after being surrounded by law enforcement. (FBI)
Even after she finally walked away, Gower said Evonitz had left her questioning whether she had any justification for doing so.
"When I left, I felt like I was leaving for no real good reason," she said. "[But] I wasn’t happy."

According to Gower's TikTok, she and Evonitz were married from August 1988 until January 1997. Multiple reports indicate that their divorce was finalized in 1998. Years later, Gower would learn just how much she hadn’t known about the man she left behind.
For 18 hours, Richard Evonitz held teenage Kara Robinson Chamberlain captive in his apartment, where he sexually assaulted her. (Investigation Discovery)

On June 24, 2002, 15-year-old Chamberlain was at a friend’s home in South Carolina when Evonitz pulled into the driveway. The stranger approached her with pamphlets and asked if her parents were home. Then, he held a gun to her neck and threatened to shoot her if she screamed. He forced Chamberlain into a dark storage container in his car.

At Evonitz’s apartment, Chamberlain was repeatedly sexually assaulted. He restrained her to a bed. After hours of torture, Chamberlain managed to free one of her hands from a pair of handcuffs with her teeth, unclip a leather leg restraint and quietly bolt out the door as Evonitz slept. As she took off, Chamberlain encountered two men who took her to a police station.
Kara Robinson Chamberlain after her medical exam. (Investigation Discovery)

Chamberlain led officers back to her captor’s apartment. But when investigators arrived, Evonitz had escaped. Police tracked Evonitz to Sarasota, Florida, but as they closed in on him, Evonitz died by suicide. He was 38.
GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL

Richard Evonitz shot and killed himself after a 100 mph car chase from Manatee County ended on Bayfront Drive across from Maria Jack in Sarasota, Florida, on June 27, 2002. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect)

Once investigators began digging into Evonitz’s past, Chamberlain’s abduction proved to be only part of the story. Evidence recovered from Evonitz’s South Carolina apartment, former Virginia residence and vehicle linked him to three unsolved murders.
Kara Robinson Chamberlain worked with law enforcement as a sex crime and child abuse investigator. (Investigation Discovery)

On Sept. 9, 1996, Evonitz abducted 16-year-old Sofia Silva from the front steps of her home in Spotsylvania County, Virginia, where he and Gower had been living. Her body was discovered about five weeks later in neighboring King George County.

Then, on May 1, 1997, sisters Kristin "Kristi" Lisk, 15, and Kathryn "Kati" Lisk, 12, vanished after returning home from school. Both girls had been sexually assaulted and strangled. Their bodies were discovered five days later in the South Anna River.
After her abduction, Kara Robinson Chamberlain went on to pursue a career in law enforcement. (Investigation Discovery)
Notes discovered by investigators indicated that Evonitz already had his eye on other potential victims, Fox News Digital previously reported.
It would be months after Chamberlain’s abduction that Gower learned of her ex-husband’s other victims.

"It felt like it wasn’t real at all," Gower admitted. "It felt like this was something that happens in the movies. This wasn’t real life. It was very hard to believe that he could hurt anybody. He had never hit me or physically abused me."
GET REAL-TIME UPDATES DIRECTLY ON THE TRUE CRIME HUB

After escaping, Kara Robinson Chamberlain went straight to law enforcement. She provided crucial information that led investigators to her captor’s apartment and helped identify him as the man responsible for at least three previously unsolved murders. (FOX Image Collection via Getty Images)
Now, Gower and Chamberlain are looking to Evonitz’s past for answers about whether there could be other victims.
Gower has helped piece together a timeline of Evonitz’s movements during their marriage, providing investigators with dates, locations and old calendars as potential cold cases are examined.
"Of course, he wasn’t always where I thought he was," said Gower.
Kara Robinson Chamberlain previously appeared in "America's Most Wanted" opposite John Walsh to raise awareness on the stories of victims. (FOX Image Collection via Getty Images)

Chamberlain, meanwhile, has been investigating whether Evonitz could be responsible for other unsolved crimes, examining cases dating back to the 1980s and tracing his movements during his years in the Navy and in the decades before her own abduction.

"I genuinely think that there is a level of escalation that we see between an indecent exposure [incident] and then three homicides in approximately nine months and then a break before me that is unexplainable to me," she said.
Today, Kara Robinson Chamberlain is a survivor advocate. (Investigation Discovery)
"Everything’s possible and nothing has been confirmed," Chamberlain stressed. "It’s a frustrating place to be, but I will not stop searching."
LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST
Kara Robinson Chamberlain is adamant that Richard Evonitz may be responsible for other crimes across the country. (Investigation Discovery)
One potential key to finding answers is DNA.

While investigating cases for the docuseries, Chamberlain said she learned that Evonitz’s DNA profile was not in CODIS, the FBI’s national DNA database. However, she said authorities in Spotsylvania County still have a blood sample that can be provided to law enforcement agencies seeking to compare his DNA with evidence from other cases.
Chamberlain said she hopes Evonitz’s DNA can ultimately be entered into CODIS, allowing for broader comparisons with evidence from unsolved crimes.

Bonnie Lou Gower (left), alongside Kara Robinson Chamberlain, is looking back at forgotten notes and old calendars to provide more information that could uncover fresh clues and leads. (Investigation Discovery)
"I genuinely believe that there’s no way he only murdered three girls and kidnapped me," she said. "I don’t think that there’s a world in which that’s true."
"The Serial Killer Connection" airs Wednesdays at 9 p.m. Episodes will be available to stream on HBO Max. (Investigation Discovery)

While making the docuseries, Gower learned that Evonitz had kept a photograph of her when she was just 11 years old — years before they began dating — hidden behind another framed picture of her. Gower said it was not a photograph she had taken with her when she left home and that she never knew Evonitz possessed it.
"It’s disturbing enough that he would have 11-year-old me in a picture behind something," she said.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE
Kara Robinson Chamberlain (left) was nervous about meeting Bonnie Lou Gower (right). They became fast friends. (Investi)
Decades after learning the truth about the man she married, Gower said she is still trying to make sense of it.
"I don’t think you ever make sense of it," she said. "There’s no tidy little box to put it in to make it make sense."
SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS
Bonnie Lou Gower is seen here embracing Kara Robinson Chamberlain. (Investigation Discovery)
"I’m still grappling with it. I’m still processing."
Stephanie Nolasco is an Entertainment Reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Alex Murdaugh's defense makes 'high risk' move to show DNA proves he didn't kill family, prosecutor says
summary: Alex Murdaugh's defense team is betting on a Y-STR DNA test by Othram that prosecutors call "high risk" ahead of his April 2027 murder retrial.
story: Criminal defense attorney and Fox News contributor Josh Ritter said that Alex Murdaugh's win in court on a motion to test DNA samples from Maggie Murdaugh could potentially backfire on him.
LEXINGTON, S.C. – Alex Murdaugh’s defense team is gambling on a "high risk" DNA test in its bid to point to another killer, a prosecutor said, citing the defense’s own expert.

Judge Debra McCaslin sided with the defense over prosecutors’ objections Friday, allowing new testing on swabs from Maggie Murdaugh’s cellphone and clippings from under her fingernails, even though the process will likely use up the last of the testable samples. McCaslin said due process requires that a defendant be given "a meaningful opportunity to present a full and complete defense."

Murdaugh was convicted in 2023 of murdering his wife, Maggie, and son, Paul, at the family's Moselle property in Colleton County. The South Carolina Supreme Court later overturned the convictions after finding that former Colleton County Clerk of Court Becky Hill improperly influenced the jury.
His retrial is scheduled to begin April 5, 2027. Murdaugh has maintained his innocence in the killings.
MURDAUGH WANTS IDAHO MURDERS DNA DREAM TEAM BEHIND KOHBERGER CASE TO HELP REWRITE SECOND MURDER TRIAL
Alex Murdaugh at a pretrial hearing in Lexington, South Carolina on Oct. 16, 2026. (Tracy Glantz of The State and Henry Taylor of The Post and Courier.)

The defense team plans to employ Othram to conduct a Y-STR test, a method that isolates DNA from the Y chromosome to generate a profile of a male contributor in samples where female DNA is predominant.

Murdaugh's attorneys contend that all three samples contain unidentified male DNA and are seeking to determine whether a single man was the source. Defense attorney Phil Barber said the findings could rule out certain individuals as contributors and may provide ancestry information, although the test cannot differentiate between men who share the same paternal ancestors.
MURDAUGH DEFENSE SAYS NEWLY DISCLOSED RESERVE DNA SAMPLES SHOULD GO TO OTHRAM BEFORE STATE ANALYSIS
Alex Murdaugh's attorney, Dick Harpootlian, speaks at a pretrial hearing on Oct. 16, 2026. (Tracy Glantz of The State and Henry Taylor of The Post and Courier)
The defense said the process will require approximately 90 days.
Creighton Waters, the lead prosecutor, said in court that the testing would be "high risk" and unlikely to generate significant evidence.
ALEX MURDAUGH'S 'WILD GOOSE CHASE' FOR MISSING MURDER GUNS TARGETS POLICE CHIEF: EXPERT

"When we talked to their expert, he said, yeah, that’s pretty much a sole source sample. This would be high risk and unlikely to generate anything, and [it] appears that that’s the case, because when we got back the quantification from [Othram], it’s goose eggs on the Y chromosome," Waters said.
Barber laid out his reasoning for the new test, acknowledging the unknown male DNA could have an innocent explanation but saying the pattern is hard to ignore.
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X
Alex Murdaugh in court on Oct. 16, 2026. (Tracy Glantz of The State and Henry Taylor of The Post and Courier)

"Maybe it’s different male DNA. Maybe it’s the same. Maybe it’s red herrings ... But as we keep progressing from one hand to two hands and now the phone, you know, it’s starting to look less and less like a red herring," Barber said. "If you have an unknown person under both her fingernails and throwing the phone out the side of the road after she’s murdered and it’s not him. I mean, that’s extremely important to the defense."
SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS
Notably, the defense and prosecution both said once the DNA test is performed, there won't be enough samples left to test again in any post-trial proceedings, which Murdaugh was OK with.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM THE FOX TRUE CRIME HUB
"To perform the test, there is enough to perform the test, but there’s not enough to perform the test and then have enough left over," Barber said.
SEND US A TIP
"My client just informed me that he will waive that," he said referring to any post-conviction retesting.
ALEX MURDAUGH DEFENSE SAYS MURDER WEAPON MAY BE TIED TO SEPARATE KILLING AS JUDGE SEEKS ANSWERS

Alex Murdaugh arrives for a judicial hearing on Monday, June 29, 2026, at the Marc H. Westbrook Judicial Center in Lexington, South Carolina. Murdaugh will be retried in the June 7, 2021, shooting deaths of his wife and son, after his original conviction was overturned due to jury tampering. (Tracy Glantz/The State via Pool)

Former prosecutor Joshua Ritter told Fox News Digital the strategy could backfire, saying the defense may have been better off leaving the DNA untested and using the unknown male profile to raise reasonable doubt at trial.
LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

"They could make an argument, hey you found samples, it was unknown male DNA. That DNA did not come back to our client, correct? There's somebody else out there who could potentially be linked to this crime," Ritter said. "Now, unless it comes back that it's a person who does have some reason to be suspicious, they've got a problem because if it comes back to a person with a rock solid alibi or a person with an innocent explanation as to why their DNA would end up underneath her fingernails, they've foreclosed any argument that they could have made."
GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL
Alex Murdaugh, right, is shown here with his family. (Fox News)
"It's one of those situations where sometimes it's better left unknown for the defense, but they seem to be determined to try to figure out who that DNA belongs to," he added.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Murdaugh is due back in court on Nov. 13.
Fox News Digital reached out to Murdaugh's defense team for comment.
Adam Sabes is a reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to Adam.Sabes@fox.com and on Twitter @asabes10.

title: Hero dad who took down Oregon school shooter identified along with teacher, student both killed in attack
summary: The teacher killed in a shooting at a Bend, Oregon, school was identified by police Friday as 25-year-old Meghan Lambert. The hero who took down the shooter was Kaylub Giamanco.
story: Bend Police Department Chief Mike Krantz shares new details about Thursday's shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, during a news conference Friday.

The good Samaritan who police in Bend, Oregon, said "neutralized" the 16-year-old shooter who killed three children and a teacher Thursday at Silver Rail Elementary School has been identified as 36-year-old Kaylub Giamanco, a law enforcement source confirmed to Fox News Digital.

During a news conference Friday, police identified the teacher who was killed in the shooting as 25-year-old Meghan Lambert, and also announced that among the youngest of the victims was 5-year-old Rhoam Summer. Police also revealed a school staff member threw a cellphone and tackled the attacker during the harrowing incident.

"Meghan was compassionate and had a huge heart. She always fought for the underdog and those with special needs. She was an incredible sister, daughter, niece and granddaughter. Her friends became her family," Lambert's family said in a statement read at the news conference.
ARMED BYSTANDER FATALLY SHOOTS SUSPECTED TEEN GUNMAN AFTER 3 CHILDREN, 1 ADULT KILLED AT OREGON SCHOOL: FEDS
"Yesterday was a terrible day for our community," Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said during the news conference. "Five people succumbed to their injuries at the scene, including the suspect.

"The deceased at the school scene included three children — ages 5, 8 and 11 — and one 25-year-old teacher. One 7-year-old child and a 54-year-old teacher were transported by Bend Fire to Saint Charles Bend with critical injuries."
The 7-year-old is in serious but stable condition, and the 54-year-old teacher suffered non-life-threatening injuries.

Krantz said that, at 12:58 p.m., a witness who was driving by the school saw the suspect throw his gun over a fence and then climb the fence onto school property. He said the witness confronted the suspect, who then fired at his truck, hitting it at least three times. The driver, who was not injured by the gunfire, went down the street and made the initial 911 call at 12:59 p.m., he said.

Giamanco, who Krantz only identified as a "36-year-old man" during the briefing, drove into the school parking lot after seeing the suspect shoot at the truck, Krantz said, and saw the suspect shoot the glass panes on two double doors to get inside.
POLICE DISPTACH AUDIO RELEASED AFTER OREGON ELEMENTARY SCHOOL SHOOTING
Police tape is placed outside Silver Rail Elementary school after a shooting Thursday in Bend, Ore. (Joe Kline/AP Photo)
Once he was inside, the shooter went straight into the classroom that was to the left and fired as many as 15 rounds.
Krantz said the shooter used three types of ammunition and that all the victims were shot in the classroom.

Giamanco grabbed a .40-caliber pistol he legally kept in his car and went into the school through the same doors. After hearing the sounds of a shooting, he went into the classroom, where he saw the suspect struggling with a teacher, who had thrown her cellphone at and tackled the shooter.
Giamanco shot him multiple times.

"In addition to the 36-year-old man who bravely stepped in to stop the suspect, I want to highlight another person whose heroic action we need to recognize," Krantz said. "A teacher in the classroom threw her cellphone at the suspect and then tackled him and fought to take the firearm from him.
"She was not injured in that incident, but she almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed."
DEMOCRATS' LATEST GUN-CONTROL PUSH RUNS INTO INCONVENIENT FACT ABOUT HOW SCHOOL KILLER WAS STOPPED
Map locating Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Ore., where three children and an adult were killed in a shooting on Thursday, according to federal law enforcement sources. (Fox News)

Police arrived at the school within minutes of the 911 call at 1:02 p.m. having been told that the "suspect had been shot by a community member who had seen the suspect enter the school and pursued him into the school and engaged him, shooting him several times," Krantz said.
Earlier Friday, Kenda Freeman said in a statement that her son, Giamanco, intervened in the attack and shot the gunman who killed three students and a teacher, The Associated Press reported.
Giamanco, a local carpenter and dad, has two daughters who attend Silver Rail, his brother, Kyle Gianmaco, told NBC News.
Kyle shared that Kaylub is shaken by the event and doesn't want to speak to the public.
"We want the bystander who intervened to know we know he is going through a rough time, but we are grateful, and we think he is a hero," Lambert's family added in the statement.
"You selflessly put yourself at risk for others. We would like the other families to know they are in our thoughts and prayers. Meghan loved those children, and so we will show you love for her."
Flowers are placed beside a sign at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Ore., Friday, a day after a deadly shooting. (Haven Daley/AP Photo)
The shooter forced his way into the school by firing a shotgun at locked doors, Krantz said, citing the initial investigation.
He said the shooter fired as many as 15 times and had about 44 rounds remaining when he was killed.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
On Thursday, Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek praised school staff, parents and first responders, along with the community member "who heroically intervened to stop further loss of life."
Silver Rail Elementary School is a public school in the Bend-La Pine Schools District with roughly 400 students, kindergarten through fifth grade, and approximately 40 staff members.
Fox News Digital's Stepheny Price, and Fox News' David Spunt and Bill Melugin contributed to this story.
Brie Stimson is a Los Angeles-based entertainment and breaking news writer for Fox News Digital.

title: Bryan Kohberger fights to remove judge who called him 'worst of the worst,' questioned his honesty
summary: Bryan Kohberger's new attorney accuses Latah County prosecutors of dodging key arguments in his motion to disqualify Judge Steven Hippler from the case.
story: Idaho prosecutors urge a judge to reject murder suspect Bryan Kohberger's attempt to withdraw his guilty plea, calling the defense's arguments a fishing expedition. Former federal prosecutor Jonathan Fahey joins to break down the latest legal maneuvers, the strength of the state's case and what lies ahead for the victims' families in the high-profile trial.
Bryan Kohberger's new lawyer is taking another swing at Idaho prosecutors in his fight to have the judge who called his client a "faceless coward" removed from post-conviction proceedings.

Court-appointed attorney Greg Rauch is accusing Latah County prosecutors of "regurgitating" rules rather than addressing concerns raised in his motion to disqualify Judge Steven Hippler from the case.
Hippler said Kohberger, 31, "slithered" into the victims' home before committing a crime that made him "the worst of the worst" after the killer admitted guilt last year.

At issue, according to Rauch, "is how [Hippler's] statements about counsel’s preparation and [Kohberger's] capacity for truthfulness bear on the disputes it may now decide, in combination with the myriad of other statements made."
KOHBERGER PROSECUTORS SAY NO AS IDAHO KILLER TRIES TO BOOT JUDGE WHO CALLED HIM A 'FACELESS COWARD'

Judge Steven Hippler of Idaho's 4th Judicial District in Ada County rejected the latest attempt by Bryan Kohberger's defense to drop the death penalty as a possible sentence if a jury convicts him of killing four University of Idaho students in 2022. (Katherine Jones/Idaho Statesman/Tribune News Service via Getty Images)
And when addressing the fact that there would be no allocution or explanation from Kohberger, the judge also questioned whether Kohberger even possessed the capacity to say something truthful.

"Even if I could force him to speak, which legally I cannot, how could anyone ever be assured that what he speaks is the truth?" Hippler asked during sentencing. "Do we really believe, after all of this, he is capable of speaking the truth, or of giving up something of himself to help the very people whose lives he destroyed? Rather, I suspect the so-called reason would be dished out in enticing self-serving and aggrandizing untruthful bits, leaving people wanting more information, more insight, and thus enhancing even further the power he seeks to hold."
BRYAN KOHBERGER DIDN'T UNDERSTAND WHAT HE WAS DOING WHEN HE PLEADED GUILTY: UNSEALED MEMO

Bryan Kohberger appeared at the Ada County Courthouse for his sentencing hearing on July 23, 2025, in Boise, Idaho. Kohberger pleaded guilty in exchange for being spared the death penalty for the stabbing of four University of Idaho students nearly three years earlier. (Kyle Green-Pool/Getty Images)
Rauch wrote that "of course" judges can deny defense motions, "condemn terrible crimes," and go on to preside over post-conviction claims.
BRYAN KOHBERGER'S NEW LAWYER SAYS KEY QUESTIONS MAY SOON GET ANSWERS IN COURT
"The question is not whether someone might criticize the Court, but whether an informed, reasonable observer could question its impartiality in light of this connected record," he wrote.

And it's not just that Hippler tore into Kohberger at sentencing. He has also taken issue with a June scheduling order days before Kohberger surprised the country and pleaded guilty to avoid the death penalty.

University of Idaho students Madison Mogen, Kaylee Goncalves, Xana Kernodle and Ethan Chapin were killed in a November 2022 attack at an off-campus house on King Road in Moscow, Idaho. (Idaho Statesman/Tribune News Service via Getty Images)

story: Former University of Kentucky cheerleader Laken Snelling was sentenced to 10 years in prison on Friday after pleading guilty to manslaughter in connection with the death of her infant child. Credit: WDKY

Laken Snelling, a former University of Kentucky cheerleader, was sentenced to 10 years in prison Friday, according to local media, after being convicted of first-degree manslaughter for the death of her infant child.
Snelling, who was indicted for manslaughter and three other charges in March, pleaded guilty in August.

Officers from the Lexington Police Department arrested Snelling in August 2025 after her roommates heard loud noises coming from her closet. When officers arrived on scene, they found the infant cold to the touch and wrapped in a trash bag placed in the closet, the city of Lexington announced in a statement.

"I was under a lot of emotional stress and my baby came unexpectedly," Snelling said through tears while in court. "And instead of helping him, I ended his life and afterward I cleaned up and didn’t tell anyone."

In addition to the manslaughter charge, Snelling pleaded guilty to charges of abuse of a corpse, tampering with physical evidence and concealing the birth of an infant.

Snelling, who was a senior at the time, told investigators that she was awake for 30 minutes after giving birth, but then passed out on top of the baby.

title: Texas woman sentenced to 7 years in prison, annual jail time during probation for deadly DUI crash
summary: Lynlee Pollis, who was sentenced to prison in a deadly DUI crash, must return to jail for 15 days each year on dates tied to the victims' birthdays and the anniversary of 2023 crash in Dallas.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.
A Texas woman convicted of killing a college student in a drunken-driving crash was sentenced to seven years in prison and ordered to return to jail for 15 days each year while on probation.

Lynlee Pollis, 30, was sentenced Wednesday after being convicted of intoxication manslaughter and intoxication assault in the September 2023 crash that killed 19-year-old Southern Methodist University student Honor Wallace and seriously injured her friend, Catherine "CeCe" Solberg, according to The Dallas Morning News.
State District Judge Jennifer Balido also ordered Pollis to serve 10 years of probation following her release from prison, including 15 days in jail annually.
Some of the required jail dates coincide with the victims' birthdays, Pollis' birthday and the anniversary of the deadly crash, according to the newspaper.
NEVADA PAROLE BOARD REJECTS HENRY RUGGS III'S BID FOR EARLY RELEASE AFTER DEADLY 156 MPH DUI CRASH
Lynlee Pollis, 30, was sentenced to seven years in prison after being convicted of intoxication manslaughter and intoxication assault in a 2023 Dallas crash that killed a college student. (Facebook)
The sentence came after roughly three hours of jury deliberations following a two-and-a-half-week trial.
During the trial, Solberg's father, Bobby Solberg, delivered an emotional victim impact statement criticizing Pollis for putting the families through the lengthy proceedings.
"You were so drunk, and you wouldn’t admit it. You made us sit through this [trial] for three weeks," Solberg said. "We’ve seen no personal accountability from you."
PROMINENT BUSINESSMAN LEARNS FATE IN BOAT CRASH CASE THAT KILLED TEEN, MAIMED ANOTHER

A Texas woman convicted in a deadly drunken-driving crash was ordered to serve additional jail time each year during her probation following her prison sentence. (Dallas County Jail/Southern Methodist University)
Wallace's father, David Wallace, also confronted Pollis in his victim impact statement.
"You took the most precious gift from us through your selfishness," he said. "Own it. Own what you did."
On Sept. 24, 2023, Wallace was driving her Volkswagen Jetta through a green light in Dallas when Pollis' Lexus SUV slammed into her vehicle.

Wallace was pronounced dead at the hospital, while Solberg, a passenger in the Jetta, suffered a shoulder injury and concussion. She was later diagnosed with a traumatic brain injury, according to The Dallas Morning News.
DRUNK REPEAT OFFENDER CALLED A 'TICKING TIME-BOMB' BEFORE 80-MPH BOATING COLLISION KILLED WOMAN: PROSECUTORS
Lynlee Pollis was convicted in connection with a September 2023 crash that killed 19-year-old Honor Wallace and seriously injured another Southern Methodist University student. (Facebook)

According to testimony from prosecution experts cited by the newspaper, Pollis was traveling approximately 67 mph in a 35-mph zone and drove through a traffic light that had been red for at least five seconds.
Pollis' husky named Tequila, who was also in the vehicle, was not hurt.
The newspaper reported that testing showed Pollis had a blood alcohol concentration of 0.294%, nearly four times Texas' legal limit of 0.08%.
According to the initial arrest affidavit, officers noticed Pollis had glassy eyes, slurred speech and an odor of alcohol when they interviewed her at the hospital.
Her attorneys had sought probation rather than prison, pointing to her lack of prior felony convictions.

Defense attorney Scott Palmer said during his closing argument that Pollis was a "good person who made a terrible decision."

title: Alex Murdaugh judge warns against courtroom 'circus' as defense wins DNA fight, loses ballistics bid
summary: Alex Murdaugh's defense claims a Yemassee police chief was seen with the murder weapons, but a former prosecutor calls it a "wild goose chase."
story: Former prosecutor Joshua Ritter said Alex Murdaugh's defense is "grasping at straws" by pursuing uncorroborated claims about missing murder weapons ahead of his retrial.

LEXINGTON, S.C. — The judge overseeing Alex Murdaugh’s double-murder retrial rebuked both sides Friday over their bitter evidence fights, warning she "will not allow these proceedings to become a circus."
During the tense hearing, Judge Debra McCaslin handed the defense a win on their DNA testing request but rejected its broader request for ballistic data.

McCaslin also corrected the record on a polygraph claim that Murdaugh attorney Dick Harpootlian made in August, which he said Murdaugh passed with "flying colors." The judge said Friday that Murdaugh actually failed that test, which was related to his financial crimes, not the murder case.

Murdaugh was convicted in 2023 of murdering his wife, Maggie, and son, Paul, at the family's Moselle property in Colleton County. The South Carolina Supreme Court later overturned the convictions after finding that former Colleton County Clerk of Court Becky Hill improperly influenced the jury. His retrial is scheduled to begin April 5, 2027. Murdaugh has maintained his innocence in the killings.
ALEX MURDAUGH MURDER SAGA LANDS RIGHT BACK WHERE IT STARTED BEFORE NEXT LOWCOUNTRY COURTROOM BATTLE
Alex Murdaugh at a pretrial hearing in Lexington, South Carolina on Oct. 16, 2026. (Tracy Glantz of The State and Henry Taylor of The Post and Courier.)

McCaslin sided with the defense over prosecutors' objections on DNA samples of swabs from Maggie Murdaugh's phone, even though the analysis will likely consume the last testable samples. She cited due process and the right to a "full and complete defense." Murdaugh's defense team said the testing will likely take about 90 days.
The judge said defense attorneys don't have to share results of the DNA tests with prosecutors unless they plan to use them at trial.

McCaslin denied Murdaugh's request for a list of every crime in the 2nd and 14th judicial circuits since 2021 involving .300 Blackout ammunition, for every such firearm recovered, and for casings from other shootings.

She found the theory that the murder weapon is tied to an unsolved crime speculative and was based solely on news reports, adding that the South Carolina Law Enforcement Division doesn't have a list like that, and a manual review would be too much work and could intrude on investigations that are ongoing.
While the judge denied Harpootlian for his expert to physically test the shell casings from the crime scene, she ordered the state to hand over all raw data to the defense.

She also said prosecutors must hand over 3D crime scene scan data by Monday, but added she won't make the state produce material several times and asked the defense to have staff sign for discovery. McCaslin issued a similar warning when the state agreed to provide the defense with cellphone extraction data from Maggie and Paul's phone, but said this would be the last time the state will hand it over.
MURDAUGH DEFENSE SAYS DETECTIVES FOUND MALE DNA UNDER VICTIM'S NAILS BUT SKIPPED KEY TESTING

Alex Murdaugh arrives for a judicial hearing on Monday, June 29, 2026, at the Marc H. Westbrook Judicial Center in Lexington, South Carolina. Murdaugh will be retried in the June 7, 2021, shooting deaths of his wife and son, after his original conviction was overturned due to jury tampering. (Tracy Glantz/The State via Pool)

To close the hearing, McCaslin granted a state motion to correct the record regarding Harpootlian's assertion at an Aug. 14 hearing that Murdaugh had passed a polygraph "with flying colors." She said Murdaugh had been administered a polygraph concerning whether he concealed other assets and failed it, and that he has never taken a polygraph related to the killings of Maggie and Paul Murdaugh.
McCaslin acknowledged that Harpootlian had submitted a letter expressing apology for any confusion, then cautioned both sides that "candor with the court is not optional."

McCaslin also ruled in prosecutors' favor on a defense motion requesting evidence related to the disposal of the murder weapons, which have never been recovered. McCaslin said the state is required to hand over the material only if it proves favorable to Murdaugh's defense.
ALEX MURDAUGH DEFENSE POINTS TO UNKNOWN MALE DNA IN PUSH FOR NEW TESTING

Murdaugh's defense team initially asked the judge to force prosecutors to turn over information it has "concerning the handling, transport, concealment, or disposal of the alleged weapons used to kill Maggie Murdaugh and Paul Murdaugh, including the statement a witness gave to agents of the South Carolina Law Enforcement Division in 2023 that a Lowcountry police chief spoke of arriving early at the scene and of providing Defendant Murdaugh a change of clothes, the reports of every interview conducted on that subject, and the testimony and exhibits presented to the State Grand Jury concerning it."
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X
Alex Murdaugh, right, is shown here with his family. (Fox News)

According to the motion, filed in late September by Murdaugh's attorneys, press reports indicate that a state grand jury received testimony alleging Yemassee Police Chief Greg Alexander was observed in possession of the murder weapons shortly after the June 7, 2021, killings.
SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

"According to those reports, witnesses have testified that the Chief of Police of the Town of Yemassee, Greg Alexander, was seen with the murder weapons in the immediate aftermath of the June 7, 2021, killings, and that second Yemassee officer is under investigation for transporting and concealing weapons and clothing," the filing states.

It cites a story from The Post and Courier, which reported that "a Lowcountry official told SLED agents that Chief Alexander 'spoke of arriving early to the murder scene and talked about providing a change of clothes to Murdaugh,' and that the official believed the guns and clothing were brought into the police station and stored there."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM THE FOX TRUE CRIME HUB

Circuit Judge Debra McCaslin addresses attorneys during a pretrial hearing ahead of Alex Murdaugh’s murder retrial in Lexington, S.C., Aug. 14, 2026. (Tracy Glantz of The (Columbia, South Carolina) State/POOL)
Notably, the allegations couldn't be corroborated by The Post and Courier.
Alexander, through his attorney, Joe McCulloch, denied accusations made in the media reports.
LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST
"The same explanation has been provided to SLED," McCulloch told Fox News Digital. "That truth will outlive any ridiculous rumors and gossip."
Former prosecutor Joshua Ritter told Fox News Digital he considers the allegation against Alexander a "wild goose chase."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"This is one of those cases that, you know, a lot of reporting was done early on, a lot of conspiracy theories swirling around this case," Ritter said. "I don't see any reason for the judge to allow for this essentially wild goose chase in regards to an uncorroborated report about law enforcement perhaps being in possession of the murder weapon."

"Obviously, the defense would love to pursue this to its absolute limit because they think that there's a snowball's chance that it might yield something, but I think that the judge is probably going to give very little leeway on something like this," he added.

title: FBI returns 'Most Wanted' fraudster to US after India arrest in alleged $600K SNAP food stamp scheme
summary: FBI Director Kash Patel announced Manjit Singh Bedi, accused of stealing over $600,000 in SNAP benefits in Tacoma, has been returned from India.
story: In the months since the establishment of the National Fraud Enforcement Division, the Department of Justice has launched over 1,000 major fraud enforcement actions across the country. Coordinated efforts aim to protect taxpayer dollars from schemes targeting Medicaid, SNAP, HUD, Social Security and SBA programs. These federal programs are designed to assist vulnerable groups, including the elderly, sick, and homeless.
A fugitive accused of stealing more than $600,000 in federal food stamp benefits has been returned to the United States after being arrested in India last month, FBI Director Kash Patel announced.

Manjit Singh Bedi, one of the FBI's Most Wanted Fraudsters, was wanted on federal charges stemming from an alleged Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) fraud scheme at a grocery store in Tacoma, Washington.
"BACK IN THE U.S. - Manjit Singh Bedi, one of the FBI’s Most Wanted Fraudsters, arrested in September in India," Patel posted on X.
Patel highlighted the FBI's recent success in bringing fugitives back to the United States.
EXCLUSIVE: FBI'S FIFTH MOST WANTED FRAUDSTER CAPTURED AFTER ALLEGED SNAP SCAM SUSPECT ARRESTED IN INDIA
Manjit Singh Bedi is seen in an undated FBI photo. Authorities arrested Bedi in India on Friday after alleging he fled the United States while facing wire fraud and SNAP benefits fraud charges. (FBI)

"This is the latest in an unprecedented stretch of success in bringing high-value targets back to the United States through strong partnerships with our foreign law enforcement counterparts," Patel said.
"Over the past 20 months, we’ve secured 260 extraditions and removals — an increase of more than 70% compared to the previous 20-month period," he added.

According to federal officials, Bedi allegedly defrauded the U.S. government of at least $600,000 through a SNAP fraud scheme between March 2024 and June 2025 while operating an Asian grocery store in Tacoma.
MILLION-DOLLAR SNAP FOOD STAMP FRAUD SCHEME IN WALZ'S BACKYARD SPARKS OUTRAGE: 'CRUEL JOKE'
FBI Director Kash Patel speaks during a press conference on Oct. 23, 2025 in New York City. (Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images)
The FBI said Bedi allegedly swiped SNAP recipients' Electronic Benefit Transfer (EBT) cards, provided cash instead of eligible food purchases and kept roughly half the benefits for himself.
After being indicted in connection with the scheme, Bedi allegedly drove to Canada before fleeing to India.
A federal arrest warrant charging him with violating the conditions of his release was issued on May 21, 2026.
Patel said Bedi is now one of six fugitives captured through the FBI's Most Wanted Fraudsters program since the list was created three months ago.
FBI ADDS 2 FUGITIVES TO 'MOST WANTED FRAUDSTERS' LIST AMID HISTORIC $6.5B HEALTHCARE TAKEDOWN: PATEL

Manjit Singh Bedi, accused of defrauding the federal food stamp program of more than $600,000, was returned to the United States after being arrested in India in September 2026, according to the FBI. (Andrew Leyden/Getty Images)
"This marks yet another significant moment for the historic FBI’s Most Wanted Fraudsters program," he said.
Bedi, a naturalized U.S. citizen, was previously the subject of an FBI reward offering up to $150,000 for information leading to his arrest and conviction.
Patel said Bedi will now face justice in the United States for his alleged crimes.
"Thank you to our outstanding partners for their assistance in this case," Patel wrote.

title: Trans neo-Nazi accused of plotting Hindu temple massacre, will receive hormone treatment in jail: officials
summary: A transgender 19-year-old alleged neo-Nazi plotted an attack on a Hindu temple, but the firearm malfunctioned and a coworker's tip led to an arrest.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

A transgender 19-year-old who authorities say identified himself as a neo-Nazi allegedly plotted a mass shooting at a Hindu temple outside Chicago, but a tip from a coworker helped authorities thwart the attack, according to police.

Alexandros Paporakis, of Palatine, was arrested on Sunday after allegedly plotting to open fire at a Hindu temple in Aurora, a suburb of Chicago, Palatine Police said at a news conference on Thursday.
Paporakis faces one felony count of making a terrorist threat and one felony count of unlawful possession of a weapon.

A Cook County judge has ordered Paporakis held without bond and has put a jailhouse healthcare order into place, saying that the teenager receives hormone injections for gender transition and is being treated for ADHD, depression and anxiety, according to NBC Chicago.
NEVADA TRANSGENDER SUSPECT WITH MASSIVE WEAPONS CACHE ACCUSED OF LAS VEGAS TERRORISM-RELATED THREATS
Alexandros Paporakis, of Palatine, was arrested on Sunday after allegedly plotting to open fire at a Hindu temple in Aurora. (Palatine Police Department)

Prosecutors allege Paporakis drove to the Hindu temple in Aurora armed with a modified rifle and about 300 rounds of ammunition and equipped with body armor and other tactical gear. Authorities said Paporakis intended to carry out a shooting, but returned home after the rifle malfunctioned.

After arriving home, the suspect searched the internet trying to learn how to unjam the gun and allegedly called a colleague informing them of the intent to carry out a mass shooting, according to police.

Paporakis' coworkers at Taco Bell reported to Mount Prospect Police that they had received a suspicious message that day from Paporakis, leading police to obtain a search warrant and detain Paporakis before the suspect could return to the scene to carry out the alleged attack.
Authorities praised those who reported the threat and encouraged others who come across something suspicious to report it to law enforcement.
MALL OF AMERICA TERROR PLOT THWARTED; SUSPECTED ISIS SYMPATHIZER ARRESTED, FBI ANNOUNCES
Authorities praised the tipster and encouraged others who come across something suspicious to report it to law enforcement. (Google Maps)

"I want to praise and offer my personal, sincerest thanks to the individual who stepped forward in many successful disruptions by law enforcement and potential acts of violence or terrorism attacks. It is a single, courageous member of the public who comes forward to prevent attacks," FBI Chicago Field Office acting special agent in charge Lucas Rothaar said at a press conference on Thursday.

Police said they identified a red Acura registered to Paporakis after receiving the tip. Surveillance video showed the suspect in the vehicle entering the parking lot at the Hindu temple at 12:25 p.m. before exiting a few minutes later.

Paporakis was later observed driving to a residence on Rand Road in Palatine shared with the suspect's mother. Police executed a search warrant and found a rifle, a loaded magazine, hundreds of rounds of rifle ammunition and other tactical gear in Paporakis' possession.
Police also found what they described as an eight-page manifesto, which authorities said detailed the alleged attack and Paporakis' White supremacist views.

The writings "expressed words of hate, violence, superior race and mass shooting of Indian people. [Paporakis'] hatred was against Jewish people, African-Americans, Indians, and 'non-white' people," according to police. Paporakis described them as "subhumans" and planned to kill as many of them as possible.
Coworkers at Taco Bell reported to police that they had received a suspicious message that day from the suspect. (Photo by Duane Prokop/Getty Images for Taco Bell)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Police said the suspect "expressed pleasure calling himself a sociopathic White supremacist Neo-Nazi filled with hatred, fantasizing about mass murder nearly every day."
The manifesto also referred to Paporakis as the "Aurora Shooter."
A judge ruled that Paporakis will remain in jail, with the next court appearance scheduled for Oct. 30.
The temple said it was aware of the recent security threat and has boosted security.

"Please know that the safety of our devotees, employees and volunteers is our highest priority, and we have implemented additional security measures effective immediately, including increased armed security presence at the Temple and are taking additional steps to ensure an ongoing safe environment for everyone at the Temple," the temple said in a message on its website.

title: Ex-OpenAI engineer charged with planting recording device had one-way flight booked to Saudi Arabia, DOJ says
summary: Abdulrahman Alfozan had a one-way flight to his native Saudi Arabia booked days before federal custody, according to the Department of Justice.
story: Fox News chief correspondent Jonathan Hunt details the arrest of a Saudi OpenAI employee accused of secretly placing a recording device inside a San Francisco conference room. Hunt discusses the alleged security breach, how the device was discovered and OpenAI’s response to the incident.

The former OpenAI engineer charged with planting a recording device inside a conference room at the AI giant's San Francisco office had a one-way flight booked to Saudi Arabia days before he was taken into federal custody, the Justice Department said.
Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old Saudi national, had a flight booked for Oct. 12 — days after his arrest — for himself, his wife, and another relative, according to court documents.

Federal prosecutors cited his travel plans when asking a federal judge to seal the criminal complaint and arrest warrant against him, arguing that public knowledge of the case would prompt him to possibly flee the country.
8 EVERYDAY THINGS THAT WOULD QUIT WORKING WITHOUT DATA CENTERS

A man described as Abdulrahman Alfozan, a Saudi national formerly employed as an OpenAI engineer, looks behind a television where a recording device had been placed in a conference room in OpenAI offices, in a still image from surveillance video. (Department of Justice/Handout via Reuters)
"Disclosure of the specified documents might jeopardize the defendant's arrest," court documents state.
In an Arabic podcast last month, Alfozan recalled meeting Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman during his 2016 visit to Silicon Valley.

Alfozan said he had been contemplating whether to return to his native country. In response, the prince advised young Saudis living and working in Silicon Valley to refine their skills at premier tech companies before bringing their expertise home, the New York Post reported.
OpenAI offices are seen in San Francisco. (Smith Collection/Gado/Getty Images)
"You learn from the source and then, God willing, bring that experience and knowledge back to the homeland," Alfozan reportedly said on the podcast.
Alfozan was arrested Oct. 9 and charged with using or attempting to use a device to intercept oral communications, according to the Department of Justice.

OpenAI discovered the encrypted device Sept. 30, plugged into a USB port on the back of a television in a conference room used for "highly confidential" discussions involving proprietary research, product plans and business opportunities, federal prosecutors said.

The OpenAI logo is displayed on a smartphone screen on a reflective surface with Dots promotional artwork projected onto it in Creteil, France, on Oct. 1, 2026, as OpenAI begins rolling out Dots in ChatGPT, its new system of autonomous AI agents. (Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

The device, concealed in toilet paper, had allegedly been installed two days earlier. OpenAI traced the device to Alfozan, and security footage showed him near the conference room multiple times, authorities said.
In addition, a chatbot associated with his wife was allegedly used to field prompts about ways to install and hide audio recording devices.

Fox News Digital has reached out to Alfozan's attorney for comment.
Louis Casiano is a reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to louis.casiano@fox.com.

title: Armed bystander fatally shoots suspected teen gunman after 3 children, 1 adult killed at Oregon school: feds
summary: Three children and a teacher were killed after a gunman forced his way into Silver Rail Elementary in Bend, Oregon, by firing at locked doors.
story: Fox News correspondent Christina Coleman says on ‘Hannity’ that four people, including three children, were killed by a suspected 16-year-old shooter, and two victims were taken to the hospital with critical injuries in Thursday's elementary school shooting in Bend, Oregon.
Three children and an adult were killed in a shooting at an Oregon elementary school Thursday, and the suspected gunman is also dead, shot by an armed good Samaritan.
The shooter was a 16-year-old Bend resident armed with a shotgun who was killed by an armed bystander with a concealed carry permit, federal law enforcement sources told Fox News.
The bystander "definitely prevented more deaths," one source said.
POLICE MAKE ARREST AFTER GUNFIRE DURING CALIFORNIA HIGH SCHOOL FOOTBALL GAME LEAVES 1 DEAD
People are seen outside Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Ore., as police respond to a reported active shooter Thursday. (KTVZ)
The children killed at Silver Rail Elementary School were ages 5, 8 and 11, Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said during an evening news conference.
A 7-year-old child and a 54-year-old teacher were taken to St. Charles Bend with critical injuries.
The shooter forced his way into the school by firing at locked doors, Krantz said, citing the initial investigation.
A "community member" saw the shooter enter, pursued him into the building and engaged him, according to Krantz.
Officers arrived within three minutes of the first emergency call. Moments later, an officer reported that the community member had shot the suspect.

"Our officers entered the building and confirmed the suspect was dead," Krantz said. "They cleared the school to ensure there were no additional threats, and then rendered emergency aid to the victims."
Scene near Silver Rail Elementary School after an Oct. 15, 2026, shooting that killed three children and an adult, according to federal law enforcement sources. (Rob Kerr/Reuters)
Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek praised school staff, parents and first responders, along with the community member "who heroically intervened to stop further loss of life."
"Your actions carry a heavy emotional burden, and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you as well," Kotek said.
REPORTED SHOOTING AT VIRGINIA ELEMENTARY SCHOOL 'CONTAINED,' SHERIFF'S OFFICE SAYS
School buses are lined up outside Silver Rail Elementary school on Thursday in Bend, Ore. (Joe Kline/AP Photo)
Krantz said he did not yet have details about the bystander’s firearm or whether he had a concealed carry permit. Federal law enforcement sources separately confirmed the permit to Fox News.

The chief said investigators did not yet know how far the shooter had gone inside the building or whether he knew anyone at the school. Police were also investigating whether the teen had previously attended Silver Rail Elementary.

The first emergency call came at 12:59 p.m. from a person in a vehicle who reported being shot at multiple times by someone carrying a long gun, Krantz said. Dispatchers then received dozens of calls reporting that a shooter had entered the school.
Dispatch sent an alert summoning all law enforcement at 1 p.m. Responding officers directed the school to lock down at 1:01 p.m., and the first officers arrived at 1:02 p.m.
TRANSGENDER EX-STUDENT IDENTIFIED AS ALLEGED SUSPECT IN DEADLY CANADA SCHOOL MASS SHOOTING
Police tape is placed outside Silver Rail Elementary school, where a shooting took place Thursday in Bend, Ore. (Joe Kline/AP Photo)
Officers found five people dead at the scene, including the shooter. All victims’ families had been notified, Krantz said.
Bend police, the Deschutes County Sheriff’s Office, Redmond police, Oregon State Police and federal law enforcement partners evacuated the building room by room.
STUDENT PERPETRATES DEADLY SHOOTING AT THAILAND HIGH SCHOOL, AUTHORITIES SAY
Students and staff were transported on Bend-La Pine school buses to Journey Church to reunite with families and guardians. That process was still underway at the evening briefing.
The FBI’s Portland field office said it was assisting local authorities with the investigation.
"We will make every resource they need available," the office wrote on X.
Krantz said every Bend police officer completed a full day of active threat training at a local high school in August.
"Unfortunately, this is something we train for on a regular basis, and we must," he said.
A large police presence would remain at the school for several days as investigators worked to establish what happened.
Bend Police Department Chief Mike Krantz provides an update after a deadly shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Ore., Thursday. (KTVZ)
"There are not really any words I can say to any of you that will make this better," Krantz said, urging residents to "lean on each other and be there for each other."
Bend-La Pine Schools Superintendent Steven Cook said the district was "heartbroken" and "horrified," and called the incident an "unthinkable tragedy."

"This is the kind of thing you hear about in other places, and pray that it never happens here. And it has happened here today," Cook said. "It happened to our children, to our teachers and to our families."
Cook choked up as he thanked staff for protecting students.
"You did what no one should ever be asked to do," he said. "I am so grateful beyond words for your efforts."
Bend Mayor Melanie Kebler said a community vigil would be held Thursday night.
"A school should be a safe place where children can learn and feel secure. What happened today should never happen," Kebler said.
"This is a horrible day. No parent should have to have this kind of day, and no community should have to live through this kind of day," Kotek said.
Silver Rail Elementary serves kindergarten through fifth grade in the Bend-La Pine school district. The school enrolled 459 students during the 2024-2025 school year.
Sen. Jeff Merkley, D-Ore., expressed support for the students and families affected.
"No one should have to fear violence at school," Merkley wrote on X.
Rep. Janelle Bynum, D-Ore., whose district includes Bend, called the shooting "every parent’s worst fear."
"Our babies are supposed to do arts and crafts at school, not use their desks as cover from gunfire," Bynum said in a statement posted on X.
"My heart and my prayers and everything else I got is with the families at Silver Rail Elementary. When will it end?"
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

All Bend-La Pine schools, activities and athletic events were canceled Friday. Cook said crisis counselors would be available at the Central Library for students, families, employees and anyone in the community needing support.
"Please hold your children. Hold your loved ones tight tonight," Cook said. "Let them talk. Let them cry."
Authorities said they planned to hold another news conference Friday afternoon.
